summary.title: Learning design rules for selective oxidation catalysts from highthroughput experimentation and artificial intelligence
summary.authors: Lucas Foppa, Christopher Sutton, Luca M Ghiringhelli, Sandip De, Patricia Löser, Stephan A Schunk, Ansgar Schäfer, Matthias Scheffler
summary.executive_summary: The design of heterogeneous catalysts is hindered by the complexity of materials and the scarcity of high-performing candidates within the vast space of possible compositions. This study demonstrates the application of subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial intelligence to a hybrid dataset combining high-throughput experimentation (HTE) and density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations to identify design rules for selective oxidation catalysts. The researchers synthesized and tested 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. Using the yield of value-added oxygenates (acrolein and acrylic acid) as the target, the SGD approach identified specific constraints on key physicochemical parameters that exclusively describe materials with outstanding performance. The identified rules constrain the reaction temperature to 280–300°C, the phosphorus content to >0.55, and the composition-weighted electronegativity to 3.910–4.002 eV. These rules not only rationalize the local reactivity patterns associated with exceptional performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts. By applying these rules, the authors designed four- and five-component catalysts containing additional elements such as tellurium and tantalum. Experimental validation showed that these new materials achieved oxygenate yields up to 60.19% and 59.60%, respectively, which are significantly higher than the maximum yield of 26.85% observed in the three-component training set. The study highlights that while the temperature rule was not directly transferable to the more complex materials, the composition-dependent rules successfully predicted high-performing candidates, demonstrating the potential of SGD for rational catalyst design in complex materials spaces.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
The design of heterogeneous catalysts is hindered by the complexity of materials and the scarcity of high-performing candidates within the vast space of possible compositions. This study demonstrates the application of subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial intelligence to a hybrid dataset combining high-throughput experimentation (HTE) and density-functional-theory (DFT) calculations to identify design rules for selective oxidation catalysts. The researchers synthesized and tested 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. Using the yield of value-added oxygenates (acrolein and acrylic acid) as the target, the SGD approach identified specific constraints on key physicochemical parameters that exclusively describe materials with outstanding performance. The identified rules constrain the reaction temperature to 280–300°C, the phosphorus content to >0.55, and the composition-weighted electronegativity to 3.910–4.002 eV. These rules not only rationalize the local reactivity patterns associated with exceptional performance but also guide the design of more complex catalysts. By applying these rules, the authors designed four- and five-component catalysts containing additional elements such as tellurium and tantalum. Experimental validation showed that these new materials achieved oxygenate yields up to 60.19% and 59.60%, respectively, which are significantly higher than the maximum yield of 26.85% observed in the three-component training set. The study highlights that while the temperature rule was not directly transferable to the more complex materials, the composition-dependent rules successfully predicted high-performing candidates, demonstrating the potential of SGD for rational catalyst design in complex materials spaces.

Research Context
Heterogeneous catalysis is governed by an intricate interplay of multiple processes. The explicit atomistic modelling of the full catalytic progression by first-principles methods is impractical. High-throughput experimentation (HTE) is used to test large amounts of materials. Utilizing the information obtained by the experiments to decide on the next promising materials is not straightforward. The number of good catalysts is very small compared to the number of possible materials. Detailed characterization of each material in large libraries is typically not feasible. Distinct catalytic mechanisms might operate depending on the materials and reaction conditions. Global models trained to describe all materials simultaneously may not allow focused modelling. Alternative approaches for catalyst design are therefore required.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to identify key physicochemical descriptive parameters and constraints on their values. These rules are particularly associated with high performance in selective oxidation. The reactivity measured by HTE is used as the target in the SGD analysis. Temperature and composition-dependent physicochemical properties evaluated with DFT are used as candidate parameters. The hypothesis is that SGD can identify local behavior reflecting specific underlying processes. The approach circumvents the need for explicit modelling of the full catalytic progression. Candidate descriptive materials parameters can be calculated by first-principles methods. The resulting SG rules can identify promising catalyst candidates not yet synthesized. The goal is to describe materials and conditions giving high yields of oxygenates.

Methodological Details
120 different three-component catalyst compositions containing ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus were synthesized. The catalysts were supported on SiO2 pseudo-liquid support. Reactions were carried out in tubular, fixed-bed reactors. The reaction feed included Ar, H2O, N2, O2, and propylene. Molar rates were 4.015, 4.015, 104.40, 20.08, and 1.57 mmol/h respectively. The same mass of catalyst was used in all reactions. Contact time was kept fixed across experiments. Reaction temperatures between 200ºC and 400ºC were examined. The target variable was the yield of oxygenates (acrolein and acrylic acid). Eleven descriptive parameters were used in the SGD analysis. Properties were calculated for isolated atoms using DFT-PBEsol and FHI-aims code. Per-element free-atom properties were converted to system-specific properties via composition-weighted average. Oxygen content was not included in the material's characterization. The quality function uses coverage and cumulative Jensen-Shannon divergence.

Procedures And Architectures
The subgroup-discovery (SGD) artificial-intelligence local approach was applied. SGD starts with the generation of a pool of propositions. Propositions are inequalities constraining the values of continuous candidate descriptive parameters. SGD identifies selectors formed by propositions and the AND connector. Selectors result in the selection of subgroups with outstanding target value distributions. The quality function measures how outstanding specific subselections of data points are. The coverage term controls the subgroup size and prevents small SGs. The Jensen-Shannon divergence measures dissimilarity between two distributions. The approach identifies a local behavior rather than a global model. For four-component materials, phosphorus content was fixed to 0.60. Ruthenium molar content was fixed to 0.05 for four-component materials. V_C elements were selected based on octahedral coordination and atomic radius difference. The maximum atomic radius difference compared to tungsten was 0.10 Å. Considered V_C elements included niobium, tantalum, chromium, molybdenum, tin, antimony, and tellurium. Lead was also included as it was experimentally tested.

Key Results
50% of the measured materials and conditions result in less than 2% oxygenates yield. Only 41 measurements out of 1220 are associated to yields of oxygenates above 20%. The average oxygenates yield over the whole data set is equal to 4.83%. The maximum oxygenates yield value is 26.85%. The selected SG contains only 15 data points, approximately 1.2% of the data set. The average yield of oxygenates in this SG is equal to 24.15%. The SG is described by rules: 280 ≤ T ≤ 300ºC, P > 0.55, and 3.910 ≤ VY < 4.002 eV. The highest yield of oxygenates for four-component materials is 60.19% at 400ºC. This highest yield contains 0.35 molar fraction of tellurium. The highest yield of oxygenates for five-component materials is 59.60% at 400ºC. This five-component catalyst contains tantalum as the V^ element. The composition-averaged electronegativity for this five-component material is 3.947 eV. The four- and five-component yields are up to twice as large as three-component materials. The SG for four- and five-component data contains 18 data points. The rules for the new SG constrain T ≥ 360ºC, L_+1 ≤ 1.001 Å, and VH < -1.593 eV.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The rules reflect the underlying processes particularly associated to high performance. High phosphorus content is needed to achieve outstanding performance. This could be related to the dilution of metal active sites. The electronegativity rule effectively limits the range of Ru contents. Ru is needed for conversion but too much leads to combustion products. The SG rules are not strongly affected by variations on the data used. The approach detects interpretable, chemically meaningful, and complex patterns. The identified rules guide the design of more complex catalysts. The local modelling approach is suitable for search of exceptional materials.

Contradictions And Limitations
The atomic structures of all the tested catalysts are not known in detail. The oxygen content is not included in the material's characterization. The SG rule on reaction temperature is not transferable to four-component materials. It is unclear if the SG rules can identify exceptional materials for arbitrary Ru content. Different mechanisms may operate on materials with significantly different radii. The analysis was focused on low ruthenium contents. The SGD analysis might need new data points for unexplored portions of materials space.

Claims
SGD identifies specific physicochemical constraints that predict high catalytic performance in selective oxidation. The SG rules describe materials with outstanding catalytic performance. The rules constrain temperature, phosphorus content, and electronegativity. The temperature rule did not transfer to four-component materials. These rules can guide the design of new catalysts.
The derived rules successfully predict high-performing four- and five-component catalysts. Four-component catalysts achieved yields up to 60.19%. Five-component catalysts achieved yields up to 59.60%. The highest yields for complex materials occurred at higher temperatures. The approach generalizes to more complex materials.

Data And Code Availability
Further calculation details and values for elemental properties are available in the ESI.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Similar SG rules are obtained when training with randomly-selected 90% of data points. Rules are similar when data points with yield lower than 3% are excluded. The ranges of variation for thresholds are similar to the main results. The SG rules are not strongly affected by variations on the data.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the SGD approach and the selective oxidation reaction. Figure 2 shows the distribution of yield and the SG rules for three-component catalysts. Figure 3 shows the ternary diagram of Ru content. Figure 4 shows the catalyst map for four-component materials and experimental results. Figure 5 shows the SG analysis for four- and five-component materials.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the application of SGD to HTE and DFT data to find catalyst design rules. 2. The strongest evidence is the successful prediction of high-yield four- and five-component catalysts. 3. The future path involves exploring unexplored portions of the materials space.

summary.title: Self-assembling materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces in cellular activities
summary.authors: Noriyuki Uchida; Takahiro Muraoka
summary.executive_summary: This Feature Article reviews recent developments in bioinspired supramolecular materials designed to mimic the dynamic functions of biological interfaces, specifically extracellular matrices (ECMs) and phospholipid bilayers. The authors highlight how self-assembling peptides and amphiphilic molecules can reconstruct these interfaces to facilitate regenerative medicine and drug delivery. A primary focus is on stiffness-controlled peptide hydrogels, such as A16G and A16G-Ncad, which mimic the structural and dynamic properties of scaffold cells to promote neuroblast migration in injured neonatal neocortex. The article details the design of JigSAP, a peptide with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces, which enables the efficient incorporation and sustained release of growth factors like VEGF, promoting angiogenesis in stroke models without cell transplantation. Additionally, the study explores redox-responsive peptides where the position of methionine residues controls the kinetics of gel-sol transitions, allowing for stimuli-responsive cargo release. The review also addresses the stabilization of phospholipid nanosheets (bicelles) using metal-chelating peptides, which enhances their stability in blood circulation compared to spherical vesicles. Finally, it introduces an amphiphilic molecular machine (AzoMEx) that induces endocytosis-like membrane fission in liposomes, enabling the encapsulation and in vivo delivery of large biomacromolecules such as M13 phage viruses to multiple organs while retaining infectivity. These approaches demonstrate that bottom-up chemical methodologies can effectively manipulate bio-interfaces to create functional biomaterials for advanced biomedical applications.

claims.description: Self-assembling peptides can mimic ECM dynamics to promote neuronal migration.
JigSAP enables efficient incorporation and sustained release of growth factors.
Metal-chelating peptides stabilize phospholipid nanosheets for blood circulation.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This Feature Article reviews recent developments in bioinspired supramolecular materials designed to mimic the dynamic functions of biological interfaces, specifically extracellular matrices (ECMs) and phospholipid bilayers. The authors highlight how self-assembling peptides and amphiphilic molecules can reconstruct these interfaces to facilitate regenerative medicine and drug delivery. A primary focus is on stiffness-controlled peptide hydrogels, such as A16G and A16G-Ncad, which mimic the structural and dynamic properties of scaffold cells to promote neuroblast migration in injured neonatal neocortex. The article details the design of JigSAP, a peptide with jigsaw-shaped hydrophobic surfaces, which enables the efficient incorporation and sustained release of growth factors like VEGF, promoting angiogenesis in stroke models without cell transplantation. Additionally, the study explores redox-responsive peptides where the position of methionine residues controls the kinetics of gel-sol transitions, allowing for stimuli-responsive cargo release. The review also addresses the stabilization of phospholipid nanosheets (bicelles) using metal-chelating peptides, which enhances their stability in blood circulation compared to spherical vesicles. Finally, it introduces an amphiphilic molecular machine (AzoMEx) that induces endocytosis-like membrane fission in liposomes, enabling the encapsulation and in vivo delivery of large biomacromolecules such as M13 phage viruses to multiple organs while retaining infectivity. These approaches demonstrate that bottom-up chemical methodologies can effectively manipulate bio-interfaces to create functional biomaterials for advanced biomedical applications.

Research Context
Various cellular functions occur through dynamic actions of biomacromolecules at bio-interfaces. Extracellular matrix (ECM) adheres to membrane protein receptors to regulate cellular functions. Phospholipid bilayers contribute to fundamental cellular activities like substance transportation. Stimuli-responsive transformation is a notable characteristic of phospholipid bilayers. Recent progress in supramolecular chemistry allows creating dynamic materials. Artificial extracellular matrices and membrane-deforming materials are introduced.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to develop bioinspired supramolecular materials mimicking dynamic bio-interfaces. It is hypothesized that mimicking dynamic actions can develop biomaterials for regenerative medicine. The research focuses on constructing artificial extracellular matrices and membrane-deforming materials. The goal is to apply these materials to injured brain regeneration. The study also targets in vivo cargo delivery for extended blood circulation. Self-assembling molecules like fibre-forming amphiphilic peptides are used for construction.

Methodological Details
Self-assembling peptide fibres are recognized as versatile supramolecular scaffolds. Peptide amphiphiles construct nanofibres by forming cylindrical micelles. RADA16 forms supramolecular nanofibres via β-sheet-type hydrogen bonding. A16G is a mutant of RADA16 with terminal alanine replaced by glycine. A16G forms curved fibres seen on transmission electron microscopy. Molecular dynamics simulations visualized similar self-assembling morphology. JigSAP consists of Ac-RIDARMRADIR-NH2 sequence with AXXXA motif. JigSAP forms nanofibres with an average width of 3.2 nm. JigSAP hydrogel exhibits a rigidity of 1.1 x 10^4 Pa. DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets are formed by mixing dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine with Chol-MBP. Chol-MBP binds to two Cu2+ ions to inhibit dissociation. AzoMEx contains a diazocine core undergoing opening-closing motion. GUVDOPC/AzoMEx uses 180 µM DOPC and 20 µM AzoMEx.

Procedures And Architectures
A16G hydrogel containing A16G-Ncad facilitates neuroblast migration in vivo. Neonatal neocortex is injured at low temperature before hydrogel injection. JigSAP is dispersed in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium. Circular dichroism spectroscopy visualizes conformational change to β-sheet. EGFP-JigSAP is incorporated at 93 mol% efficiency. VEGF-JigSAP and JigSAP are injected into ischaemic stroke mouse models. DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets are diluted to 0.2 wt% for stability testing. Cu2+ ions are added to maintain nanosheet structure upon dilution. Fluorescent Cy5-labeled vesicles and nanosheets are administered via tail vein. Blood circulation profiles are observed by confocal laser scanning microscopy. AzoMEx undergoes photoisomerization to change distance between cationic moieties. M13 phage virus is incorporated into deforming membrane area.

Key Results
Migration rate of neuroblasts was significantly higher on A16G-Ncad hydrogel. Dcx+ neuroblasts were abundantly observed in A16G-Ncad hydrogel. EGFP-JigSAP incorporation efficiency was 93 mol% compared to 3 mol% untagged. 21 mol% of EGFP-JigSAP was released after 24-hour incubation. Released protein increased to 39 mol% after 168 hours. Double-positive cells increased when VEGF-JigSAP and JigSAP were used. Nanosheet structure was maintained after dilution with Cu2+ ions. FL DPPC vesicles were aggregated and clogged in blood vessels. FL DPPC/Chol-MBP/Cu nanosheets were homogeneously dispersed in blood vessels. M13 phages were efficiently incorporated into GUVDOPC/AzoMEx. Spleen infectivity was [25.6 ± 13.2] × 10^9 virions/mg. Liver infectivity was [18.3 ± 3.2] × 10^9 virions/mg.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Fibrous self-assembly mimics structure and dynamic function of scaffold cells. This provides a novel strategy for neuro-regenerative therapy. JigSAP demonstrates wide applicability to controlled sustained release. Stabilization of bicelle morphology enables prolonged blood circulation. AzoMEx functionalizes GUV for endocytosis-like fission. This technology can be applied to in vivo phage display.

Contradictions And Limitations
The mammalian brain has a very limited capability of regeneration. Delivering sufficient neuroblasts to distant injury sites is a challenge. Incorporating and releasing secreted proteins are generally incompatible. Bicelles composed of surfactants are essentially unstable. A molecular approach for endocytosis-like transport remains unexplored. The materials science to reconstruct biomimetic interfaces is in its infancy.

Claims
Self-assembling peptides can mimic ECM dynamics to promote neuronal migration. A16G-Ncad hydrogel facilitates neuroblast migration. Dcx+ neuroblasts are abundant in A16G-Ncad hydrogel. Neuroblasts are sparse in A16G alone hydrogel. This offers a strategy for neuro-regenerative therapy.
JigSAP enables efficient incorporation and sustained release of growth factors. EGFP-JigSAP incorporation is 93 mol%. Release increases to 39 mol% after 168 hours. Untagged EGFP incorporation is only 3 mol%. Useful for artificial scaffolds for tissue regeneration.
Metal-chelating peptides stabilize phospholipid nanosheets for blood circulation. Nanosheets remain stable with Cu2+ ions. Nanosheets are homogeneously dispersed in blood. Vesicles are aggregated and clogged. Suitable carrier for whole body blood administration.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A16G shows lower stiffness than RADA16. JigSAP hydrogel shows strain thinning profile. Redox-responsive peptides show contrasting macroscopic properties. JigSAP-IMI-Ox remains dispersed in solution.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 3 shows neuroblast migration on A16G-Ncad hydrogel. Figure 4 shows JigSAP nanofibre formation and protein release. Figure 6 shows stability of DPPC/Chol-MBP nanosheets. Figure 7 shows M13 phage encapsulation and organ distribution.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is bioinspired supramolecular materials mimicking bio-interfaces. 2. The strongest evidence is efficient VEGF release and neuroblast migration. 3. The future path is developing regenerative medicines and drug delivery.

summary.title: GUIDEMOL: a Python graphical user interface for molecular descriptors based on RDKit
summary.authors: Joao Aires
summary.executive_summary: GUIDEMOL is a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) designed to facilitate the calculation of molecular descriptors and 3D grid representations using the RDKit chemoinformatics toolkit. The primary objective of this software is to lower the barrier to entry for scientists and students who lack programming skills, providing an intuitive interface for routine chemoinformatics tasks. The application leverages the tkinter package to create a minimalist interface that allows users to process molecular structures, specifically generating 3D models from SMILES strings and calculating a variety of descriptors. Key features include the computation of standard RDKit descriptors such as RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA. Additionally, GUIDEMOL implements direct 3D representations of molecules, which are increasingly relevant for deep learning applications. These representations include grids encoding electrostatic potential (EP) and voxel-based encodings of atomic properties like atomic number, partial charges, and contributions to refractivity and logP. The software supports both a graphical interface for interactive use and a command-line interface (CLI) for batch processing of grid calculations. The 3D structure generation utilizes the MMFF94 force field with specific optimization parameters. The source code is released under the three-clause BSD license, allowing for both commercial and non-commercial use and easy extension for other descriptors or tasks. This tool addresses the need for accessible software in chemoinformatics education and research, bridging the gap between powerful computational libraries like RDKit and non-programmer users.

GUIDEMOL supports 3D grid representations for deep learning.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
GUIDEMOL is a Python-based graphical user interface (GUI) designed to facilitate the calculation of molecular descriptors and 3D grid representations using the RDKit chemoinformatics toolkit. The primary objective of this software is to lower the barrier to entry for scientists and students who lack programming skills, providing an intuitive interface for routine chemoinformatics tasks. The application leverages the tkinter package to create a minimalist interface that allows users to process molecular structures, specifically generating 3D models from SMILES strings and calculating a variety of descriptors. Key features include the computation of standard RDKit descriptors such as RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA. Additionally, GUIDEMOL implements direct 3D representations of molecules, which are increasingly relevant for deep learning applications. These representations include grids encoding electrostatic potential (EP) and voxel-based encodings of atomic properties like atomic number, partial charges, and contributions to refractivity and logP. The software supports both a graphical interface for interactive use and a command-line interface (CLI) for batch processing of grid calculations. The 3D structure generation utilizes the MMFF94 force field with specific optimization parameters. The source code is released under the three-clause BSD license, allowing for both commercial and non-commercial use and easy extension for other descriptors or tasks. This tool addresses the need for accessible software in chemoinformatics education and research, bridging the gap between powerful computational libraries like RDKit and non-programmer users.

Research Context
Molecular descriptors are central to QSPR/QSAR methodologies used by scientists with varying computer skills. Chemoinformatics is permeating curricula in chemistry, biology, and material science, creating a need for teaching software. Existing tools include CDK-based GUIs like PaDEL and BlueDesc, as well as web services like OCHEM and ChemDes. Proprietary software such as MOE and VolSurf+ also offer descriptor calculation capabilities. RDKit is a widely used open-source Python software for chemoinformatics and machine learning projects. Python's tkinter package enables easy development of GUIs for chemoinformatics tools. Previous work like JRgui combined RDKit and tkinter for specific descriptor calculations. Direct 3D representations like voxel grids are gaining attention for deep learning applications.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to provide an easy access to RDKit tools for users without programming skills. The application is designed to calculate descriptors already implemented in RDKit. It also aims to calculate grid representations of 3D molecular structures. The tool supports representations using electrostatic potential or voxels. The interface is intended to be adaptable for other descriptors or procedures. A command-line interface is provided specifically for grid representation calculations. The software serves as a template for GUIs to other chemoinformatics tasks.

Methodological Details
The GUI is built using tkinter widgets controlled by the grid geometry manager. Buttons trigger calculations for 3D structure generation or descriptor calculation. Checkbuttons enable YES/NO options for specific descriptor inclusion. Radiobuttons allow choices among mutually exclusive options like atomic properties. Entries are used to submit numbers such as 3D grid coordinates. File selection uses native look-and-feel dialog windows via tkinter.filedialog. A log file is created to register successful processing and failures. 3D models are generated using RDKit's MMFFOptimizeMolecule function. The MMFF94 variant is used with a maximum of 5000 iterations. Options include removing metals, keeping the largest fragment, or neutralizing charges. Hydrogen atoms are added using the Chem.AddHs() function. Available 3D descriptors include RDF, MORSE, WHIM, AUTOCORR3D, GETAWAY, PEOE_VSA, and SMR_VSA. Electrostatic potential grids use Gasteiger or MMFF partial atomic charges. Voxelization uses atomic properties like atomic number, charge, refractivity, and logP. Descriptors are saved in a CSV output file with molecule name and ID.

Procedures And Architectures
The electrostatic potential at each cube is calculated using a summation formula. The formula excludes atoms closer than 1 Å from the cube center. Atoms further than a user-defined cutoff distance are also excluded. Grid parameters include center coordinates, side size, and cube size. Voxel grid values are calculated using a Gaussian decay function. The sigma parameter determines how fast atomic contribution decreases with distance. Missing hydrogen atoms can be added with calculated 3D coordinates. The CLI command requires specifying input, output, grid type, and properties. CLI parameters include grid center coordinates, cube size, and cutoff/sigma. An example CLI command calculates an EP grid with Gasteiger charges. The example uses a 5 Å grid size and 0.5 Å resolution. The source code is available on GitHub under a BSD license.

Key Results
The software successfully calculates descriptors implemented in RDKit. It generates 3D grid representations using electrostatic potential. It generates 3D grid representations using voxel encoding. The GUI allows users to specify parameters for these grids. The CLI provides an alternative method for grid calculation. The application requires no programming skills to operate. The source code is released for easy detection and fixing of bugs.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
GUIDEMOL facilitates access to descriptors for scientists and students. The 3D grid representations are useful for deep learning algorithms. The tool bridges the gap between RDKit capabilities and non-programmer users. The minimalist interface supports routine chemoinformatics tasks. The BSD license allows for commercial and non-commercial use. The software can be extended for other molecular descriptors.

Contradictions And Limitations
Inconsistencies were observed in GETAWAY, MORSE, and WHIM descriptors. These inconsistencies occurred with the same RDKit version (2022.9.5). The issue was observed in different runs or operating systems. An example was provided with the molecule COc1ccc(cc1(OC))Br.

Claims
GUIDEMOL provides an accessible interface for RDKit descriptor calculation. The app provides easy access to RDKit tools. It is designed for users with no programming skills. Some descriptors showed inconsistent values across runs. It lowers the barrier for chemoinformatics education and research.
GUIDEMOL supports 3D grid representations for deep learning. It calculates grids using electrostatic potential. It calculates grids using voxel encoding.  These representations are useful for AI algorithms.

Data And Code Availability
The source code is available at a specific GitHub URL. The code is released under the three-clause BSD license.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The paper notes inconsistencies in specific descriptor calculations. These inconsistencies were observed in RDKit version 2022.9.5.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the GUIDEMOL interface.

Three Takeaways
1. GUIDEMOL is a Python GUI for RDKit descriptors and 3D grids. 2. It supports electrostatic potential and voxel grid calculations. 3. The code is open-source under a BSD license.

summary.title: Visualization of π-hole in molecules by means of Kelvin probe force microscopy
summary.authors: B Mallada, M Ondráček, M Lamanec, A Gallardo, A Jiménez-Martín, B De La Torre, P Hobza, P Jelínek
summary.executive_summary: This study presents the first direct experimental visualization of the π-hole, a submolecular charge distribution feature in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbons, using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). While the existence of π-holes has been theoretically predicted and indirectly inferred from spectroscopic data, direct real-space observation has remained elusive. The authors investigate 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and anthracene (An) self-assembled on an Au(111) surface. Using non-contact atomic force microscopy (nc-AFM) to resolve molecular structures, they demonstrate that FCl-An molecules exhibit a distinct bow-tie pattern in the local contact potential difference (LCPD) maps, corresponding to the π-electron-deficient cavity. In contrast, anthracene lacks this feature. The study further elucidates the impact of the π-hole on molecular adsorption. Force-distance spectroscopy reveals that FCl-An adsorbs at a greater height (360 pm) compared to anthracene (330 pm) on the Au(111) surface. Theoretical calculations, including DFT and SAPT0, indicate that the π-hole increases the ionization potential of FCl-An, thereby suppressing charge density induction at the molecule-metal interface. This reduction in induced electrostatic interactions leads to weaker adsorption and a higher adsorption height. The work confirms that the π-hole significantly modulates non-covalent interactions, specifically affecting the electrostatic component of molecule-surface binding. By combining high-resolution imaging with theoretical modeling, the paper establishes KPFM as a powerful tool for mapping submolecular charge distributions and understanding their role in physical-chemical properties. The findings expand the understanding of π-hole systems and open avenues for studying how internal charge distributions influence molecular interactions and stability in supramolecular assemblies.

Executive Summary
This study presents the first direct experimental visualization of the π-hole, a submolecular charge distribution feature in halogen-substituted polyaromatic hydrocarbons, using Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). While the existence of π-holes has been theoretically predicted and indirectly inferred from spectroscopic data, direct real-space observation has remained elusive. The authors investigate 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and anthracene (An) self-assembled on an Au(111) surface. Using non-contact atomic force microscopy (nc-AFM) to resolve molecular structures, they demonstrate that FCl-An molecules exhibit a distinct bow-tie pattern in the local contact potential difference (LCPD) maps, corresponding to the π-electron-deficient cavity. In contrast, anthracene lacks this feature. The study further elucidates the impact of the π-hole on molecular adsorption. Force-distance spectroscopy reveals that FCl-An adsorbs at a greater height (360 pm) compared to anthracene (330 pm) on the Au(111) surface. Theoretical calculations, including DFT and SAPT0, indicate that the π-hole increases the ionization potential of FCl-An, thereby suppressing charge density induction at the molecule-metal interface. This reduction in induced electrostatic interactions leads to weaker adsorption and a higher adsorption height. The work confirms that the π-hole significantly modulates non-covalent interactions, specifically affecting the electrostatic component of molecule-surface binding. By combining high-resolution imaging with theoretical modeling, the paper establishes KPFM as a powerful tool for mapping submolecular charge distributions and understanding their role in physical-chemical properties. The findings expand the understanding of π-hole systems and open avenues for studying how internal charge distributions influence molecular interactions and stability in supramolecular assemblies.

Research Context
Non-covalent interactions are crucial in chemical and biological processes. The nature of these bonds is determined by dispersion and electrostatic forces. Electrostatic components are highly directional and linked to internal charge distribution. In polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, carbon electronegativity creates electron-rich π-bonds. Substituting hydrogens with electronegative atoms reverses electron population. This creates a π-electron-deficient cavity known as a π-hole. The presence of π-holes affects non-covalent intermolecular interactions. Previously, π-hole existence was proven only indirectly via measured data. Direct experimental observation of π-holes was lacking. Scanning probe microscopy is the most appropriate tool for visualization. KPFM has previously resolved sigma-holes with atomic resolution.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to experimentally confirm the existence of the π-hole. It specifically investigates 9,10-Dichlorooctafluoroanthracene (FCl-An) and anthracene (An). The hypothesis is that FCl-An possesses a π-hole while An does not. The presence of different substituents rules charge transfer between orbitals. Molecular orbitals in FCl-An extend to halogen substituents. This extension gives rise to a π-hole on the carbon skeleton. The study also hypothesizes that π-holes affect adsorption on surfaces. It predicts that the π-hole influences electrostatic interactions with the substrate. The expected outcome is a measurable difference in adsorption height. The π-hole is predicted to increase ionization potential. This should suppress charge density induction at the interface.

Methodological Details
Experiments were conducted at 4.2 K using a Createc STM/nc-AFM microscope. Pt/Ir tips were sharpened by focused ion beam and cleaned. A qPlus sensor with 30 kHz frequency was used for nc-AFM. The Au(111) substrate was prepared by Ar+ sputtering and annealing. FCl-An and An were sublimated simultaneously in UHV at room temperature. Molecular self-assemblies were formed on the Au(111) surface. STM images were acquired at a base temperature of 4.8 K. nc-AFM used a functionalized carbon monoxide (CO) tip. KPFM recorded spatial variation of local contact potential difference. LCPD maps were fitted to parabolic expressions of frequency shift. Data was collected on a 64 x 80 pixel grid. Theoretical calculations used DFT methods in the FHI-AIMS code. The PBE version of GGA was employed for exchange-correlation. SAPT0 analysis was performed using the PSI4 program.

Procedures And Architectures
STM topography was acquired in constant current mode. nc-AFM imaging operated in frequency modulation mode. Oscillation amplitude for nc-AFM was set to 200 pm. KPFM images were captured in constant height mode. The tip-sample height was chosen near Δf minima. This choice ensures the absence of tip relaxation. KPFM simulations used the PP-AFM code. Simulated images matched experimental evidence well. DFT calculations used a 4-layer Au(111) slab. The surface supercell corresponded to a 6×6 unit cell. Van der Waals correction used Tkatchenko-Scheffler method. Geometries were optimized when forces were under 2 meV/Å. The CO tip termination had a charge quadrupole of -0.2 e/Å². SAPT0 cluster models used a single layer of 38 gold atoms.

Key Results
FCl-An and An formed ordered molecular islands on Au(111). The supramolecular assembly has a rhombic periodic structure. The unit cell contains one An and two FCl-An molecules. KPFM revealed a bow-tie pattern in FCl-An molecules. This pattern corresponds to the π-hole charge distribution. Anthracene molecules did not exhibit this submolecular contrast. Force-distance spectroscopy showed a 30 pm difference in minima. The adsorption height of An was determined to be 330 pm. The adsorption height of FCl-An was determined to be 360 pm. FCl-An adsorbs higher than An on the Au(111) surface. DFT calculations confirmed these adsorption heights reasonably well. Induced electron density was higher for An than FCl-An. SAPT0 analysis showed induction energy is larger for An. The π-hole increases the ionization potential of FCl-An.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The π-hole creates a positive electrostatic potential in the center. This affects non-covalent intermolecular interactions significantly. The π-hole increases the ionization potential of the molecule. Higher ionization potential inhibits charge density induction. Weaker induced electrostatic interactions result in larger adsorption height. The study confirms the theoretical prediction of π-hole existence. It demonstrates the importance of submolecular charge distribution. KPFM is validated as a tool for real-space charge mapping. The findings expand understanding of π-hole systems. It opens possibilities for studying chemical properties influenced by charge.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study compared FCl-An with anthracene as a control. KPFM simulations were compared with experimental data. SAPT0 and DFT calculations gave similar adsorption energies. The effect of tip-sample distance was analyzed.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the charge distribution in PAHs. Figure 2 shows the molecular self-assembly structure. Figure 3 presents KPFM images and simulations. Figure 4 displays force-distance spectroscopy and induced density. Table S2 presents adsorption energies from DFT and SAPT0. Table S3 presents SAPT0 energy decomposition.

summary.title: Non-idealities in CO2 electroreduction mechanisms revealed by automation-assisted kinetic analysis
summary.authors: Joy S Zeng, Vineet Padia, Joseph H Maalouf, Aditya M Limaye, Alexander H Liu, Michael A Yusov, Ian W Hunter, Karthish Manthiram
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the limitations of traditional linearized kinetic analyses (Tafel and order dependence) in electrocatalysis, which often fail to capture complex reaction phenomena such as surface coverage effects and mixed control. The authors introduce a robotic system that automates the sequential testing of up to ten electrochemical cells, allowing for varied electrodes, electrolytes, gas compositions, and voltages. This automation facilitates cohesive kinetic analysis, a robust strategy requiring extensive data over wide reaction conditions. Using this platform, the team investigated the mechanism of CO2 electroreduction to carbon monoxide (CO) at immobilized metal tetrapyrroles: cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc). The results reveal significant non-idealities in reaction rate data, specifically non-linear and potential-dependent bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences. For CoPc and CoTPP, bicarbonate inhibition is attenuated at more reductive potentials, consistent with models involving bicarbonate poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control. In contrast, FePc exhibits stronger bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials, suggesting a different mechanism where the most abundant reactive intermediate is a species prior to the unoccupied site. The study demonstrates that complex mechanisms, unexplainable by standard Tafel analysis, are prevalent in this class of catalysts. The robotic workflow proved more time-efficient and reliable, with data correlating well with previous manual studies despite lower absolute rates. The work highlights the importance of considering electrolyte poisoning, coverage effects, and mixed control in interpreting CO2RR kinetics, suggesting that apparent contradictions in literature may stem from limited operating condition ranges. Future work will focus on incorporating membranes and automated mechanism enumeration to further standardize and accelerate electrocatalytic research.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the limitations of traditional linearized kinetic analyses (Tafel and order dependence) in electrocatalysis, which often fail to capture complex reaction phenomena such as surface coverage effects and mixed control. The authors introduce a robotic system that automates the sequential testing of up to ten electrochemical cells, allowing for varied electrodes, electrolytes, gas compositions, and voltages. This automation facilitates cohesive kinetic analysis, a robust strategy requiring extensive data over wide reaction conditions. Using this platform, the team investigated the mechanism of CO2 electroreduction to carbon monoxide (CO) at immobilized metal tetrapyrroles: cobalt phthalocyanine (CoPc), cobalt tetraphenylporphyrin (CoTPP), and iron phthalocyanine (FePc). The results reveal significant non-idealities in reaction rate data, specifically non-linear and potential-dependent bicarbonate and CO2 order dependences. For CoPc and CoTPP, bicarbonate inhibition is attenuated at more reductive potentials, consistent with models involving bicarbonate poisoning and potential-dependent mixed control. In contrast, FePc exhibits stronger bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials, suggesting a different mechanism where the most abundant reactive intermediate is a species prior to the unoccupied site. The study demonstrates that complex mechanisms, unexplainable by standard Tafel analysis, are prevalent in this class of catalysts. The robotic workflow proved more time-efficient and reliable, with data correlating well with previous manual studies despite lower absolute rates. The work highlights the importance of considering electrolyte poisoning, coverage effects, and mixed control in interpreting CO2RR kinetics, suggesting that apparent contradictions in literature may stem from limited operating condition ranges. Future work will focus on incorporating membranes and automated mechanism enumeration to further standardize and accelerate electrocatalytic research.

Research Context
Traditional electrocatalysis kinetics rely on linearized rate data. These methods assume independent factorization of voltage and concentration. Complex phenomena like coverage effects break these assumptions. Cohesive kinetic analysis offers a more robust alternative. This approach requires large datasets over wide conditions. Manual data collection is slow and error-prone. Existing automation focuses on high-throughput screening. Miniaturization limits product quantification for kinetic analysis. Parallelization often lacks individual online product detection. Sequential testing with online quantification is ideal.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to automate electrochemical rate data collection. The robotic system accommodates varied experimental parameters. The primary goal is to investigate CO2RR mechanisms. Specific catalysts include CoPc, CoTPP, and FePc. The hypothesis is that non-idealities are prevalent. These non-idealities manifest as changing order dependences. The authors predict complex mechanisms explain these trends. Phenomena like electrolyte poisoning are expected to be key. The study seeks to reconcile conflicting literature reports. It is hypothesized that standard Tafel analysis is insufficient.

Methodological Details
CoPc catalysts were drop-casted onto Toray060 carbon paper. CoPc loading was 5.98 x 10^-11 mol/cm2. CoTPP and FePc used carbon black-containing DMF. CoTPP loading was 5.11 x 10^-10 mol/cm2. FePc loading was 8.04 x 10^-10 mol/cm2. Electrolytes were prepared from Na2CO3 and NaClO4 stocks. Stock solutions were bubbled overnight with CO2. Final electrolytes had 1 mol/L ionic strength. Electrolyses were queued in batches of ten. A leak-free Ag/AgCl reference electrode was used. The reference electrode was calibrated daily. Data was uploaded to an SQL database. A python script processed the data files. The robot houses a single cell body. Ten cell pan pairs house working electrodes. The cell body moves horizontally and vertically. Online product quantification used a gas chromatograph. The working electrode exposed a 10 mm diameter circle. A 0.25 mm platinum wire counter electrode was used.

Procedures And Architectures
The robot sequentially tests each cell pan. Electrolyte is pumped through the 'electrolyte in' port. Gas flow is initiated before voltage application. Voltage is applied after a few minutes. Online detection of CO and H2 occurs. Electrolyte is pumped out via 'electrolyte out' tubing. Cell body cleaning uses a wash station. MilliQ water is pumped for cleaning cycles. The cell body is rinsed after ten electrolyses. The setup is a three-electrode, undivided compartment cell. No membrane separates anode and cathode. Oxygen crossover can cause parasitic ORR current. Average Faradaic efficiency closure was ~60%. Pt counter electrode prevents anode product attribution. High HER Faradaic efficiencies were observed. CO2 was bubbled into the electrolyte. Currents were below mass transport limits.

Key Results
Newly measured CO rates were up to ten times lower. Faradaic efficiencies toward CO were typically under 30%. Previous kinetic trends in CO production were preserved. New data correlated well with previous work. Non-ideal mechanisms showed curvature in data. Bicarbonate inhibition was voltage-dependent for all catalysts. CoPc and CoTPP showed negative bicarbonate dependence at less reductive potentials. CoPc and CoTPP showed positive dependence at more reductive potentials. FePc showed greater bicarbonate inhibition at more reductive potentials. CoPc CO2 order dependence appeared ideal and first order. CoTPP CO2 order was slightly below one. CoTPP CO2 order decreased at more reductive potentials. FePc CO2 order was more attenuated at less reductive potentials. FePc CO2 order curves intersected at low pressures. Voltage inhibited the reaction at low CO2 pressures for FePc.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CoPc and CoTPP mechanisms involve bicarbonate poisoning. These mechanisms also involve potential-dependent mixed control. Poisoning is described by positive electrosorption valency. FePc mechanism involves a species prior to the unoccupied site. This explains the contrasting bicarbonate trend in FePc. On-cycle poisoning species can also explain trends. Complex mechanisms are prevalent in metal tetrapyrroles. Standard Tafel analysis misses these complexities. Literature contradictions may arise from limited condition ranges. Automation enables robust cohesive kinetic analysis.

Contradictions And Limitations
The undivided cell design allows oxygen crossover. This leads to incomplete Faradaic efficiency closure. High HER Faradaic efficiencies were observed. Pt deposition might affect HER sites. Bubbling CO2 may influence measured kinetics. New rates were lower than previously reported. Models only qualitatively capture observed trends. Models do not quantitatively fit all data. Specific reaction mechanisms were not definitively proposed. The study relies on conceptual and generalized analyses.

Claims
Automation enables robust cohesive kinetic analysis for electrocatalysis. The robotic system automates sequential testing. It accommodates varied experimental conditions. Data collection is more time-efficient. The undivided cell design has limitations. Oxygen crossover affects Faradaic efficiency. This approach can reveal complex mechanisms. It standardizes and accelerates data collection.
CO2RR at metal tetrapyrroles involves complex, non-linearizable mechanisms. Bicarbonate order dependences change with potential. CO2 order dependences are non-linear. These trends are unexplainable by standard models. CoPc CO2 order appeared ideal. Standard Tafel analysis is insufficient. Electrolyte poisoning and mixed control are key.

Data And Code Availability
All experimental data is available as xlsx. Supporting information includes protocols and data. The work is licensed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Data robustness was evaluated against literature precedent. New data correlated well with previous work. Kinetic trends were preserved despite lower rates. Models were tested for goodness-of-fit. Some models could not fit observed trends.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the robot design and cell assembly. Figure 2 illustrates bicarbonate dependence and mechanisms. Figure 3 shows CO2 dependence and mechanisms. Figure S5 shows Faradaic efficiency closure. Figure S7 compares new and previous kinetic trends. Figure S8 shows correlation with previous data. Figure S10 shows Faradaic efficiencies toward CO and H2.

Three Takeaways
1. A robotic system automates electrochemical kinetic data collection. 2. CO2RR at metal tetrapyrroles exhibits complex, non-linear kinetics. 3. Future work will improve automation and mechanism enumeration.

summary.title: Biological activity of Ajuga iva extracts against the African cotton leafworm Spodoptera littoralis
summary.authors: Leena Taha-Salaime, Galina Lebedev, Jackline Abo-Nassar, Sally Marzouk, Moshe Inbar, Murad Ghanim, Radi Aly
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the biological activity of crude extracts from Ajuga iva against the African cotton leafworm, Spodoptera littoralis, a major agricultural pest. The research focuses on the potential of phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes, natural compounds found in Ajuga plants, as green alternatives to synthetic pesticides. The authors hypothesized that these compounds, which mimic insect molting hormones, would disrupt larval development and survival. Using first and third instar larvae, the study demonstrated that A. iva crude leaf extract significantly increased mortality, reduced larval weight gain (LWG), and decreased relative growth rate (RGR) in a dose-dependent manner. Specifically, the highest concentration (250 µg/µl) resulted in 85% mortality in first instars and prevented pupation in third instars. Histological analysis using DAPI and phalloidin staining revealed severe gut damage, including nuclear abnormalities and reduced actin filament organization, suggesting a direct toxic effect on gut epithelial cells. The study also confirmed that purified phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) isolated from the extract retained significant biological activity, causing similar developmental disruptions. In contrast, commercial standards at low concentrations showed no significant effect, highlighting the potency of the plant-derived mixture. The findings support the use of A. iva extracts in Integrated Pest Management (IPM) programs, offering a safer, environmentally friendly option for controlling S. littoralis while minimizing risks to human health and the environment.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the biological activity of crude extracts from Ajuga iva against the African cotton leafworm, Spodoptera littoralis, a major agricultural pest. The research focuses on the potential of phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes, natural compounds found in Ajuga plants, as green alternatives to synthetic pesticides. The authors hypothesized that these compounds, which mimic insect molting hormones, would disrupt larval development and survival. Using first and third instar larvae, the study demonstrated that A. iva crude leaf extract significantly increased mortality, reduced larval weight gain (LWG), and decreased relative growth rate (RGR) in a dose-dependent manner. Specifically, the highest concentration (250 µg/µl) resulted in 85% mortality in first instars and prevented pupation in third instars. Histological analysis using DAPI and phalloidin staining revealed severe gut damage, including nuclear abnormalities and reduced actin filament organization, suggesting a direct toxic effect on gut epithelial cells. The study also confirmed that purified phytoecdysteroids (20-hydroxyecdysone, makisterone A, and cyasterone) isolated from the extract retained significant biological activity, causing similar developmental disruptions. In contrast, commercial standards at low concentrations showed no significant effect, highlighting the potency of the plant-derived mixture. The findings support the use of A. iva extracts in Integrated Pest Management (IPM) programs, offering a safer, environmentally friendly option for controlling S. littoralis while minimizing risks to human health and the environment.

Research Context
Insects cause severe damage to crops, and current control methods rely on pesticides with negative environmental impacts. Green control is gaining popularity due to concerns about pesticide side effects. Phytoecdysteroids are plant-produced steroids that mimic insect molting hormones. These compounds are present in 5-6% of plant species at higher concentrations than in arthropods. Ajuga plants contain high levels of phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes. Previous studies showed Ajuga extracts inhibit ecdysis and cause mortality in other pests. The study aims to evaluate A. iva extracts against Spodoptera littoralis.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether A. iva crude leaf extract affects S. littoralis larvae. A second question examines if isolated phytoecdysteroids have different effects than the crude extract. A third question investigates if phytoecdysteroids have a direct effect on the larvae's gut. The hypothesis is that A. iva extracts containing phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes are promising pest-control agents. It is predicted that these compounds will interfere with molting and metamorphosis. The study expects the extracts to reduce damage caused by S. littoralis larvae.

Methodological Details
Young and mature leaves and stems of A. iva were collected after blooming. Plant material was oven-dried at 55°C for 3-4 days and homogenized. Crude extracts were prepared by soaking 24 g of powder in 240 ml MeOH. The extract was homogenized at 2500 rpm for 1 hour and centrifuged. LC-TOF-MS was used to identify phytoecdysteroids and clerodanes in three concentrations. First and third instar S. littoralis larvae were reared on castor bean leaves. Larvae were exposed to 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl of crude leaf extract. Experiments were conducted in a climate-controlled room at 25°C. Gut morphology was analyzed using DAPI and phalloidin staining. Statistical analyses included t-tests, mixed-model ANOVA, and Friedman tests.

Procedures And Architectures
Castor bean leaves were smeared with aqueous A. iva crude leaf extract. Tween 20 was added as a surfactant to the extract solution. Treated leaves were dried in a chemical hood for 2 hours. First instar larvae were placed on treated leaves for 3 days. Third instar larvae were fed on treated leaves for 4 or 8 days. Freshly treated leaves were provided after 4 days to avoid decay. Larval mortality, survival, and relative growth rate were recorded. Pupation rate was evaluated for an additional 15 days. Guts were dissected, fixed in paraformaldehyde, and stained. Images were captured using Leica and Olympus confocal microscopes.

Key Results
First instar larvae showed significant mortality increases at 50, 100, and 250 µg/µl. Mortality rates were 25%, 65%, and 85% respectively, compared to 5% in controls. Third instar larvae showed reduced larval weight gain at all concentrations. Relative growth rate was significantly decreased compared to controls. At 250 µg/µl, RGR decreased by 0.05 and 0.20 g/g day on days 6 and 8. None of the treated larvae survived more than 8 days at the highest concentration. Purified phytoecdysteroid mixture also significantly reduced RGR and survival. Larvae fed on 250 µg/µl extract or phytoecdysteroid mixture lost weight and died. Gut nuclei were smaller and abnormally shaped in treated larvae. Actin filaments were smaller and reduced in amount in treated guts. Treated larvae were unable to complete pupation after 15 days.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results support the hypothesis that A. iva extracts disrupt S. littoralis development. Phytoecdysteroids likely interfere with molting and metamorphosis processes. Gut damage suggests a direct toxic effect on epithelial cells. Reduced growth and weight gain prevent larvae from reaching pupation threshold. The findings align with previous studies on phytoecdysteroid toxicity in insects. A. iva extracts offer a potential green control method for IPM programs.

Claims
Ajuga iva crude leaf extract significantly reduces the survival and development of Spodoptera littoralis larvae. Mortality increased to 85% at the highest concentration. Relative growth rate was significantly decreased. Larvae were unable to pupate. Commercial standards at 100 ppm had no significant effect. A. iva extracts are promising for pest control.
Phytoecdysteroids in A. iva cause direct damage to the larval gut. Gut nuclei were abnormally shaped. Actin filaments were reduced in amount.  Gut damage contributes to larval mortality.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used multiple concentrations to assess dose-dependency. Purified phytoecdysteroids were tested to confirm specific activity. Control treatments with water and Tween 20 were included.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows TLC analysis of phytoecdysteroids. Figure 2 displays larval mortality and weight gain. Figure 3 illustrates relative growth rate and survival. Figure 4 shows the effect of treatment order. Figure 5 presents the effect of purified phytoecdysteroids. Figure 6 shows gut histology with DAPI and phalloidin. Figure 7 depicts incomplete pupae.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating the efficacy of A. iva extracts against S. littoralis. 2. The strongest evidence is the dose-dependent mortality and gut damage. 3. The future path is the integration of A. iva into IPM programs.

summary.title: Sorry, we're open: Golden Open Access and inequality in the natural sciences
summary.authors: Russell J Gray
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the relationship between Article Processing Charges (APC) and journal impact metrics within the context of Golden Open Access (GOA) publishing in the natural sciences. The author argues that while GOA increases accessibility, the associated costs create significant inequalities, particularly for researchers in developing countries or those without institutional funding. The study analyzes metadata from 237 open-access natural science journals, focusing on APC, Impact Factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), and citability. The data was sourced from the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) and analyzed using R statistical software. Key findings reveal significant positive correlations between APC and IF (r = 0.391), EF (r = 0.303), and citability (r = 0.323). Furthermore, publishers from developed countries were found to have higher APCs and impact metrics compared to those from developing countries. The author discusses the implications of these trends, highlighting how high APCs may prioritize publisher profit over scientific integrity and create barriers for researchers in the Global South. The paper concludes that the current GOA model exacerbates global scientific inequality, potentially marginalizing important research from tropical regions and independent researchers, and calls for a more inclusive publishing environment.

claims.description: There is a positive correlation between Article Processing Charges and journal impact metrics.
Golden Open Access exacerbates inequality between developed and developing countries.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the relationship between Article Processing Charges (APC) and journal impact metrics within the context of Golden Open Access (GOA) publishing in the natural sciences. The author argues that while GOA increases accessibility, the associated costs create significant inequalities, particularly for researchers in developing countries or those without institutional funding. The study analyzes metadata from 237 open-access natural science journals, focusing on APC, Impact Factor (IF), Eigen Factor (EF), and citability. The data was sourced from the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) and analyzed using R statistical software. Key findings reveal significant positive correlations between APC and IF (r = 0.391), EF (r = 0.303), and citability (r = 0.323). Furthermore, publishers from developed countries were found to have higher APCs and impact metrics compared to those from developing countries. The author discusses the implications of these trends, highlighting how high APCs may prioritize publisher profit over scientific integrity and create barriers for researchers in the Global South. The paper concludes that the current GOA model exacerbates global scientific inequality, potentially marginalizing important research from tropical regions and independent researchers, and calls for a more inclusive publishing environment.

Research Context
The rise of Sci-Hub and ResearchGate has increased article availability. High-impact journals transitioned to mandatory open access to maintain profitability. Publication fees in GOA journals can be costly for many researchers. Researchers from developing countries often pay full prices for high-impact journals. Publishing in lower-impact or predatory journals is a common alternative.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to determine links between publication costs and impact metrics. It examines the relationship between APC, Impact Factor, and Eigen Factor. The study also analyzes citability in relation to publication costs. It investigates disparities based on the country of the journal publisher. The goal is to discuss implications for global scientific inequality.

Methodological Details
Data was collected from the Directory of Open Access Journals. The initial dataset contained 14,275 journal records. A subset of 1,047 journals related to biological sciences was queried. Journals with an Impact Factor greater than 40 were excluded. The final analysis used a vetted dataset of 237 journals. R statistical software was used for all data analyses. The scholar package was used to generate impact factors. The quantmod package converted all currencies to USD. Pearson's correlation coefficient was used to analyze correlations.

Procedures And Architectures
Keywords like ecology and conservation were used to filter journals. Excluded journals were checked to ensure they were not natural sciences. APC was examined in relation to citability and impact metrics. Country of publisher was examined against cost and impact. The ggpubr package was used for statistical analysis.

Key Results
A linear trend was found between IF, EF, and citability vs APC. Publishers from developed countries had higher APC and impact metrics. The mean APC of the analyzed journals was $1344.27 USD. The mean Impact Factor was 2.855. The mean Eigen Factor was 0.017. The mean total citation count was 5925.92. APC was significantly positively correlated with IF (r = 0.391, p < .001). APC was significantly positively correlated with EF (r = 0.303, p < .001). APC was significantly positively correlated with citability (r = 0.323, p < .001).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Increasing publishing costs are linked to higher impact and citations. Developed country publishers dominate high-impact, high-cost journals. Research from developing countries is less likely to gain exposure. High APCs may prioritize publisher profit over scientific integrity. The GOA system may create an environment of editorial complacency.

Contradictions And Limitations
Expensive APCs are not linked to the reliability of research. Impact factor creates a false perception of reliability. The study focuses only on natural sciences journals. Personal experience is cited regarding funding rejection. The criteria for APC assistance can be restrictive.

Claims
There is a positive correlation between Article Processing Charges and journal impact metrics. APC is positively correlated with Impact Factor. APC is positively correlated with Eigen Factor. APC is positively correlated with citability. High cost does not guarantee research reliability. Higher costs may signal higher prestige but not quality.
Golden Open Access exacerbates inequality between developed and developing countries. Developed country publishers have higher APCs and impact. Developing country researchers pay full prices. Some funding assistance exists for developing countries. Research from the Global South may be marginalized.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates disparities between developed and developing publishers.

Three Takeaways
1. APCs are positively correlated with journal impact and citability. 2. Publishers from developed countries dominate high-impact GOA journals. 3. The GOA model creates barriers for researchers in developing countries.
