summary.title: Machine learning force field ranking of candidate solid electrolyte interphase structures in Li-ion batteries
summary.authors: James M Stevenson; Garvit Agarwal; Leif D Jacobson
summary.executive_summary:
This study addresses the critical gap in understanding the Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in lithium-ion batteries, a complex passivating layer that remains poorly characterized due to the limitations of existing simulation methods. Traditional Density Functional Theory (DFT) methods are too slow for the necessary length and time scales, while classical force fields lack the accuracy for complex redox reactions. The authors propose a novel approach using a multitask machine learning force field (MLFF) based on the QRNN architecture to simulate SEI formation and rank candidate structures by predicted energy.

The methodology involves a combination of classical sampling and active learning. Initial SEI candidate structures were generated using the Schrödinger SEI Simulator with OPLS4 molecular dynamics, starting with 1 M LiPF6 in ethylene carbonate (EC). These candidates were then annealed using a reactive QRNN model under extreme conditions (400 K, 1000 atm) to ensure stability and reaction completion. The model was trained on a diverse dataset including periodic and non-periodic systems, labeled with PBE-D3 and wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD levels of theory, as well as a supplemental SPICE dataset for general organic chemistry to shape the latent space.

Key results demonstrate that the MLFF can stably simulate complex redox reactions, producing the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by energy. Statistical analysis of the bonding in these structures reveals that P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable configurations, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with less stability. The study validates the model against surface reaction energy barriers, showing reasonable accuracy. The authors conclude that this approach provides a quantitative foundation for understanding SEI chemistry and suggests future work on comparing multiple electrolyte formulations and applying other MLFF architectures like Nequip and MACE. This work represents a significant step toward using machine learning to model complex battery interphases, offering a pathway to optimize SEI composition for next-generation batteries.

claims.description: Multitask training with QRNN allows accurate simulation of complex SEI reactions.
Specific bond types correlate with SEI structural stability.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the critical gap in understanding the Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) in lithium-ion batteries, a complex passivating layer that remains poorly characterized due to the limitations of existing simulation methods. Traditional Density Functional Theory (DFT) methods are too slow for the necessary length and time scales, while classical force fields lack the accuracy for complex redox reactions. The authors propose a novel approach using a multitask machine learning force field (MLFF) based on the QRNN architecture to simulate SEI formation and rank candidate structures by predicted energy.

The methodology involves a combination of classical sampling and active learning. Initial SEI candidate structures were generated using the Schrödinger SEI Simulator with OPLS4 molecular dynamics, starting with 1 M LiPF6 in ethylene carbonate (EC). These candidates were then annealed using a reactive QRNN model under extreme conditions (400 K, 1000 atm) to ensure stability and reaction completion. The model was trained on a diverse dataset including periodic and non-periodic systems, labeled with PBE-D3 and wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD levels of theory, as well as a supplemental SPICE dataset for general organic chemistry to shape the latent space.

Key results demonstrate that the MLFF can stably simulate complex redox reactions, producing the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by energy. Statistical analysis of the bonding in these structures reveals that P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable configurations, while C-O and Li-F bonds correlate with less stability. The study validates the model against surface reaction energy barriers, showing reasonable accuracy. The authors conclude that this approach provides a quantitative foundation for understanding SEI chemistry and suggests future work on comparing multiple electrolyte formulations and applying other MLFF architectures like Nequip and MACE. This work represents a significant step toward using machine learning to model complex battery interphases, offering a pathway to optimize SEI composition for next-generation batteries.

Research Context
The Solid-Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) is a vital but poorly-understood material class in lithium-ion batteries. Key questions about SEIs, such as their amorphous or crystalline nature, remain unanswered. Existing pure density functionals underestimate reaction barriers and are too slow for SEI scales. Hybrid functionals struggle with metals and have poor computational scaling for periodic systems. Machine learning force fields (MLFFs) promise DFT accuracy with classical force field speed. Previous MLFFs have predicted properties of Li metal and organic liquids but not SEI interactions. Traditional force fields are difficult to fit for complex systems like the SEI.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to simulate and rank SEI candidate structures using machine learning. The hypothesis is that a multitask MLFF can model complex SEI reactions with sufficient accuracy. The study aims to produce the first set of SEI structures ranked by predicted energy. It is hypothesized that specific bond types correlate with the energetic stability of SEI structures. The authors predict that MLFFs can bridge the gap between DFT accuracy and classical speed. The goal is to enable future machine learning applications and comparison with experimental results.

Methodological Details
The reference level of theory for non-periodic systems is wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD. The reference level of theory for periodic systems is PBE-D3 in a plane wave basis. The study uses multiple rounds of active learning for data generation. Enhanced reaction sampling uses Artificial Force Induced Reactions (AFIR) and Nudged Elastic Band (NEB). A supplemental dataset of general organic chemistry, SPICE, was added to shape the latent space. The SPICE subset consists of elements H, Li, C, O, F, and P. The hidden layers of the neural networks were doubled to increase model capacity. Initial SEI candidates were generated using the Schrödinger SEI Simulator with OPLS4 MD. Each system starts with 700 molecules of EC and 52 ions each of Li+ and PF6-. The total number of atoms in each initial system is 7416. Four sets of candidates were defined with 5, 12, 23, and 33 added Li+ ions. Lithium oxide, carbonate, fluoride, and hydroxide were added to the training set. Non-equilibrium geometries were sampled by adding Gaussian noise to Cartesian coordinates. Periodic DFT was performed using Quantum Espresso with PBE functional and D3 correction. Gas-phase DFT was performed using Psi4 v1.6 with wB97X-D3BJ/def2-TZVPD.

Procedures And Architectures
The model architecture is a multitask QRNN with four output levels of theory. The loss function includes energy, force, and charge mean squared error. The Adamax optimizer with decoupled weight decay was used for training. The final model used a learning rate of 2e-3. Hidden layers of size 256, 224, and 192 were used for all elements. The batch size was set to 64. A weight decay of 1e-3 was used for the final model. The final model is an exponential moving average of training parameters. Initial liquid geometries were equilibrated using NPT ensemble for 1 ns. Solid-liquid interfaces started from a BCC lattice of lithium with optimized lattice constant. Candidates were annealed using reactive QRNN MD at 400 K and 1000 atm for 100 ps. Structures were ranked by mean potential energy over a 20 ps MD trajectory at 300 K. Lewis structures were recalculated using Schrödinger Materials Science Suite for bond analysis.

Key Results
The QRNN models gave stable dynamics despite extreme conditions applied during annealing. The study produced the first set of SEI candidate structures ranked by predicted energy. P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures. C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable structures. Adding SPICE data resulted in only an 8% increase in hybrid-head RMSE. The model was validated against surface reaction energy barriers. The lowest-energy SEI candidate from the 33 added Li subgroup was identified as the best. The model does not have enough capacity to overfit, so early stopping had little effect.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results suggest that specific bond types determine the energetic stability of SEI structures. Multitask training allows the model to handle diverse chemical systems without heavy capacity cost. The latent space of MLFF models contains unused capacity for broadening chemical applicability. This work provides a quantitative foundation for understanding lithium-ion battery interphases. The approach enables the ranking of candidate SEI structures for future optimization. The study demonstrates the feasibility of simulating complex redox reactive systems with MLFFs.

Contradictions And Limitations
The difficulty of characterizing the SEI experimentally is an obstacle to validation. Experimental values for density, diffusivity, viscosity, or elastic modulus do not exist for SEI. The model is not final, as its scope is still small compared to requirements. The study only used a single formulation of electrolyte, 1M LiPF6 in EC. The probability of being proven wrong by future events is high. The model was not trained on DFT-generated MD, AFIR, or NEB geometries to avoid test set leakage.

Claims
Multitask training with QRNN allows accurate simulation of complex SEI reactions. The model stably simulated extreme conditions and complex redox reactions. The model produced ranked SEI structures with reasonable energy predictions. The model's scope is limited and not yet final. This enables quantitative understanding of SEI chemistry.
Specific bond types correlate with SEI structural stability. P-F and Li-O bonds are associated with more stable structures. C-O and Li-F bonds are associated with less stable structures. The correlation is based on predicted energies, not experimental validation. This guides the design of more stable SEI formulations.

Data And Code Availability
The list of SEI candidate structures and energies is available on Figshare. Plotting scripts and initial solution structures are also provided in the repository.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Adding SPICE data did not significantly increase PBE-head validation RMSE. Higher weight decay reduced reaction barrier heights, so a conventional value was used. The model was validated against surface reaction energy barriers.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 4 shows bond counts with respect to total system energy for the most lithiated SEI set. Table 1 validates the model against surface reaction energy barriers.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first MLFF-based ranking of SEI candidate structures. 2. The strongest evidence is the stable simulation of complex redox reactions and bond stability correlations. 3. The future path involves comparing multiple electrolyte formulations and applying other MLFF architectures.

summary.title: A Workflow for Identifying Viable Crystal Structures with Partially Occupied Sites Applied to Solid Electrolyte: Cubic Li 7 La 3 Zr 2 O 12
summary.authors: Julian Holland; Tom Demeyere; Arihant Bhandari; Felix Hanke; Victor Milman; Chris-Kriton Skylaris
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the lack of consensus regarding the ground state configuration of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), a prominent solid electrolyte candidate. Previous experimental and theoretical works have failed to identify the stable structure due to the vast combinatorial space of possible Li site occupancies. The authors present a novel methodology to identify energetically favorable configurations by systematically generating and ranking all possible structures. The workflow begins by eliminating physically impossible structures where Li atoms overlap, using a minimum Li-Li distance constraint of 1.7 Å. This geometric constraint significantly reduces the configuration space by limiting the possible 24d:96h site ratios. Further reduction is achieved by removing symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH), which scales linearly with the number of structures. The remaining unique structures are then energetically ordered using a machine learning model, specifically a multiple linear regression (MLR) trained on Density Functional Theory (DFT) data. The DFT calculations were performed using the ONETEP code with the PBE functional. The study finds that the lowest energy structures predominantly feature an 8:48 ratio of 24d to 96h site occupancy. Four structures are identified within 0.026 eV of the global minimum energy. The authors demonstrate that a large portion of previously reported structures in the literature may not be feasible or stable due to violating the minimum Li-Li distance constraint. The generated structures are made available in a public database to improve reproducibility and accuracy in future c-LLZO research. This work provides a robust framework for identifying viable crystal structures in materials with partially occupied sites, extending beyond c-LLZO to other ion conductors.

claims.description: A significant portion of previously reported c-LLZO structures are not physically feasible due to Li-Li overlap.
The 8:48 ratio of 24d to 96h site occupancy is energetically preferred.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the lack of consensus regarding the ground state configuration of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12 (c-LLZO), a prominent solid electrolyte candidate. Previous experimental and theoretical works have failed to identify the stable structure due to the vast combinatorial space of possible Li site occupancies. The authors present a novel methodology to identify energetically favorable configurations by systematically generating and ranking all possible structures. The workflow begins by eliminating physically impossible structures where Li atoms overlap, using a minimum Li-Li distance constraint of 1.7 Å. This geometric constraint significantly reduces the configuration space by limiting the possible 24d:96h site ratios. Further reduction is achieved by removing symmetry-equivalent duplicates using local sensitive hashing (LSH), which scales linearly with the number of structures. The remaining unique structures are then energetically ordered using a machine learning model, specifically a multiple linear regression (MLR) trained on Density Functional Theory (DFT) data. The DFT calculations were performed using the ONETEP code with the PBE functional. The study finds that the lowest energy structures predominantly feature an 8:48 ratio of 24d to 96h site occupancy. Four structures are identified within 0.026 eV of the global minimum energy. The authors demonstrate that a large portion of previously reported structures in the literature may not be feasible or stable due to violating the minimum Li-Li distance constraint. The generated structures are made available in a public database to improve reproducibility and accuracy in future c-LLZO research. This work provides a robust framework for identifying viable crystal structures in materials with partially occupied sites, extending beyond c-LLZO to other ion conductors.

Research Context
Experimental and theoretical works have failed to uncover the ground state configuration of cubic Li7La3Zr2O12. Computational studies typically rely on an initial low-energy structure as a reference point. There is no consensus on the Li occupancy of c-LLZO in the literature. Previous studies often use experimental values as starting points for idealised unit cells. The range of predicted structures indicates disagreement about the ground state. Without knowing if structures are close to the ground state, properties may not be well described.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to find and rank all possible Li site occupancies for c-LLZO. The authors intend to produce all possible structures of a c-LLZO unit cell. They seek to ascertain if there is a significant energy difference in structure choice. The study hopes to elicit if structural properties like 24d:96h ratio indicate energy. The methodology aims to identify energetically favourable configurations of c-LLZO. The method is designed to be extended to other ion conductors.

Methodological Details
The total number of ways to populate 120 sites with 56 Li is approximately 7.4 × 10^34. A brute-force combinatorial method is unviable due to this large number. Structures with overlapping Li atoms are eliminated using a minimal Li-Li distance. The chosen minimal Li-Li distance is 1.7 Å. This distance is less than 2 times the ionic radius of a Li atom. The 48g site is neglected as it is not reported in most refinements. The crystal structure sites reported by Buschmann et al. are used as the framework. The total number of generated structures is approximately 2.3 × 10^8. Symmetry-equivalent duplicates are removed using local sensitive hashing (LSH). LSH optimizes pairwise comparison from O(N^2) to O(N). Only approximately 1% of structures are symmetrically unique. The configuration space is reduced to around 2 × 10^6 structures. DFT calculations were performed on 1235 single point structures. The first subset consisted of the 200 energetically lowest structures according to COMPASSIII. The second subset was a random selection of approximately 1000 structures. DFT calculations were performed with the ONETEP code. The PBE GGA exchange correlation functional was used. A kinetic energy cutoff of 830 eV was applied. A multiple linear regression (MLR) model was fitted to the DFT energies. Structures were represented by a frequency occurrence list of Li-Li interactions. Data were split into test and training sets with a 1:3 ratio.

Procedures And Architectures
All possible 24d permutations are generated for a given 24d occupancy. Directly neighbouring 96h sites are eliminated from consideration. Remaining 96h sites are populated such that no two nearest neighbours are occupied. An upper triangular connectivity matrix of the Li sub-lattice is constructed. The matrix is flattened and sorted to ensure uniformity. LSH is used to perform fast approximate similarity searches. The method is limited to comparison of monoatomic sub-lattices with predefined positions. The method was validated for 13:43 and 12:44 ratios. DFT calculations were performed on small subsets to fit the MLR model. The COMPASSIII forcefield was used to pre-select the lowest energy structures. ONETEP was used for DFT calculations with linear scaling. CASTEP on-the-fly generated pseudopotentials were used. Geometry optimisation calculations were performed on the final four structures. Broyder-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno (BFGS) was used for geometry optimisation.

Key Results
The MLR model achieved a correlation of 0.9996 on the test set. All structures occur within a range of 5.8 eV of the lowest energy structure. 19 out of the 20 lowest energy structures have a ratio of 8:48. The 19th lowest energy structure has a ratio of 9:47. The average energy for all structures is 1.47 eV higher than the ground state. The average energy for each ratio increases with increasing 24d occupancy. There is an energetic preference to avoid 24d occupation where possible. Four structures, all 8:48, are within 0.026 eV of the lowest energy structure. The four lowest energy structures have very similar atomic coordinates. All four lowest structures have the same 24d configuration. Only slight variations exist in the 96h configuration of the lowest structures. Geometry optimisation narrows the energy gap between the final four structures. A large proportion of experimental and theoretical literature structures are not feasible. The 96h to 24d transition yielded the lowest overall energy structure. This lowest energy structure was 0.58 eV lower than the single point minimum.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The methodology enables the isolation of low-energy structures for crystallographically predicted structures. Geometrical constraints from the methodology determine that many reported structures may not be feasible. The method can be extended to other ion conductors and partially occupied crystals. Providing all structures aims to improve accuracy and reproducibility in c-LLZO research. The study highlights that a large portion of literature structures are not reflective of real systems. The workflow provides a fast evaluation procedure for crystals with partially occupied sites.

Contradictions And Limitations
The energetic ordering procedure does not include entropic contributions. The study assumes a reasonable retention of ordering upon geometry relaxation. A large-scale energy prediction of geometry optimised structures is outside the scope. The LSH method is limited to monoatomic sub-lattices with predefined positions. The trade-off for increased speed is the high specificity of the method. COMPASSIII predicts a more pronounced separation of energies than ONETEP. The issue with COMPASSIII was considered too large to surmount in this paper. The choice of initial structure in previous studies was mostly for convenience. Coulombic forces alone are not sufficient to energetically order c-LLZO structures.

Claims
A significant portion of previously reported c-LLZO structures are not physically feasible due to Li-Li overlap. The study eliminates structures involving overlapping Li atoms. A minimal Li-Li distance of 1.7 Å is imposed. A large portion of literature structures may not be feasible. Some literature structures might be valid if dopants are considered. Future research should verify structures against this geometric constraint.
The 8:48 ratio of 24d to 96h site occupancy is energetically preferred. 19 of the 20 lowest energy structures have an 8:48 ratio. Average energy increases with increasing 24d occupancy. One of the lowest structures has a 9:47 ratio. This ratio should be prioritized in future computational studies.

Data And Code Availability
All structures generated are published in a freely accessible database. The database aims to improve accuracy and reproducibility in c-LLZO research. Scripts for symmetry checking are provided with the database.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The symmetry checking method was validated against ASE for 12:44 and 13:43 ratios. The same number of structures were produced using both methods. Including symmetry in the MLR model made a negligible difference. Geometry relaxation was tested on a small dataset of 20 structures. A negative correlation was found between distance moved and final energy.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the 24d:96h ratios that cannot exist without Li-Li interaction. Figure 2b shows the energy distribution of structures. Figure 3 shows the workflow to find the 4 final structures. Table 1 gives the number of structures for each 24d:96h ratio. Figure S3 compares DFT energies to COMPASSIII predictions. Figure S4 shows the energy of a Li Dimer with changing distance. Figure S5 plots MLR energies against space group order.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a workflow to identify viable crystal structures with partially occupied sites. 2. The strongest evidence is the identification of four low-energy structures with an 8:48 ratio. 3. The future path is the extension of this method to other ion conductors.

summary.title: Highly sensitive and full-genome interrogation of SARS-CoV-2 using multiplexed PCR enrichment followed by next-generation sequencing
summary.authors: Chenyu Li, David N Debruyne, Julia Spencer, Vidushi Kapoor, Lily Y Liu, Bo Zhou, Utsav Pandey, Moiz Bootwalla, Dejerianne Ostrow, Dennis T Maglinte, David Ruble, Alex Ryutov, Lishuang Shen, Lucie Lee, Rounak Feigelman, Grayson Burdon, Jeffrey Liu, Alejandra Oliva, Adam Borcherding, Hongdong Tan, Alexander E Urban, Xiaowu Gai, Jennifer Dien Bard, Guoying Liu, Zhitong Liu
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the limitations of standard RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 detection, which often misses low-viral-load cases due to sampling timing or RNA degradation. The authors developed a highly sensitive multiplex PCR-based method using 343 specific primer pairs to amplify the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome. A mathematical model predicts this approach can detect as few as 0.29 copies of the virus at 95% probability, significantly outperforming RT-PCR's limit of 4.8 copies. The method was validated using plasmids and 13 clinical nasopharyngeal swab specimens with viral loads ranging from 8 to 675,885 copies per microliter. The assay successfully amplified full genomes, allowing for next-generation sequencing (NGS) to identify mutations, including the dominant D614G variant. The study also introduces a multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method using random hexamers, which achieved over 96% coverage of the SARS-CoV-2 genome in the presence of human genomic DNA with only ~0.6 million reads. This metagenomic approach offers a pathway for detecting novel or emerging pathogens without requiring deep sequencing. The results demonstrate that multiplex PCR enrichment provides a robust, sensitive, and specific alternative to RT-PCR for both diagnosis and genomic surveillance, capable of distinguishing SARS-CoV-2 from other respiratory viruses with high specificity.

claims.description: The multiplex PCR method is more sensitive than RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 detection.
The metagenomic method can identify SARS-CoV-2 in complex human backgrounds.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the limitations of standard RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 detection, which often misses low-viral-load cases due to sampling timing or RNA degradation. The authors developed a highly sensitive multiplex PCR-based method using 343 specific primer pairs to amplify the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome. A mathematical model predicts this approach can detect as few as 0.29 copies of the virus at 95% probability, significantly outperforming RT-PCR's limit of 4.8 copies. The method was validated using plasmids and 13 clinical nasopharyngeal swab specimens with viral loads ranging from 8 to 675,885 copies per microliter. The assay successfully amplified full genomes, allowing for next-generation sequencing (NGS) to identify mutations, including the dominant D614G variant. The study also introduces a multiplex-PCR-based metagenomic method using random hexamers, which achieved over 96% coverage of the SARS-CoV-2 genome in the presence of human genomic DNA with only ~0.6 million reads. This metagenomic approach offers a pathway for detecting novel or emerging pathogens without requiring deep sequencing. The results demonstrate that multiplex PCR enrichment provides a robust, sensitive, and specific alternative to RT-PCR for both diagnosis and genomic surveillance, capable of distinguishing SARS-CoV-2 from other respiratory viruses with high specificity.

Research Context
RT-PCR is the current gold standard but has limited sensitivity in clinical settings. Only 47-59% of true positive cases are identified by RT-PCR methods. Low viral load and RNA degradation hinder efficient downstream diagnosis. Full-length genome sequencing is essential for surveillance of viral evolution. Multiplex PCR offers higher sensitivity by targeting hundreds of genomic regions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to develop a more sensitive detection method than RT-PCR. The hypothesis is that multiplex PCR can detect lower copy numbers of SARS-CoV-2. The method should accommodate various application settings including surveillance. A metagenomic approach should identify novel pathogens with moderate sequencing depth. The assay should distinguish SARS-CoV-2 from other respiratory pathogens.

Methodological Details
The study utilized 343 pairs of specific primers for multiplex PCR. Two pools of primers were designed to cover the entire genome. The average amplicon length was 99bp with a 76bp gap. Validation used plasmids containing S and N gene sequences. Plasmid copy numbers were determined using droplet-based digital PCR. Thirteen nasopharyngeal swab specimens were used for clinical validation. Viral loads in clinical samples ranged from 8 to 675,885 copies/uL. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina MiSeq platform. A metagenomic method used random hexamer-adapters for amplification. Human gDNA was spiked with viral plasmids for metagenomic testing.

Procedures And Architectures
Multiplex PCR products were amplified in a secondary PCR for indexing. Electrophoresis was used to visualize potential positives by peak size. NGS libraries were interrogated for definitive virus identification. The mathematical model assumed 99% efficiency for RT-PCR. The multiplex PCR efficiency was estimated at 26% with UMIs. For single-strand cDNA, an efficiency of 6% was assumed. Mutations were detected using two independently developed algorithms. Mutations with frequencies greater than 60% were considered true. Intra-host mutations were analyzed with a 20% frequency cutoff. Background removal reagents were used to clean metagenomic libraries.

Key Results
RT-PCR was modeled to detect 4.8 copies at 95% probability. The multiplex PCR panel predicted a detection limit of 1.15 copies. Using both primer pools, the detection limit was 0.29 copies. Plasmid validation showed library peaks from 8,900 to 2.8 copies. Experimental detection probability for 1.1 copies was 56%. 95% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies. 98-99% coverage was achieved for samples with 22 to 675,885 copies. Sub-sampling to 150,000 reads maintained 93% genome coverage at 100X. The D614G mutation was found in 11 of 13 specimens. The metagenomic method recovered 96% of the SARS-CoV-2 genome. Viral bases constituted 16% of total recovered bases in metagenomics.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Multiplex PCR significantly improves sensitivity over standard RT-PCR. The method tolerates mutations in primer binding sites. High specificity was demonstrated against other human coronaviruses. The metagenomic method allows detection of novel pathogens. Low copy numbers require cautious interpretation of intra-host mutations.

Contradictions And Limitations
Low viral copy numbers may introduce false intra-host mutations. Sequencing depth affects the accuracy of low-frequency mutation detection. The saturation point for library yield may be lower in clinical samples. Metagenomic detection of other viruses requires further validation. Heat inactivation of samples can cause loss of viral particles.

Claims
The multiplex PCR method is more sensitive than RT-PCR for SARS-CoV-2 detection. The detection limit is 0.29 copies compared to 4.8 for RT-PCR. The method detects degraded viral genome fragments. Efficiency may be lower for single-strand cDNA templates. This improves diagnostic accuracy for low-viral-load cases.
The metagenomic method can identify SARS-CoV-2 in complex human backgrounds. 96% genome coverage was achieved with 0.6M reads. Viral targets were preferentially amplified over human genome. Validation for other respiratory viruses is still needed. This enables surveillance of emerging pathogens.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Sub-sampling analysis confirmed sufficient coverage at lower read depths. Two independent algorithms were used to validate mutation calls. Specificity was tested against other human coronaviruses.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the mathematical models for RT-PCR and multiplex PCR. Figure 2 shows validation results using plasmids. Figure 3 presents genome coverage and mutation analysis of clinical samples. Figure 4 details the metagenomic method performance. Supplemental Table 2 lists viral loads of the 13 specimens.

Three Takeaways
1. A multiplex PCR method detects SARS-CoV-2 at 0.29 copies. 2. Full genome sequencing was achieved from 8 to 675,885 copies. 3. A metagenomic approach enables detection of novel pathogens.

summary.title: A Combined Evidence Approach to Prioritize Nipah Virus Inhibitors
summary.authors: Nishi Kumari, Ayush Upadhyay, Kishan Kalia, Rakesh Kumar, Kanika Tuteja, Rani Paul, Eugenia Covernton, Tina Sharma, Vinod Scaria, Anshu Bhardwaj
summary.executive_summary: Nipah Virus (NiV) is a lethal pathogen with a case fatality rate exceeding 75%, yet no approved treatments exist. Current containment relies on isolation, and existing antivirals like ribavirin show contradictory or limited efficacy. This study addresses the lack of systematic evaluation for Nipah Virus Inhibitors (NVIs) by developing the Nipah Virus Inhibitor Knowledgebase (NVIK). The authors conducted a rigorous literature search, curating 182 NVIs, of which 98 are unique small molecule inhibitors. To prioritize these compounds for drug discovery, a combined evidence strategy was employed. This involved computing over 1800 physicochemical descriptors and comparing them against FDA-approved drugs and antiviral libraries. Additionally, compounds were filtered using PAINS and DruLito to assess toxicity and drug-likeness. An independent prioritization was performed based on the robustness of the assays used to identify the inhibitors. The results show that the NVIK library is chemically diverse, with most compounds being cyclic. While many NVIs exhibit physicochemical properties similar to FDA-approved drugs, only a few passed all DruLito filters. Specifically, NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 were highlighted for passing multiple filters and showing drug-like features. The study provides a web-based platform for the community to browse, search, and submit new NVIs, aiming to accelerate the development of therapeutic interventions for NiV and potentially other viruses.

claims.description: A combined evidence approach effectively prioritizes Nipah Virus Inhibitors.
The NVIK platform provides a comprehensive and accessible resource for NVIs.

To prioritize these compounds for drug discovery, a combined evidence strategy was employed. This involved computing over 1800 physicochemical descriptors and comparing them against FDA-approved drugs and antiviral libraries. Additionally, compounds were filtered using PAINS and DruLito to assess toxicity and drug-likeness. An independent prioritization was performed based on the robustness of the assays used to identify the inhibitors. The results show that the NVIK library is chemically diverse, with most compounds being cyclic. While many NVIs exhibit physicochemical properties similar to FDA-approved drugs, only a few passed all DruLito filters. Specifically, NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 were highlighted for passing multiple filters and showing drug-like features. The study provides a web-based platform for the community to browse, search, and submit new NVIs, aiming to accelerate the development of therapeutic interventions for NiV and potentially other viruses.

Research Context
Nipah Virus is a severe public health concern with high mortality. Current treatment options are limited and ineffective. Ribavirin has shown contradictory results in reducing mortality. Previous inhibitor databases lack systematic evaluation for NiV. There is an urgent need for accelerated R&D for NiV.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to systematically evaluate reported Nipah virus inhibitors. A combined evidence strategy is used to prioritize drug-like compounds. The hypothesis is that robust assays and drug-likeness filters can identify viable candidates. The goal is to create a structured knowledgebase for further development. The platform allows for continuous community curation and analysis.

Methodological Details
PubMed and Google were used to collect inhibitor data. 838 papers were initially shortlisted using the keyword 'Nipah'. A scoring system was applied to prioritize papers for curation. The final knowledgebase contains 182 entries. 98 unique small molecule inhibitors were identified from the 125 small molecule entries. EC50/IC50 values were available for 70 of the compounds. Data quality was ensured by an independent re-curation team. The platform was built using LAMP server technology. 1875 descriptors were calculated using PaDel software. Clustering was performed using Jarvis-Patrick clustering with a 0.15 threshold.

Procedures And Architectures
The NVIK platform allows for simple, query, and structure-based searches. Users can query using SMILES, SDF, and MOL formats. Near neighbours were identified using NNeib version 5.12.0. Clusters were obtained using Jarp version 6.0.2. Visualization was done using customized CIRCOS and Cytoscape. DruLito was used to screen compounds based on eight filters. PAINS filter was applied to study toxicity profiles. Compounds were compared to FDA approved drugs and Enamine antivirals. An independent evaluation based on assay robustness was performed. The web interface provides browsing of physicochemical properties.

Key Results
The IC50/EC50 values range from 0.47 nM to 7562710 nM. Clustering of 98 NVIs resulted in 90 clusters. 84 clusters were singletons, indicating high chemical diversity. 34 NVIs showed structural similarity to 76 FDA approved drugs. Only two of 91 compounds passed all DruLito filters except CMC. 11 NVIs were prioritized based on assay robustness. NVIC0025, NVIC0032, and NVIC0048 passed 6 DruLito filters. NVIC0048 displayed high overlap with physicochemical parameter ranges. NVIC0032 exhibited better activity among the shortlisted compounds. The platform currently hosts 182 NVIs with 98 small molecules.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The high diversity of NVIs offers a wide spectrum for drug development. Near neighbours with different molecular weights may share pharmacophore features. Prioritization based on assay robustness adds a layer of reliability. The platform serves as a centralized resource for the scientific community. These compounds may also be useful for other viruses.

Contradictions And Limitations
Ribavirin results are contradictory, with optimistic ones below 50% reduction. 57 entries were peptides or lacked complete information. Only a few compounds passed all DruLito filters. The study relies on literature curation, which may have gaps. No clinical trials are currently underway for NiV.

Claims
A combined evidence approach effectively prioritizes Nipah Virus Inhibitors. 11 NVIs were prioritized based on assay robustness. 3 compounds passed 6 DruLito filters. Only two compounds passed all filters except CMC. This strategy can accelerate drug discovery for NiV.
The NVIK platform provides a comprehensive and accessible resource for NVIs. The platform allows submission of new inhibitors. It contains 182 entries with detailed physicochemical data. Some entries lack complete information. It facilitates community-driven curation and analysis.

Data And Code Availability
Data is available at http://vinodscaria.rnabiology.org/nipah. The platform allows for public submission of new compounds.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Data quality was checked by an independent team. Errors were marked and verified by both teams.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the unique fields in the database. Figure 2 depicts the distribution of physicochemical properties. Figure 3 compares NVIs with FDA approved drugs and antivirals. Figure 4 shows the DruLito filter results. Table 2 lists the prioritized NVIs and their properties.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the NVIK knowledgebase with 182 NVIs. 2. The strongest evidence is the prioritization of 11 NVIs via robust assays. 3. The future path is community-driven curation and drug development.

summary.title: ProNetView-ccRCC: A web-based portal to interactively explore clear cell renal cell carcinoma proteogenomics networks
summary.authors: Selim Kalayci; Francesca Petralia; Pei Wang; Zeynep H Gümüş
summary.executive_summary: The National Cancer Institute's Clinical Proteomics Tumor Analysis Consortium (CPTAC) has generated comprehensive proteogenomic data for various cancer types, including clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). While gene/protein regulatory networks derived from these profiles offer system-level insights, visualizing and navigating these complex, high-dimensional networks remains a significant challenge. Existing tools often provide static 2D visualizations that are ill-suited for interactive exploration or integrating clinical metadata. To address this gap, the authors introduce ProNetView-ccRCC, an open-access, web-based portal designed for the intuitive visual exploration of ccRCC phosphopeptide co-expression networks. The portal features a 3D network exploration interface built on the Three.js framework, allowing users to rotate and zoom through a network comprising 3,614 genes and 30 functional pathway-enriched modules. Users can interactively query specific genes, such as the oncogene ERG, to view their connections, associated phosphopeptides, and correlations with clinical variables like tumor grade. The tool integrates metadata from CPTAC studies, including pathway enrichment results and clinical outcomes, enabling researchers to link molecular network structures with phenotypic data. By utilizing standard client-side libraries like D3.js and Bootstrap, ProNetView-ccRCC runs on modern web browsers without requiring additional plugins. This resource aims to facilitate hypothesis generation and data interpretation for the cancer research community by providing a centralized, interactive environment for exploring the complex regulatory factories underlying ccRCC.

claims.description: ProNetView-ccRCC provides an effective interactive environment for exploring complex proteogenomic networks.

Research Context
CPTAC has performed comprehensive proteogenomic characterizations of multiple cancer types. Gene/protein regulatory networks derived from these profiles serve as useful tools for system-level understanding. It remains a challenge to effectively visualize and navigate the resulting network models. There is a pressing need for a new open community resource tool. Current network visualization tools are mainly used for static 2D images. These tools are not well suited for user-initiated interactive network explorations. A centralized platform customized for CPTAC co-expression networks is necessary.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to provide an intuitive visual exploration tool for CPTAC ccRCC networks. The tool should allow users to navigate complex phosphopeptide co-expression networks. Users need to query associations between phosphopeptide abundance and clinical variables. The portal must integrate functional pathway-enriched network modules with the main network. The system should enable quick, user-intuitive interactions with the network topology. The goal is to facilitate hypothesis generation for future studies.

Methodological Details
The network characterizes co-expression patterns among 20,976 phosphopeptides in ccRCC. The network was derived using a random-forest based network construction algorithm. Network modules were derived using the Glay clustering algorithm. 30 modules containing at least 20 genes were identified. Pathway enrichment analysis was performed via Fisher Exact test. The portal displays 3,614 genes in the co-expression network.

The portal displays a network comprised of 3,614 genes. The network includes 30 functional pathway-enriched network modules. Six modules were significantly associated with biological pathways. The oncogene ERG is associated with VEGF response. ERG shows an association with tumor grade with p-value 0.003. The FDR for the ERG-tumor grade association is 0.118. ERG is directly connected to 11 genes within the Angiogenesis module. ERG maps to 5 different peptides.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The tool helps understand the phosphopeptide network in the context of markers. It guides hypothesis generation for future studies. The portal facilitates researchers with varying computational skill levels. It allows sharing and communicating results effectively. The integration of clinical variables aids in interpreting molecular mechanisms.

Contradictions And Limitations
The tool relies on standard libraries and does not require plug-ins. The network is based on phosphopeptide co-expression, which may not capture all regulatory mechanisms. The study focuses specifically on ccRCC, limiting generalizability to other cancer types.

Claims
ProNetView-ccRCC provides an effective interactive environment for exploring complex proteogenomic networks. The portal enables quick, user-intuitive visual interactions. The portal is an open-access freely available resource. The URL is http://ccrcc.cptac-network-view.org/.

Figure 1A displays the global ccRCC tumor phosphoproteomics co-expression network. Figure 1B links the network to functional network modules. Figure 1C shows the query for the oncogene ERG. Figure 2A displays the Angiogenesis enriched module network. Figure 2B displays associated gene-level meta-data for a node. Figure 3A displays the interactive table listing enriched pathways.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is an interactive 3D web portal for ccRCC proteogenomic networks. 2. The strongest evidence is the integration of 3,614 genes and clinical metadata. 3. The future path is facilitating hypothesis generation for the research community.

summary.title: 3D Genome Analysis Identifies Enhancer Hijacking Mechanism for High-Risk Factors in Human T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
summary.authors: Lu Yang; Fengling Chen; Haichuan Zhu; Yang Chen; Bingjie Dong; Minglei Shi; Weitao Wang; Qian Jiang; Leping Zhang; Xiaojun Huang; Michael Q Zhang; Hong Wu
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the role of 3D genome alterations in the pathogenesis and prognosis of T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). By integrating Hi-C and RNA-seq data from 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy controls, the authors demonstrate that 3D genome organization hierarchically classifies T-ALL subtypes according to T cell differentiation trajectories. The analysis reveals that 3D genome alterations are associated with nearly 45% of upregulated genes in T-ALL. A key finding is the identification of 34 previously unrecognized translocations in noncoding regions and 44 new translocation-mediated loops. These structural changes facilitate enhancer hijacking, particularly of the HOXA cluster, leading to ectopic expression of specific transcription factors. The study further dissects the heterogeneity of HOXA-positive T-ALLs, distinguishing between 3'HOXA+ and 5'HOXA+ subgroups based on TAD boundary shifts and enhancer interactions. Clinically, the authors show that ectopic expression of HOXA11-A13, but not other HOXA genes, is associated with immature phenotypes and poor survival outcomes. The findings suggest that 3D genome rewiring, specifically through translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking, drives the specific pathogenic gene expression profiles of T-ALL subgroups. Furthermore, the association of HOXA11-A13 positivity with JAK-STAT pathway mutations and poor prognosis suggests that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this high-risk patient group. This work provides a mechanistic framework linking chromatin architecture to oncogene activation and clinical outcomes in T-ALL.

claims.description: 3D genome alterations are a major driver of gene dysregulation in T-ALL.
Translocations cause enhancer hijacking, leading to specific T-ALL subtypes.
Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression is a marker for poor prognosis.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the role of 3D genome alterations in the pathogenesis and prognosis of T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). By integrating Hi-C and RNA-seq data from 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy controls, the authors demonstrate that 3D genome organization hierarchically classifies T-ALL subtypes according to T cell differentiation trajectories. The analysis reveals that 3D genome alterations are associated with nearly 45% of upregulated genes in T-ALL. A key finding is the identification of 34 previously unrecognized translocations in noncoding regions and 44 new translocation-mediated loops. These structural changes facilitate enhancer hijacking, particularly of the HOXA cluster, leading to ectopic expression of specific transcription factors. The study further dissects the heterogeneity of HOXA-positive T-ALLs, distinguishing between 3'HOXA+ and 5'HOXA+ subgroups based on TAD boundary shifts and enhancer interactions. Clinically, the authors show that ectopic expression of HOXA11-A13, but not other HOXA genes, is associated with immature phenotypes and poor survival outcomes. The findings suggest that 3D genome rewiring, specifically through translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking, drives the specific pathogenic gene expression profiles of T-ALL subgroups. Furthermore, the association of HOXA11-A13 positivity with JAK-STAT pathway mutations and poor prognosis suggests that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this high-risk patient group. This work provides a mechanistic framework linking chromatin architecture to oncogene activation and clinical outcomes in T-ALL.

Research Context
Recent studies have demonstrated that 3D genome alterations play important roles in tumorigenesis. However, how such alterations may provide key insights into T-ALL patients is largely unknown. The study aims to integrate 3D genome alterations with differentially expressed genes. Previous work established that 3D genome changes affect hematological malignancies.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how 3D genome alterations influence T-ALL development and prognosis. The authors hypothesize that 3D genome organization classifies T-ALL subtypes by differentiation stage. They predict that translocations will lead to enhancer hijacking of oncogenic genes. The study tests if ectopic HOXA expression correlates with poor clinical outcomes.

Methodological Details
The study recruited 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy T cell controls. Leukemia blast cells were purified by FACS using specific antibody markers. RNA-seq libraries were prepared using the TruSeq RNA Library Prep Kit v2. Paired-end RNA-seq reads were generated with an average depth of 15 million read pairs. Hi-C was performed on one million cells per sample using the BL-Hi-C protocol. Hi-C raw data were processed using the in-house HiCpipe framework. Compartment analysis used eigenvector command of Juicer under 100 kb resolution. TAD boundaries were calculated by the Insulation score method on pooled 40 kb matrices. Loops were called by HiCCUPS and differential loops adapted from Douglas et al. Translocations were detected using an adapted version of hic_breakfinder. The average depth of patient Hi-C samples was 486 million read pairs. ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data were processed using Bowtie2 and MACS2. DESeq2 was applied to identify differentially expressed genes with FDR <0.01.

Procedures And Architectures
The study utilized a multi-omics approach integrating Hi-C and RNA-seq. 3D genome features included compartments, TADs, and loops. Translocation-mediated loops were manually recorded on interchromosome Hi-C maps. Breakpoints were refined to single base-pair resolution using chimeric reads. Enhancer hijacking was identified by linking translocated enhancers to target genes. The HOXA cluster was analyzed for TAD boundary shifts and enhancer interactions. Clinical outcomes were analyzed in a cohort of T-ALL patients. Multivariate analysis was used to assess independent predictors of survival.

Key Results
3D genome alterations were associated with nearly 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL. Approximately 29% of the DEGs were associated with 3D genome alterations. The study identified 34 previously unrecognized translocations in noncoding regions. 44 new loops were formed between translocated chromosomes. Nearly 78% of translocation-mediated loops with CTCF motifs were linked to convergent motifs. ETP ALL samples were arrested at the LMPP to Thy1 stages. Non-ETP samples were arrested at the Thy2 to Thy4 stages. A strong positive correlation (0.685) was found between gene expression and loop strength. HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity was associated with poor overall and event-free survivals. HOXA13+ status served as an independent predictor for overall survival. HOXA11-A13+ cases were characterized by DN and ETP phenotypes. A higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations was observed in HOXA11-A13+ cases.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
3D genome organization represents different frozen stages of T cell development. Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking drives ectopic transcription factor activation. Different fusion events preferentially alter the 3D genome interactome within the HOXA cluster. The findings highlight the role of 3D genome alterations in T-ALL etiology.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study relies on a small sample size of 18 T-ALL patients. The association of HOXA9 with poor prognosis was not supported in this cohort. The mechanism for diverse HOXA expression patterns by fusion proteins is complex. The study focuses on newly diagnosed patients, limiting generalizability to relapsed cases.

Claims
3D genome alterations are a major driver of gene dysregulation in T-ALL. 3D genome alterations were associated with nearly 45% of upregulated genes. Structural changes at all 3 levels were seen in key transcription factors. Only 29% of all DEGs were associated with 3D genome alterations. 3D genome analysis can serve as a biological readout for functional impact.
Translocations cause enhancer hijacking, leading to specific T-ALL subtypes. 34 novel translocations and 44 new loops were identified. Enhancer hijacking of HOXA cluster was observed.  Translocation-mediated loops may be mediated by loop extrusion.
Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression is a marker for poor prognosis. HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity was associated with poor survival. HOXA13+ was an independent predictor for overall survival. HOXA9, a previous biomarker, was not associated with poor outcomes. Anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this high-risk group.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used multiple levels of 3D genome analysis (compartment, TAD, loop). Differential loop detection was adapted to minimize bias by distance ranges. Translocations were manually assessed to filter false positives.

Ethical Considerations
Samples were collected under the protocol approved by the ethics committee. Healthy donor samples were obtained under ethics committee approval.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows 3D genome and transcriptome clustering of T-ALL subtypes. Figure 2 illustrates the T cell developmental trajectory projection. Figure 3 details translocation-mediated loops and enhancer hijacking. Figure 4 analyzes HOXA cluster TAD boundaries and enhancer interactions. Figure 5 maps breakpoints for HOXA translocation cases. Figure 6 presents clinical outcome associations with HOXA expression.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of 3D genome alterations driving T-ALL heterogeneity. 2. The strongest evidence is the link between HOXA11-A13 expression and poor survival. 3. The future path involves using anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors for high-risk T-ALL.

summary.title: The Foster method: Rapid and non-invasive detection of clinically significant American Foulbrood disease levels using eDNA sampling and a dual-target qPCR assay, with its potential for other hive pathogens
summary.authors: John F Mackay, Rebecca E Hewett, Noa T Smith, Tammy L Waters, John S Scandrett
summary.executive_summary: American Foulbrood (AFB), caused by Paenibacillus larvae, is a devastating honeybee disease often missed due to subjective visual diagnosis and laborious sampling methods requiring hive dismantling. This study introduces the 'Foster method,' a rapid, non-invasive environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling technique using hive entrance swabs combined with a dual-target qPCR assay (AFBduo) to detect clinically significant AFB levels. The AFBduo assay targets the single-copy ftsZ gene and the multi-copy 16S gene, offering high sensitivity (down to 4 copies) and specificity. The study evaluated P. larvae levels in nurse bees, whole baseboard swabs, and entrance swabs across three cohorts of hives in New Zealand quarantine apiaries. Results demonstrated that entrance swab spore levels correlated strongly with clinical disease status. A spore quantity of 565,000 or more indicated a 95% probability of clinical signs. Notably, the method detected pre-clinical infections in hives without visible symptoms, allowing for early intervention. The study also validated a pooling strategy for swab eluates to reduce costs and time. The Foster method eliminates the need to dismantle hives, offering a scalable solution for AFB surveillance and potential application to other bee pathogens and incursion pests.

claims.description: The Foster method enables rapid, non-invasive detection of clinically significant AFB levels.
The dual-target qPCR assay provides high sensitivity and specificity.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
American Foulbrood (AFB), caused by Paenibacillus larvae, is a devastating honeybee disease often missed due to subjective visual diagnosis and laborious sampling methods requiring hive dismantling. This study introduces the 'Foster method,' a rapid, non-invasive environmental DNA (eDNA) sampling technique using hive entrance swabs combined with a dual-target qPCR assay (AFBduo) to detect clinically significant AFB levels. The AFBduo assay targets the single-copy ftsZ gene and the multi-copy 16S gene, offering high sensitivity (down to 4 copies) and specificity. The study evaluated P. larvae levels in nurse bees, whole baseboard swabs, and entrance swabs across three cohorts of hives in New Zealand quarantine apiaries. Results demonstrated that entrance swab spore levels correlated strongly with clinical disease status. A spore quantity of 565,000 or more indicated a 95% probability of clinical signs. Notably, the method detected pre-clinical infections in hives without visible symptoms, allowing for early intervention. The study also validated a pooling strategy for swab eluates to reduce costs and time. The Foster method eliminates the need to dismantle hives, offering a scalable solution for AFB surveillance and potential application to other bee pathogens and incursion pests.

Research Context
American Foulbrood is a destructive disease caused by Paenibacillus larvae spores. Current diagnosis relies on subjective visual symptoms and laborious hive dismantling. Previous molecular methods often lacked quantitative data or required invasive sampling. There is a need for rapid, non-invasive detection of clinically significant infections.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to evaluate a novel eDNA sampling method using hive entrance swabs. It hypothesizes that entrance swab spore levels correlate with clinical AFB status. The goal is to detect infections before visual symptoms appear. The method is intended to be applicable to other bee pathogens.

Methodological Details
Samples were collected from five quarantine apiaries in New Zealand. Sampling occurred two-monthly from late 2018 to early 2020. Sample types included nurse bees, whole baseboard swabs, and entrance swabs. Bees were collected from brood frames using 50 mL sterile containers. Swabs were moistened in sterile water and swabbed for three to five seconds. DNA extraction used a column-based kit with beadbeating. Ten bees were used per sample for ease of handling. A synthetic DNA standard was used for quantification. Quantification standards ranged from 10^6 to 2 copies per µL. Statistical analysis used binary logistic regression in Minitab.

Procedures And Architectures
The AFBduo assay is a dual-target qPCR for P. larvae. Targets include the single-copy ftsZ gene and multi-copy 16S gene. Hydrolysis probe qPCR allows quantification via fluorescent wavelengths. An internal control is included in an additional detection channel. Bee DNA extraction involved homogenization in a Mini Beadbeater 16. Swab extraction used zirconia silica beads and DXL buffer. Spore levels were calculated using the ftsZ gene amplification efficiency. Pooling of swab eluates was tested to reduce costs.

Key Results
The assay detected down to 4 copies per 10 µL reaction. Amplification efficiencies were 94% for ftsZ and 96% for 16S. Linearity was excellent over 7 orders of magnitude (r = 0.998). 45 hives were sampled in the first cohort. 8 hives showed clinical signs in the first cohort. 23 hives were tested in the second cohort. 4 hives showed clinical signs in the second cohort. A spore quantity of 565,000 indicated 95% probability of clinical signs. Binary logistic regression showed a strong relationship (p = 0.00). Hive 11 showed pre-clinical infection detected by qPCR.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The Foster method allows non-invasive detection of clinically significant AFB. Entrance swabs provide predictive information comparable to bee samples. The method can detect pre-clinical infections before visual symptoms. This approach is applicable to other bee pathogens and pests.

Contradictions And Limitations
New hiveware may delay spore accumulation on the entrance. Bees may carry high spore levels while hiveware shows low levels. Further research is needed to refine clinical spore thresholds. The accumulation rate of spores on the hive requires assessment.

Claims
The Foster method enables rapid, non-invasive detection of clinically significant AFB levels. Entrance swabs correlated with clinical disease status. Pre-clinical infections were detected in Hive 11. New hiveware may delay spore detection on the entrance. Infected hives can be dealt with more quickly.
The dual-target qPCR assay provides high sensitivity and specificity. Detection limit was 4 copies per 10 µL. Efficiencies were high for both targets. 16S copy number variability affects quantification reliability. The assay is suitable for diagnostic and surveillance purposes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Pooling swab eluates into groups of eight and twelve was tested. Single hives with high AFB were detected within pools. Internal controls confirmed DNA quality in swab samples.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 shows progression of P. larvae levels in three colonies. Table 2 compares nurse bee and entrance swab levels. Table 3 shows results of pooled swab eluate testing. Table 4 compares P. larvae levels in different sample types.

Three Takeaways
1. The Foster method uses entrance swabs for non-invasive AFB detection. 2. A spore count of 565,000 predicts 95% clinical probability. 3. The method is applicable to other bee pathogens and pests.

summary.title: Efficient and Flexible Integration of Variant Characteristics in Rare Variant Association Studies Using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation
summary.authors: Hana Susak, Laura Serra-Saurina, Raquel Rabionet Janssen, Laura Domènech, Mattia Bosio, Francesc Muyas, Xavier Estivill, Georgia Escaramís, Stephan Ossowski
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces BATI, a novel Bayesian rare variant association test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA), and the rvGWAS framework. Rare variant association studies (RVAS) often lack power in small to medium-sized cohorts, particularly when genetic variation explains a small fraction of phenotypic variance. Existing methods like burden tests and variance component tests (e.g., SKAT, MiST) have limitations regarding heterogeneous effects or computational intensity. BATI addresses these by allowing the integration of individual or variant-specific features as covariates while efficiently performing inference based on full model estimation. The authors demonstrate that BATI outperforms established RVAS methods on realistic, semi-synthetic whole-exome sequencing cohorts, especially when using meaningful biological context such as functional annotation. Specifically, BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios where competing tests fail, such as when risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. The rvGWAS framework integrates BATI with five existing tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR) to support rare variant association for genes or other biological units. Applying rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study, the authors identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The study highlights that leveraging variant characteristics and fast INLA estimation significantly improves detection power for rare variants in complex diseases.

claims.description: BATI outperforms existing RVAS methods when using biological context.
rvGWAS facilitates user-friendly analysis of RVAS.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces BATI, a novel Bayesian rare variant association test using Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (INLA), and the rvGWAS framework. Rare variant association studies (RVAS) often lack power in small to medium-sized cohorts, particularly when genetic variation explains a small fraction of phenotypic variance. Existing methods like burden tests and variance component tests (e.g., SKAT, MiST) have limitations regarding heterogeneous effects or computational intensity. BATI addresses these by allowing the integration of individual or variant-specific features as covariates while efficiently performing inference based on full model estimation. The authors demonstrate that BATI outperforms established RVAS methods on realistic, semi-synthetic whole-exome sequencing cohorts, especially when using meaningful biological context such as functional annotation. Specifically, BATI achieves power above 75% in scenarios where competing tests fail, such as when risk variants explain less than 0.5% of phenotypic variance. The rvGWAS framework integrates BATI with five existing tests (Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR) to support rare variant association for genes or other biological units. Applying rvGWAS to a Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study, the authors identified eight candidate predisposition genes, including EHMT2 and COPS7A. The study highlights that leveraging variant characteristics and fast INLA estimation significantly improves detection power for rare variants in complex diseases.

Research Context
Rare variants play an important role in the etiology of complex diseases. Next-generation sequencing facilitates association of rare variants with complex diseases. Rare variant association studies still lack power in small to medium-sized cohorts. Traditional statistical methods like GWAS require extremely large sample sizes for rare variants. Burden tests are powerful when effects are one-sided, which is rarely the case. Variance component tests like SKAT address heterogeneous effects among rare variants. MiST proposed a mixed effects test considering biological characteristics of variants. MiST requires multiple integration, making it computationally intensive for genome-wide scans. INLA is a non-sampling based numerical approximation procedure faster than MCMC. INLA is more accurate than MCMC when given the same computational resources.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to efficiently integrate variant characteristics in RVAS. The hypothesis is that a Bayesian approach using INLA improves power. BATI allows integration of individual or variant-specific features as covariates. BATI performs inference based on full model estimation efficiently. It is predicted that BATI outperforms existing methods with biological context. BATI should achieve high power when risk variants explain small variance. The framework rvGWAS supports analysis of genes or other biological units. BATI should cope with complex population structure and confounders. Difference in deviance information criterion is proposed for model selection.

Methodological Details
The study uses a novel Bayesian rare variant Association Test using INLA. INLA was implemented using the R-INLA project version 17.06.20. The method builds a hierarchical Bayesian approach to the GLMM. BATI integrates categorical and numeric characteristics of genetic variants. Realistic semi-synthetic simulations of whole-exome sequencing case-control studies were developed. The simulator combines real WES datasets with known risk variants. Predisposition variants from ClinVar were introduced into VCF files of cases. Two large datasets were used: 1000GP and an Iberian cohort. From 1000GP, half of the samples were selected as cases. For the Iberian cohort, one third were selected as cases. Breast cancer risk variants annotated as exonic or splicing were queried. Variants with MAF higher than 0.01 were removed. RVAS tests were performed on randomly split cohorts without risk variants. Significance thresholds were obtained for 5%, 0.1%, and 0.01% TIER. The median from 10 random splits was used as thresholds. A Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia study was analyzed using rvGWAS.

Procedures And Architectures
The model assumes N individuals with observed phenotypes in an exponential family. INLA produces a numerical approximation to the posteriors of interest. The null hypothesis assumes no genetic effects on the phenotype. The alternative hypothesis assumes a genetic effect on the phenotype. Deviance Information Criteria (DIC) is used for model goodness of fit. Difference in DIC between H0 and H1 is used for model selection. Simulations are used to evaluate the ability of ΔDIC to choose models. Individuals are randomly assigned to cases or controls for type I error. S datasets are generated by shuffling cases and controls. S = 10 was used for model selection in the benchmark study. rvGWAS integrates quality control, filtering, and detection of data stratification. rvGWAS includes Burden, SKAT-O, KBAC, MiST, HBMR, and BATI. The simulator introduces predisposition variants into the VCF files. Power analysis was conducted across 100 simulations for each gene.

Key Results
BATI outperforms established RVAS methods on realistic semi-synthetic cohorts. BATI achieves power above 75% when risk variants explain <0.5% variance. BATI's performance is stable despite smaller cohort size in Iberian cohort. At 0.5% VE and 0.01% TIER, BATI achieves power close to 100%. BATI calls most genes with TIER 0.01% even at VE of 0.5%. BATI calls all genes at TIER 0.1% with >80% power. Burden, KBAC, and SKAT-O fail to call BRCA2 at low VE. HBMR fails to call BARD1, CHEK2, and PALB2 at TIER 0.1%. MiST failed to identify any risk gene at low VE or low TIER. Applying rvGWAS to CLL identified eight candidate predisposition genes. EHMT2 and COPS7A were identified as candidate predisposition genes. BATI strongly benefits from inclusion of variant characteristics as covariates.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
BATI leverages both categorical and numerical variant characteristics. BATI gains power if risk genes contain mostly LoF variants. BATI performs at least as good as other methods for missense variants. Semi-synthetic benchmarks provide more realistic noise levels than pure simulations. Differences between methods are profound when variance explained is low. MiST performed poorly due to zero-inflated p-values from low variant counts. Combining Burden and SKAT-type methods with different approaches is beneficial. BATI represents a flexible testing approach for future extension.

Contradictions And Limitations
MiST showed favorable results on purely artificial benchmark sets. MiST performed poorly on realistic WES cohorts. Simulated variant data lacks complexity and noise-level of real data. Previous benchmarks resulted in overly optimistic performances. Model estimation with complex data structures is computationally heavy. The study focuses on case-control studies using WES or WGS.

Claims
BATI outperforms existing RVAS methods when using biological context. BATI outperforms established RVAS methods on realistic cohorts. BATI achieves power above 75% in low variance scenarios. MiST showed favorable results on purely artificial benchmark sets. BATI is a flexible testing approach for future extension.
rvGWAS facilitates user-friendly analysis of RVAS. rvGWAS integrates quality control and filtering. rvGWAS includes multiple existing and new tests.  Applying rvGWAS to CLL identified eight candidate genes.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
BATI's performance is stable despite smaller cohort size. BATI calls most genes at TIER 0.01% even at low VE. BATI calls all genes at TIER 0.1% with >80% power.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 3 shows gene-wise power analysis for the 1000GP cohort. Table 2 presents power results for different tests and genes. Supplementary S6 Fig shows estimated significance thresholds. Supplementary S8 Fig shows benchmark results for the Iberian cohort.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the BATI test using INLA for RVAS. 2. The strongest evidence is BATI's power above 75% in low variance scenarios. 3. The future path is extending BATI with more covariates.
