summary.title: Activation of Macrophages by CpG DNA and LPS: an FTIR Spectroscopic Study
summary.authors: Emrulla Spahiu, Senol Dogan, Jörg Schnauß, Mayda Gursel, Feride Severcan
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the global molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells upon activation with CpG DNA and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) using Attenuated Total Reflectance (ATR) Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. While CpG DNA and LPS are known to trigger innate immune responses, their impact on the relative amounts of nucleic acids, lipids, and proteins has not been previously characterized using bulk spectroscopic methods. The researchers employed ATR-FTIR to monitor cellular dynamics at 10 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours, and 6 hours post-treatment. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) revealed that PC-1 accounted for 83% of the variability, guiding the selection of specific spectral peaks for detailed analysis. The results indicate that both CpG DNA and LPS treatments lead to an early increase in total nucleic acid concentration. Specifically, RNA synthesis, identified by the ribose vibration peak at 915 cm⁻¹, occurs rapidly in the first two hours, followed by DNA synthesis starting around 6 hours post-CpG stimulation. In contrast, LPS treatment primarily induced RNA synthesis without significant DNA changes, consistent with its anti-proliferative nature. Protein analysis, using Amide I and II bands, showed a rapid initial increase in total protein concentration that leveled off after two hours. Furthermore, both stimuli triggered a significant increase in fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol, suggesting a shared pathway of de novo lipogenesis during macrophage activation. This study demonstrates that FTIR spectroscopy serves as a rapid, non-destructive, and independent modality to monitor the activation dynamics of macrophages, providing a holistic view of metabolic shifts that complement traditional omics techniques.

claims.description: FTIR spectroscopy can detect global molecular changes in macrophages upon CpG DNA and LPS activation.
RNA synthesis precedes DNA synthesis during CpG DNA-induced macrophage activation.
Both CpG DNA and LPS induce de novo lipogenesis in macrophages.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the global molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells upon activation with CpG DNA and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) using Attenuated Total Reflectance (ATR) Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy. While CpG DNA and LPS are known to trigger innate immune responses, their impact on the relative amounts of nucleic acids, lipids, and proteins has not been previously characterized using bulk spectroscopic methods. The researchers employed ATR-FTIR to monitor cellular dynamics at 10 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours, and 6 hours post-treatment. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) revealed that PC-1 accounted for 83% of the variability, guiding the selection of specific spectral peaks for detailed analysis. The results indicate that both CpG DNA and LPS treatments lead to an early increase in total nucleic acid concentration. Specifically, RNA synthesis, identified by the ribose vibration peak at 915 cm⁻¹, occurs rapidly in the first two hours, followed by DNA synthesis starting around 6 hours post-CpG stimulation. In contrast, LPS treatment primarily induced RNA synthesis without significant DNA changes, consistent with its anti-proliferative nature. Protein analysis, using Amide I and II bands, showed a rapid initial increase in total protein concentration that leveled off after two hours. Furthermore, both stimuli triggered a significant increase in fatty acids, triglycerides, and cholesterol, suggesting a shared pathway of de novo lipogenesis during macrophage activation. This study demonstrates that FTIR spectroscopy serves as a rapid, non-destructive, and independent modality to monitor the activation dynamics of macrophages, providing a holistic view of metabolic shifts that complement traditional omics techniques.

Research Context
FTIR spectroscopy allows non-destructive, rapid, and high-throughput analysis of biological systems. The infrared spectrum serves as a fingerprint for all metabolites of the cell system. Macrophages constitute the front line of the immune system defending the organism. CpG DNA triggers proliferation of macrophages and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines. LPS is a main constituent of the cell wall of gram-negative bacteria. How CpG ODN-mediated immune activation impacts relative amounts of metabolites has not been studied. Omics techniques require complex sample preparation steps that can alter chemical ratios. Bulk FTIR analysis provides a broad view of relative amounts of metabolites.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to monitor molecular changes in murine macrophage RAW 264.7 cells. The cells were activated with CpG DNA and lipopolysaccharide (LPS). The hypothesis is that CpG ODN-mediated activation leads to global molecular changes. These changes are expected to be detectable by FTIR spectroscopy. The study seeks to identify sources of variation using PCA analysis. It predicts that CpG DNA and LPS increase total nucleic acid concentration. DNA synthesis is hypothesized to follow RNA synthesis in time. Both stimuli are expected to increase concentrations of fatty acids and cholesterol.

Methodological Details
Murine macrophage-like RAW 264.7 cells were cultured at 37 °C. Cells were grown in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium supplemented with 10% FBS. Cells were resuspended at a concentration of 2x10^6/mL. The control group was treated with phosphate-buffered saline (0.9% PBS). The CpG DNA group was treated with 1 µM K3 ODN. The LPS group was treated with 0.5 µg/ml LPS. Measurements were taken at 10 min, 30 min, 2 h, and 6 h. Samples were washed with sterile PBS to remove organic compounds. Infrared interferograms were collected using a Perkin-Elmer Spectrum One FTIR spectrometer. The ATR unit used a Diamond-ZnSe crystal. Spectra were recorded in the 4000-650 cm -1 region at 25°C. Cell samples of 1 µl were dried with mild N2 flux. The best signal-to-noise ratio was achieved with 128 scans. Spectral resolution was set to 2 cm -1. Replicates (n=5) were used in data analysis.

Procedures And Architectures
Post-processing included 13-point Savitzky-Golay smoothing and baseline correction. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was performed using Unscrambler 11.0 software. PCA was conducted on the 3000-650 cm -1 region. Peak assignment used center of weight measurements and literature comparison. Concentration studies were carried out by integrating curves under peaks. Shapiro-Wilk and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests determined the normality of datasets. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 8.3. The ATR surface was cleaned using a water-ethanol-water sequence.

Key Results
PC-1 gave a variability of 83% in the PCA analysis. PC-2 had a variability of 11%. CpG DNA stimulation induced significant changes in nucleic acid content from 10 min to 6 h. The RNA-specific peak at 915 cm -1 increased significantly from the first minutes. This RNA increase was maintained until 2 h after stimulation. DNA synthesis started from 6 h after stimulation with CpG DNA. LPS increased total RNA concentration up to 2 h post-stimulation. Total protein content of CpG DNA treated cells increased from 10 min to 2 h. The initial increase in protein concentration reduced starting from 2 h. There was a very significant increase in triglycerides and cholesterol from the first minutes. LPS stimulation elevated triglycerides and cholesterol concentration after 10 min. A significant increase was observed in fatty acid concentration.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The RNA-specific peak allows defining the activation state at the first minutes. LPS inhibits DNA synthesis and elicits cell cycle arrest in macrophages. The decrease in protein content may be due to secretion or oxidative stress. The increase in lipids points to de novo lipogenesis in pro-inflammatory reactions. A shared metabolite (Acetoacetyl-CoA) links fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis. FTIR spectroscopy serves as an independent modality to monitor activation dynamics. The study provides an aerial view of total protein fate.

Contradictions And Limitations
The absorbance of IR light by water is a limitation of infrared spectroscopy. The degree to which specific pathways contribute to protein loss is unknown.

Claims
FTIR spectroscopy can detect global molecular changes in macrophages upon CpG DNA and LPS activation. PCA identified sources of variation to follow with detailed spectral analysis. CpG DNA and LPS treatment increase total nucleic acid concentration. Water absorbance superimposes other signals of the aqueous cell systems. FTIR is a rapid, non-invasive tool for monitoring immune activation.
RNA synthesis precedes DNA synthesis during CpG DNA-induced macrophage activation. RNA-specific peak shows activation state in early periods. DNA synthesis starts from 6 h after stimulation. LPS does not show significant DNA changes after 6 h. This temporal sequence helps define the kinetics of immune response.
Both CpG DNA and LPS induce de novo lipogenesis in macrophages. Both activated groups increase concentration of fatty acids and cholesterol. This points to a shared synthesis pathway.  Lipid metabolism is a key component of macrophage activation.

Data And Code Availability
The protocol is available online.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
PCA was used to reduce dimensionality and draw logical conclusions. Replicates (n=5) were used to ensure statistical significance.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows PCA Scores and Loadings Plots. Figure 2 shows nucleic acid peak integrations. Figure 3 shows Amide I and II peak integrations. Figure 4 shows lipid peak integrations. Table 1 shows the study groups and treatments.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is demonstrating FTIR as a tool for monitoring macrophage activation. 2. The strongest evidence is the time-resolved increase in RNA and lipid peaks. 3. The future path involves studying mechanisms of CpG-induced protein loss.

summary.title: EcoEvoApps: Interactive Apps for Theoretical Models in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology
summary.authors: Rosa M Mcguire, Kenji T Hayashi, Xinyi Yan, Marcel Caritá Vaz, Damla Cino Glu, Madeline C Cowen, Alejandra Martínez-Blancas, Lauren L Sullivan, Sheila Vazquez-Morales, Gaurav S Kandlikar
summary.field_subfield: Ecology and Evolutionary Biology (EEB) / Educational Technology
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces EcoEvoApps, an open-source R package and website designed to bridge the gap between theoretical and empirical research in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology (EEB). The primary motivation is to address the barrier that mathematical models often present to empiricists, who may find equation-heavy literature intimidating or less accessible. EcoEvoApps provides a collection of 11 interactive Shiny apps that simulate fundamental EEB models, such as predator-prey dynamics, island biogeography, and resource competition. These apps allow users to explore model structures and outcomes by manipulating parameters, thereby fostering a deeper conceptual understanding without requiring extensive coding or analytical skills. The package also includes underlying R functions for simulating and visualizing model dynamics, serving as a gateway for users to transition from interactive exploration to command-line implementation. The authors evaluated the educational utility of these apps in classroom settings at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and the University of Missouri (MU). Surveys of 51 students at UCLA indicated that an overwhelming majority (40/51) found the apps moderately to very helpful for understanding the models. Similar positive results were observed at MU, with notable gains in student confidence, particularly among those with higher initial interest in the topics. The project is designed to be collaborative and inclusive, with apps available in multiple languages including English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The authors invite community contributions to expand the model library, add new features, and develop teaching plans. By leveraging the R ecosystem, EcoEvoApps offers a customizable, accessible, and open-source alternative to existing educational resources, aiming to facilitate communication and collaboration between theoretical and empirical researchers in the EEB community.

claims.description: Interactive Shiny apps effectively facilitate the understanding of theoretical EEB models in classroom settings.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces EcoEvoApps, an open-source R package and website designed to bridge the gap between theoretical and empirical research in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology (EEB). The primary motivation is to address the barrier that mathematical models often present to empiricists, who may find equation-heavy literature intimidating or less accessible. EcoEvoApps provides a collection of 11 interactive Shiny apps that simulate fundamental EEB models, such as predator-prey dynamics, island biogeography, and resource competition. These apps allow users to explore model structures and outcomes by manipulating parameters, thereby fostering a deeper conceptual understanding without requiring extensive coding or analytical skills. The package also includes underlying R functions for simulating and visualizing model dynamics, serving as a gateway for users to transition from interactive exploration to command-line implementation. The authors evaluated the educational utility of these apps in classroom settings at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) and the University of Missouri (MU). Surveys of 51 students at UCLA indicated that an overwhelming majority (40/51) found the apps moderately to very helpful for understanding the models. Similar positive results were observed at MU, with notable gains in student confidence, particularly among those with higher initial interest in the topics. The project is designed to be collaborative and inclusive, with apps available in multiple languages including English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. The authors invite community contributions to expand the model library, add new features, and develop teaching plans. By leveraging the R ecosystem, EcoEvoApps offers a customizable, accessible, and open-source alternative to existing educational resources, aiming to facilitate communication and collaboration between theoretical and empirical researchers in the EEB community.

Research Context
Integrating theory with observations is a fundamental driver of progress in life sciences. Mathematical models enable generalization and clarify biological factors. Equation-heavy papers are often cited less frequently. Instructors of quantitative courses often receive worse student evaluations. Previous calls for quantitative training focused on statistics or programming. Interactive tools help increase student interest in quantitative concepts. There is a need for better pedagogy of theoretical models.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to provide a platform for interactive simulations of EEB models. The hypothesis is that interactive apps facilitate communication between theoretical and empirical researchers. The apps are expected to help users gain familiarity with model structure. The package serves as a bridge to coding and implementing theoretical models. The study evaluates the utility of these apps in classroom settings. It is predicted that apps will help students understand specific model topics.

Methodological Details
The core of the package consists of 11 interactive Shiny apps. Models were selected by surveying undergraduate ecology syllabi and textbooks. Apps include descriptions, parameter tables, and literature references. Nine apps are available in English, Spanish, Chinese, Turkish, and Portuguese. Apps are hosted on RStudio's shinyapps.io servers. The package includes functions with the prefix shiny_ for local deployment. Simulations are conducted by functions with the prefix run_. Plotting functions are prefixed with plot_ and return ggplot2 objects. A classroom survey was conducted with 51 students at UCLA. The survey used a scale of 1-7 to rate helpfulness. Similar surveys were conducted at the University of Missouri.

Procedures And Architectures
The package is an open-source R package named ecoevoapps. The website is hosted at https://ecoevoapps.gitlab.io. The predator-prey app includes tabs for Lotka-Volterra and extensions. Extensions include logistic growth and type II functional response. The run_predprey_model() function takes params, init, and time as inputs. The function returns a dataframe of population sizes over time. Users can customize and deploy their own app instances. Model-specific vignettes provide instructions for simulating dynamics in R. The package can be installed from GitLab. The project invites contributions for new apps and translations.

Key Results
An overwhelming majority of students (40/51) found the apps helpful. Students rated the apps as moderately to very helpful (6 or 7). Students reported better understanding of concepts like carrying capacity. Similar results were found in surveys at the University of Missouri. Using interactive apps led to substantial gains in student confidence. Confidence gains were especially high among students with higher interest. The paradox of enrichment can be visualized by altering carrying capacity. Low carrying capacity results in stable oscillations or equilibrium. High carrying capacity results in unstable oscillations.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Interactive tools help disentangle complex interactions and feedbacks. The apps bridge the gap between theoretical and empirical researchers. Simulation-based learning provides easier access to theoretical insights. The open-source nature allows for community customization and expansion. The project aims to complement existing educational web resources. Future work will prioritize evolutionary biology and population genetics models.

Contradictions And Limitations
Simulation-based learning may not provide all insights of analytical solutions. The current release focuses primarily on ecological models. The study relies on self-reported student surveys for efficacy. The sample size for the primary survey was 51 students. The package is in its first release and expected to grow.

Claims
Interactive Shiny apps effectively facilitate the understanding of theoretical EEB models in classroom settings. 40 out of 51 students rated the apps as helpful. Students reported improved understanding of specific concepts. Confidence in models increased after using the apps. Simulation may not replace analytical solutions entirely. Educators can use these apps to teach quantitative models. The apps lower the barrier to entry for theoretical models.

Data And Code Availability
The package is available as an open-source R package. The website is hosted on GitLab. Apps are available on RStudio's shinyapps.io.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The package includes functions for simulating and visualizing dynamics. Users can customize app instances for specific lessons.

Ethical Considerations
Classroom surveys were reviewed by UCLA and MU IRBs. The studies were determined to constitute exempt studies.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the predator-prey dynamics app with model extensions. Figure 2 illustrates the paradox of enrichment with varying K. Figure 3 presents survey results on student helpfulness ratings. Table 1 lists the models and functions included in the package.

Three Takeaways
1. EcoEvoApps provides interactive Shiny apps for fundamental EEB models. 2. Classroom surveys show high student satisfaction and improved understanding. 3. The open-source R package invites community contributions for expansion.

summary.title: Translational accuracy of a tethered ribosome
summary.authors: Celine Fabret; Olivier Namy
summary.executive_summary: Ribosomes are essential ribonucleoprotein complexes that typically function as two separate subunits, the 30S and 50S, which associate during translation initiation and dissociate after termination. Recently, a tethered ribosome variant, Ribo-T, was engineered in Escherichia coli by covalently linking the small and large subunit rRNAs. While Ribo-T supports cell growth, its translational fidelity and efficiency have not been fully characterized. This study investigates the translational properties of Ribo-T, specifically focusing on programmed recoding events such as -1 and +1 frameshifting, stop codon readthrough, and internal translation initiation. The authors utilized a dual-reporter system (lacZ-luc) to measure translational efficiency and accuracy in strains expressing Ribo-T. The results reveal that Ribo-T ribosomes exhibit distinct defects in utilizing Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequences. Specifically, Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to SD sequences during -1 frameshifting, maintaining high efficiency regardless of the SD type. However, they are severely impaired in +1 frameshifting, showing only 2% efficiency compared to 33% in wild-type ribosomes. Furthermore, Ribo-T ribosomes initiate translation less efficiently using SD sequences and terminate translation less accurately, displaying higher rates of stop codon readthrough for UAG, UGA, and UAA codons. These findings suggest that the covalent tethering of subunits alters the conformational dynamics of the ribosome, particularly affecting the geometry of helix 44 and the A-site, thereby impairing the recognition of SD sequences and the accommodation of release factors. The study highlights the unexpected flexibility of ribosomes and the specific structural consequences of subunit tethering on translational fidelity.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
Ribosomes are essential ribonucleoprotein complexes that typically function as two separate subunits, the 30S and 50S, which associate during translation initiation and dissociate after termination. Recently, a tethered ribosome variant, Ribo-T, was engineered in Escherichia coli by covalently linking the small and large subunit rRNAs. While Ribo-T supports cell growth, its translational fidelity and efficiency have not been fully characterized. This study investigates the translational properties of Ribo-T, specifically focusing on programmed recoding events such as -1 and +1 frameshifting, stop codon readthrough, and internal translation initiation. The authors utilized a dual-reporter system (lacZ-luc) to measure translational efficiency and accuracy in strains expressing Ribo-T. The results reveal that Ribo-T ribosomes exhibit distinct defects in utilizing Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequences. Specifically, Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to SD sequences during -1 frameshifting, maintaining high efficiency regardless of the SD type. However, they are severely impaired in +1 frameshifting, showing only 2% efficiency compared to 33% in wild-type ribosomes. Furthermore, Ribo-T ribosomes initiate translation less efficiently using SD sequences and terminate translation less accurately, displaying higher rates of stop codon readthrough for UAG, UGA, and UAA codons. These findings suggest that the covalent tethering of subunits alters the conformational dynamics of the ribosome, particularly affecting the geometry of helix 44 and the A-site, thereby impairing the recognition of SD sequences and the accommodation of release factors. The study highlights the unexpected flexibility of ribosomes and the specific structural consequences of subunit tethering on translational fidelity.

Research Context
Ribosomes are evolutionary conserved ribonucleoprotein complexes that function as two separate subunits in all kingdoms. During translation initiation, the two subunits assemble to form the mature ribosome, which is responsible for translating the messenger RNA. A tethered ribosome, called Ribo-T, in which the two subunits are covalently linked to form a single entity, was recently described in Escherichia coli. The ribosome with inseparable subunits generated in this way was shown to be functional and to sustain cell growth. The rate protein synthesis with Ribo-T catalysis was 50% that with wild-type ribosomes. Cell viability depends on a balance between rapid protein synthesis and accurate decoding of the genetic information. Signals present in specific mRNAs at defined locations can program a high rate of errors. These recoding events can occur during translation elongation (frameshifting) or at the termination step (stop codon readthrough). These sequences have specific impacts on translation fidelity, and are therefore powerful tools for investigations of the translation accuracy of Ribo-T ribosomes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
In this study, we investigated the translational properties of Ribo-T ribosomes. Do these ribosomes maintain the correct reading frame as faithfully as wild-type ribosomes? Do they terminate translation accurately at stop codons? Do they translate messenger RNA accurately? We investigated the behavior of Ribo-T ribosomes with recoding signals instructing the ribosome to change translational reading frame (frameshifting) or to read stop codons as sense codons (stop codon readthrough). We also investigated the preferential mode of translation used by Ribo-T ribosomes to express adjacent open reading frames on the same mRNA, given that the two subunits were inseparable. Our data reveal an impairment of tethered ribosomes for +1 frameshifting and termination, but show that these ribosomes are otherwise as effective as wildtype ribosomes.

Methodological Details
The experiments were performed with the E. coli BL21 (DE3) strain (Invitrogen), with and without the poRibo-T2 vector carrying the Ribo-T ribosomal DNA for the expression of Ribo-T ribosomes. The ASD sequence of the Ribo-T 16S rRNA was altered from the wildtype sequence (5'-UCACCUCCUUA-3') to an orthogonal sequence (5'-UCAUUGUGGUA-3'). We used the bacterial pCL99 dual reporter system. This plasmid carries the lacZ-luc fusion gene, encoding the b-galactosidase and luciferase enzymes, under the control of the T7 promoter. The various target sequences tested for translation accuracy were inserted by oligocloning into the MscI restriction site of pCL99. The translational efficiency of the ribosomes was calculated as the ratio of luciferase activity to β-galactosidase activity for the target, divided by the ratio of luciferase activity to βgalactosidase activity for the corresponding in-frame construct. We calculated the median value for at least six independent experiments. The significance of differences was determined in Student's t-tests. We used constructs with a lacZ gene carrying a wild-type SD sequence AGGAGG to analyze the translational efficiency of wild-type ribosomes. For assessments of the translational efficiency of Ribo-T ribosomes, we used the corresponding constructs with a mutated SD sequence CACCAC upstream from the lacZ gene. In strains containing this vector, both wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes are present, but only the Ribo-T ribosomes can initiate lacZ translation, because of the mutated SD sequence. We checked the level of crosstalk in our system, and found that it was too low to affect the results. We selected three programmed -1 frameshifting sites from the IS911 and IS3 insertion sequence elements and the E. coli dnaX gene. For +1 frameshifting, we selected the site from the E. coli prfB gene. We used the 46-nucleotide intergenic E. coli lacZ-lacY sequence, which carries the SD sequence promoting initiation at the lacY start codon. We therefore used the stop codon sequence of the mtmB1 gene encoding monomethylamine methyltransferase from the archaea Methanosarcina barkeri.

Procedures And Architectures
The hybrid ribosomal RNA (rRNA) consisted of the small and large subunit rRNA sequences, linked by short RNA linkers. The resulting ribosome, Ribo-T, with its inseparable subunits, was shown to be functional and able to sustain the cell growth. The slow growth of Ribo-T cells was probably due to Ribo-T biogenesis being slower than the biogenesis of wild-type ribosomes, rather than impaired Ribo-T activity. Frameshifting is stimulated by two elements: an RNA structure (a stem-loop for IS911 and dnaX, a pseudoknot for IS3) located downstream from the slippery site, and an SD sequence located upstream from the slippery site. The combination of these elements, together with the highly efficient slippery sequence, gave a -1 frameshifting efficiency of about 13%, 8% and 60% for IS911, IS3 and dnaX, respectively. We first measured frameshifting efficiencies with WT sequences (i.e. with a WT SD). As Ribo-T ribosomes cannot base pair to the WT SD, we assumed that they would be unable to frameshift. We investigated this possibility by performing the reverse experiment. We replaced the dnaX SD sequence with an SD recognized by Ribo-T ribosomes (dnaXRibo-T). This modification greatly decreased the frameshifting efficiency of WT ribosomes (11% versus 43%; p-value of 1.7x10 -3 ), but this change had no significant impact on Ribo-T ribosome frameshifting (45% vs. 44%; p-value 0.85). We addressed this possibility, by replacing the wild-type SD sequence with a sequence recognized by Ribo-T ribosomes. We used the 46-nucleotide intergenic E. coli lacZ-lacY sequence, which carries the SD sequence promoting initiation at the lacY start codon to address this question. We modified this sequence by deleting the SD sequence or replacing it with the Ribo-T SD sequence recognized only by Ribo-T ribosomes. We investigated whether the type of ribosomes translating lacZ influenced the rate of translation initiation for the luc gene, by replacing the wild-type SD sequence upstream from lacZ with a Ribo-T SD sequence. We inserted a stable stem loop structure immediately downstream from lacZ, to act as a roadblock for potential scanning ribosomes. We therefore used the stop codon sequence of the mtmB1 gene encoding monomethylamine methyltransferase from the archaea Methanosarcina barkeri, which allows the insertion of a pyrrolysine, to estimate the accuracy of Ribo-T ribosomes during translation termination.

Key Results
The efficiency of -1 ribosomal frameshifting was 13% for IS911 with wild-type ribosomes and 14% with Ribo-T ribosomes (p-value of 0.54). The efficiency was 33% for IS3 with either type of ribosome (p-value of 0.77). The efficiency was 43% for dnaX with wild-type ribosomes and 45% with Ribo-T ribosomes (p-value of 0.77). This modification greatly decreased the frameshifting efficiency of WT ribosomes (11% versus 43%; p-value of 1.7x10 -3 ). This change had no significant impact on Ribo-T ribosome frameshifting (45% vs. 44%; p-value 0.85). We obtained a +1 frameshifting efficiency of 33% for the WT ribosome, confirming previous results. However, Ribo-T ribosomes frameshift inefficiently on this sequence, with an efficiency of only 2% (p-value of 8.9x10 -9 versus wild-type ribosomes). Interestingly, this did not restore the +1 frameshifting efficiency of Ribo-T ribosomes (1.8%, p-value of 0.56 relative to the previous finding). It did strongly decrease the +1 frameshifting activity of wild-type ribosomes (0.6% versus 33%, p-value of 1.6x10 -5 ). In the absence of Ribo-T, we observed almost no luciferase activity when the SD sequence upstream from the luc gene was removed. By contrast, when the wild-type SD sequence was used, we obtained high levels of luciferase activity. In the presence of the Ribo-T SD sequence, we observed no statistically significant difference (p-value 0.04, versus no SD) in luciferase activity. Interestingly, in the presence of Ribo-T ribosomes, luciferase induction was increased by a factor of four (p-value 4.7x10 -4 ). We found that expression of the luciferase reporter gene was four times stronger when the Ribo-T SD sequence was placed in front of the start codon for the upstream lacZ than in the total absence of an SD sequence (no-SD; p-value 9.8x10 -6 ). We found that structure had no effect on the initiation of luc translation (p-value 0.22). We found that Ribo-T ribosomes terminated translation less efficiently than wild-type ribosomes (Figure 5 ; 0.07% vs. 0.013%, p-value of 4.7x10 -7 ; 0.26% vs. 0.11%, p-value of 5x10 - 3 ; 0.04% vs. 0.01%, p-value of 2.5x10 -4 , for UAG, UGA and UAA stop codons, respectively).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
These results suggest that Ribo-T ribosomes frameshift independently of the SD. These results confirm that Ribo-T ribosomes are unable to sense SD sequences and use them as stimulatory elements for frameshifting to either the -1 or +1 frame. Overall, our results indicate that Ribo-T ribosomes do not use SD sequence efficiently during either initiation or programmed frameshifting. The mechanism of translation initiation by Ribo-T ribosomes in the absence of the SD sequence remains unclear. The two subunits are linked together via helix 44 (H44) in these ribosomes. This helix is known to play an important role in the fidelity of translation initiation. The tethering of ribosomes may allow sufficient translation for cell viability, but it probably also has structural consequences for the geometry of H44. We therefore suggest that its orientation is modified in Ribo-T ribosomes, preventing them from using SD sequences in a normal manner during translation initiation and elongation. The structure of Ribo-T ribosomes, in which the rRNA molecules are covalently linked, may be less dynamic, and associated with an A-site less able to bind termination factors. These results are consistent with a previous ribosome profiling analysis in Ribo-Texpressing cells, which highlighted an increase in ribosome density at start codons and close to the 3' ends of genes. The tethering of the ribosomal subunits had mild effects on the initiation and termination/recycling steps of translation. Our work reveals the specific behavior of tethered ribosomes and highlights the greater-than-expected flexibility of ribosomes.

Contradictions And Limitations
Surprisingly, this turned out not to be the case, as the efficiency of -1 ribosomal frameshifting was 13% for IS911 with wild-type ribosomes and 14% with Ribo-T ribosomes. This may be because the stimulatory SD sequence is wild-type and is not, therefore, recognized by Ribo-T ribosomes. Interestingly, this did not restore the +1 frameshifting efficiency of Ribo-T ribosomes (1.8%, p-value of 0.56 relative to the previous finding). The mechanism of translation initiation by Ribo-T ribosomes in the absence of the SD sequence remains unclear. The elucidation of a high-resolution structure for Ribo-T ribosomes would help to resolve this question. One question of interest concerns whether tethered ribosomes would be efficient in eukaryotes, which have a different mechanism of translation initiation not involving SD-ASD interaction.

Claims
Ribo-T ribosomes are insensitive to Shine-Dalgarno sequences during -1 frameshifting. The efficiency of -1 ribosomal frameshifting was 13% for IS911 with wild-type ribosomes and 14% with Ribo-T ribosomes (p-value of 0.54). This change had no significant impact on Ribo-T ribosome frameshifting (45% vs. 44%; p-value 0.85). This modification greatly decreased the frameshifting efficiency of WT ribosomes (11% versus 43%; p-value of 1.7x10 -3 ). These results suggest that Ribo-T ribosomes frameshift independently of the SD.
Ribo-T ribosomes are severely impaired in +1 frameshifting. However, Ribo-T ribosomes frameshift inefficiently on this sequence, with an efficiency of only 2% (p-value of 8.9x10 -9 versus wild-type ribosomes). Interestingly, this did not restore the +1 frameshifting efficiency of Ribo-T ribosomes (1.8%, p-value of 0.56 relative to the previous finding). We obtained a +1 frameshifting efficiency of 33% for the WT ribosome, confirming previous results. These results confirm that Ribo-T ribosomes are unable to sense SD sequences and use them as stimulatory elements for frameshifting to either the -1 or +1 frame.
Ribo-T ribosomes terminate translation less efficiently than wild-type ribosomes. We found that Ribo-T ribosomes terminated translation less efficiently than wild-type ribosomes (Figure 5 ; 0.07% vs. 0.013%, p-value of 4.7x10 -7 ; 0.26% vs. 0.11%, p-value of 5x10 - 3 ; 0.04% vs. 0.01%, p-value of 2.5x10 -4 , for UAG, UGA and UAA stop codons, respectively).  Thus, Ribo-T ribosomes display a slight impairment of stop codon recognition.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
We calculated the median value for at least six independent experiments. The significance of differences was determined in Student's t-tests. We checked the level of crosstalk in our system, and found that it was too low to affect the results. In-frame controls were constructed for each target sequence.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the programmed -1 frameshifting sites from the IS911 and IS3 insertion sequence elements and the E. coli dnaX gene. Figure 2A shows the efficiency of -1 ribosomal frameshifting for IS911, IS3, and dnaX with wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes. Figure 2B shows the effect of replacing the dnaX SD sequence with an SD recognized by Ribo-T ribosomes. Figure 3A shows the site from the E. coli prfB gene for +1 frameshifting. Figure 3B shows the +1 frameshifting efficiency for WT and Ribo-T ribosomes. Figure 3C shows the effect of replacing the wild-type SD sequence with a sequence recognized by Ribo-T ribosomes on +1 frameshifting. Figure 4A shows the luciferase activity in the absence of Ribo-T with and without the SD sequence. Figure 4B shows the luciferase activity in the presence of Ribo-T with various SD sequences. Figure 4C shows the effect of the Ribo-T SD sequence upstream from lacZ on luciferase expression. Figure 4D shows the effect of a stable stem loop structure downstream from lacZ on luc translation. Figure 5 shows the stop codon readthrough efficiency for UAG, UGA, and UAA stop codons with wild-type and Ribo-T ribosomes. Table 1 lists the target sequences used in the study.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the characterization of the translational accuracy of tethered Ribo-T ribosomes, revealing specific defects in SD sequence usage and termination. 2. The strongest evidence is the significant impairment of +1 frameshifting (2% vs 33%) and increased stop codon readthrough in Ribo-T ribosomes. 3. The future path involves determining the high-resolution structure of Ribo-T ribosomes to understand the structural consequences of subunit tethering on helix 44 geometry.

summary.title: SPOT-Contact-Single: Improving Single-Sequence-Based Prediction of Protein Contact Map using a Transformer Language Model
summary.authors: Jaspreet Singh, Thomas Litfin, Jaswinder Singh, Kuldip Paliwal, Yaoqi Zhou
summary.executive_summary: This paper introduces SPOT-Contact-Single, a novel method for predicting protein contact maps using single-sequence inputs, addressing the limitation of evolutionary-profile-based methods that require homologous sequences. The core innovation is the integration of attention maps from the pre-trained transformer language model ESM-1b as input features, combined with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs. The model architecture consists of an ensemble of six 12-block ResNet models, trained using both direct contact prediction and distogram-based strategies. The study utilized a large training set of 34,691 proteins from the ProteinNet benchmark, with stringent independent test sets including SPOT-2018 (669 proteins) and CASP14-FM (15 targets). Results demonstrate significant improvements over existing single-sequence predictors like SSCpred, with a 15% improvement in F1-score on the CASP14-FM set. More notably, SPOT-Contact-Single outperforms evolutionary-profile-based methods TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact by 48.7% and 48.5% respectively in F1-score on proteins without homologs (Neff=1). The method is also computationally efficient, being 22 times faster than TrRosetta on CPU. These findings suggest that unsupervised learning features from language models can effectively replace evolutionary information for contact map prediction, particularly for proteins with few homologs, offering a scalable solution for large-scale genomic prediction.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper introduces SPOT-Contact-Single, a novel method for predicting protein contact maps using single-sequence inputs, addressing the limitation of evolutionary-profile-based methods that require homologous sequences. The core innovation is the integration of attention maps from the pre-trained transformer language model ESM-1b as input features, combined with one-hot encoding and SPOT-1D-Single outputs. The model architecture consists of an ensemble of six 12-block ResNet models, trained using both direct contact prediction and distogram-based strategies. The study utilized a large training set of 34,691 proteins from the ProteinNet benchmark, with stringent independent test sets including SPOT-2018 (669 proteins) and CASP14-FM (15 targets). Results demonstrate significant improvements over existing single-sequence predictors like SSCpred, with a 15% improvement in F1-score on the CASP14-FM set. More notably, SPOT-Contact-Single outperforms evolutionary-profile-based methods TrRosetta and SPOT-Contact by 48.7% and 48.5% respectively in F1-score on proteins without homologs (Neff=1). The method is also computationally efficient, being 22 times faster than TrRosetta on CPU. These findings suggest that unsupervised learning features from language models can effectively replace evolutionary information for contact map prediction, particularly for proteins with few homologs, offering a scalable solution for large-scale genomic prediction.

Research Context
Protein contact map prediction is essential for structure and function prediction. Most existing methods rely on protein-sequence-evolutionary information. Evolutionary profiles may not exist for many proteins. Generating evolutionary profiles is computationally intensive. Single-sequence methods like SSCpred perform poorly compared to MSA-based techniques. Unsupervised deep learning methods inspired by NLP language models have emerged. ESM-1b is an unsupervised method using a Transformer-34 model.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to improve single-sequence-based contact map prediction. The hypothesis is that ESM-1b attention maps can enhance prediction accuracy. The method predicts contact maps without using homologous information. The approach uses an ensemble of residual neural networks. The goal is to outperform single-sequence and MSA-based predictors for low Neff proteins. The study examines the use of ESM-1b's attention map as a feature.

Methodological Details
The training dataset was curated from the ProteinNet benchmark. The dataset consists of 50,914 proteins with high-resolution structures. Proteins were clustered at a 95% sequence identity cut-off. 100 proteins were separated for validation to minimize over-fitting. Homologs were removed using HHblits with an e-value cut-off of 0.1. The final training set contained 34,691 proteins. The validation set contained 88 proteins. The independent test set SPOT-2018 contains 669 proteins. A subset of 46 proteins with Neff=1 formed the Neff1-2018 set. The CASP14-FM test set includes 15 free modelling targets. Input features included one-hot encoding, SPOT-1D-Single outputs, and ESM-1b attention maps. Attention maps were symmetrized and applied average product corrections.

Procedures And Architectures
The neural network architecture was inspired by ResNet. A 12-block ResNet was used as the maximum trainable depth. Convolutional layers had a channel size of 64 and kernel size of 3. Six models were trained with different input feature combinations. Three models predicted contacts as binary classification. Three models predicted inter-residue distances as distance bins. Direct contact models used Binary Cross-Entropy loss. Distogram-based models used Cross-Entropy loss. The Adam optimizer was used with a learning rate of 0.001. The batch size was set to 1. Early stopping was applied with a patience of 3. The ensemble was formed by taking the mean of individual models.

Key Results
SPOT-Contact-Single improved F1-score by 15% over SSCpred on CASP14-FM. The method outperformed TrRosetta by 48.7% in F1-score on Neff=1 proteins. The method outperformed SPOT-Contact by 48.5% in F1-score on Neff=1 proteins. One-hot encoding alone yielded an F1-score of 0.15. Adding SPOT-1D-Single improved F1-score by 22.90%. ESM-1b last-layer attention maps achieved an F1-score of 0.51. This represented a 242% improvement over one-hot encoding. The ensemble achieved a 4% improvement over the second-best individual model. SPOT-Contact-Single achieved an F1-score of 0.32 on Neff=1 proteins. ESM-1b achieved an F1-score of about 0.22 on Neff=1 proteins. SPOT-Contact-Single was 22 times faster than TrRosetta on CPU. SPOT-Contact-Single was 42 times faster than TrRosetta on GPU.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Unsupervised learning features from language models can replace evolutionary information. The method is effective for proteins with few homologs. SPOT-Contact-Single serves as a reasonably accurate screening tool. The method is suitable for large-scale genomic prediction. The use of ESM-1b limits prediction to proteins under 1024 amino acids. Future improvements may involve Transformer or Performer architectures.

Contradictions And Limitations
The method cannot directly predict contact maps for proteins over 1024 amino acids. SPOT-1D-Single is not yet as competitive as evolution-based methods for high Neff. The study relies on the ProteinNet benchmark for training data. The comparison with SSCpred was limited to the CASP14-FM dataset. The method does not employ evolutionary information, limiting its use for high Neff proteins.

Claims
SPOT-Contact-Single significantly improves single-sequence-based contact map prediction using ESM-1b attention maps. The method achieved a 15% improvement in F1-score over SSCpred. It outperformed TrRosetta by 48.7% on Neff=1 proteins. ESM-1b attention maps boosted F1-score to 0.51. The method is limited to proteins under 1024 amino acids. It is not as competitive as evolution-based methods for high Neff proteins. The method offers a faster alternative to evolution-based methods. It is useful for large-scale prediction.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Ablation studies showed ESM-1b attention maps significantly boost performance. Direct contact prediction performed slightly better than distogram-based prediction. The ensemble of six models improved over individual models.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the neural network architecture. Figure 2 shows precision for top predictions. Figure 3 plots F1-score as a function of Neff. Figure 4 shows native and predicted contact-maps. Table 1 describes feature combinations for the ensemble. Table 2 shows feature importance on the validation set. Table 3 compares direct vs distance contact-map prediction. Table 4 presents results of individual models and the ensemble. Table 5 compares methods on proteins without homologs. Table 6 compares SPOT-Contact-Single, SSCpred, and ESM-1b on CASP14-FM.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a single-sequence contact map predictor using ESM-1b attention maps. 2. The strongest evidence is the 48.7% F1-score improvement over TrRosetta on Neff=1 proteins. 3. The future path involves using more advanced architectures like Transformers.

summary.title: CCN2 activates ERK-signaling via integrin av and enhances the interaction of ERK and DUSP6 in lymphatic endothelial cells
summary.authors: Shiho Hashiguchi, Tomoko Tanaka, Ryosuke Mano, Seiji Kondo, Shohta Kodama
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the intracellular signaling mechanisms of Cellular Communication Network Factor 2 (CCN2) in primary cultured lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) and its impact on lymphangiogenesis. While CCN2 is a known angiogenic factor, its role in lymphatic vessel formation and specific signaling pathways in LECs remained unclear. The researchers demonstrated that CCN2 upregulates the expression of lymphatic markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4) in a dose-dependent manner. Mechanistically, CCN2 was found to activate the ERK signaling pathway, a process partially mediated by integrin av. Knockdown of integrin av reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK levels, whereas suppression of integrin a9 had no significant inhibitory effect. Interestingly, CCN2 did not promote LEC proliferation in vitro; instead, it slightly suppressed cell growth. This growth inhibition was linked to an enhanced interaction between ERK and the dual-specificity phosphatase DUSP6. Immunoprecipitation assays confirmed that CCN2 strengthens the binding of ERK to DUSP6, and knockdown of DUSP6 increased phospho-ERK levels, suggesting DUSP6 acts as a negative regulator of ERK signaling in this context. In vivo, using a Matrigel plug assay in mice, exogenous CCN2 significantly increased the number of Podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessels. Immunostaining revealed that both phospho-ERK and DUSP6 were elevated in the CCN2-treated plugs, localizing to Podoplanin-positive cells. These findings suggest that CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo through ERK signaling, which is modulated by integrin av and negatively regulated by DUSP6 to prevent excessive activation. The study highlights the complex interplay between pro-lymphangiogenic signals and inhibitory phosphatases in LECs, providing potential therapeutic targets for diseases involving abnormal lymphangiogenesis, such as cancer metastasis.

claims.description: CCN2 activates ERK signaling in LECs via integrin av.
DUSP6 negatively regulates CCN2-induced ERK phosphorylation.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the intracellular signaling mechanisms of Cellular Communication Network Factor 2 (CCN2) in primary cultured lymphatic endothelial cells (LECs) and its impact on lymphangiogenesis. While CCN2 is a known angiogenic factor, its role in lymphatic vessel formation and specific signaling pathways in LECs remained unclear. The researchers demonstrated that CCN2 upregulates the expression of lymphatic markers (Lyve1, Podoplanin, Prox1) and lymphangiogenic factors (Vegfc, Vegfd, Flt4) in a dose-dependent manner. Mechanistically, CCN2 was found to activate the ERK signaling pathway, a process partially mediated by integrin av. Knockdown of integrin av reduced CCN2-induced phospho-ERK levels, whereas suppression of integrin a9 had no significant inhibitory effect. Interestingly, CCN2 did not promote LEC proliferation in vitro; instead, it slightly suppressed cell growth. This growth inhibition was linked to an enhanced interaction between ERK and the dual-specificity phosphatase DUSP6. Immunoprecipitation assays confirmed that CCN2 strengthens the binding of ERK to DUSP6, and knockdown of DUSP6 increased phospho-ERK levels, suggesting DUSP6 acts as a negative regulator of ERK signaling in this context. In vivo, using a Matrigel plug assay in mice, exogenous CCN2 significantly increased the number of Podoplanin-positive lymphatic vessels. Immunostaining revealed that both phospho-ERK and DUSP6 were elevated in the CCN2-treated plugs, localizing to Podoplanin-positive cells. These findings suggest that CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo through ERK signaling, which is modulated by integrin av and negatively regulated by DUSP6 to prevent excessive activation. The study highlights the complex interplay between pro-lymphangiogenic signals and inhibitory phosphatases in LECs, providing potential therapeutic targets for diseases involving abnormal lymphangiogenesis, such as cancer metastasis.

Research Context
CCN2 is a modular matricellular protein known for its role in angiogenesis. However, its specific roles in lymphangiogenesis and LEC signaling were previously unclear. CCN2 activates MAPKs like ERK in other cell types via integrins. Integrins are cell surface receptors that trigger intracellular signaling pathways. Previous studies linked CTGF to lymphangiogenesis in fibrosis models. The downstream signaling of CCN2 in primary LECs had not been elucidated.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aimed to investigate CCN2 signaling in LECs and its effects on lymphangiogenesis. It was hypothesized that CCN2 influences lymphatic markers and growth factors. The researchers sought to determine the intracellular signaling downstream of CCN2. Specifically, the role of integrins in CCN2-mediated ERK activation was examined. The study also investigated the regulation of ERK by phosphatases like DUSP6. In vivo effects on lymphangiogenesis were tested using Matrigel plug assays.

Methodological Details
Primary cultured LECs from C57BL/6 mice were used for in vitro experiments. Cells were cultured in EGM2 medium up to 6 passages. LECs were treated with various concentrations of recombinant rat CCN2. Gene expression was analyzed using quantitative RT-PCR. siRNA was used to knockdown integrins and DUSP6. Western blotting was performed to detect phosphorylated proteins. A phospho-RTK array was used to assess receptor tyrosine kinase phosphorylation. Immunoprecipitation assays were conducted to study ERK-DUSP6 interactions. In vivo experiments used male 8-week-old C57BL/6 mice. Matrigel plugs containing CCN2 were subcutaneously injected into mice. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism software.

Procedures And Architectures
Cells were plated in 24-well plates for proliferation assays. Proliferation was assessed by crystal violet staining and absorbance measurement. Total RNA was prepared using the Purelink RNA purification Kit. cDNA was prepared using the QuantiTect RT Kit. siRNAs were designed using the siDirect ver.2 website. Transfection was performed using Lipofectamine RNAiMAX. Protein lysates were prepared in RIPA Buffer with inhibitors. Proteins were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred to PVDF membranes. The phospho-RTK array involved incubating protein with a spotted membrane. Immunoprecipitation used anti-ERK or anti-DUSP6 antibodies and magnetic beads. Matrigel plugs were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and embedded in paraffin. Immunohistochemistry was performed using specific primary and secondary antibodies.

Key Results
CCN2 upregulated Lyve1, Podoplanin, and Prox1 expression in a dose-dependent manner. CCN2 increased Vegfc, Vegfd, and Flt4 expression but not Kdr. VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 phosphorylation was unchanged by CCN2. Phospho-ERK was significantly increased in response to CCN2. Knockdown of integrin av partially decreased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. Suppression of integrin a9 did not decrease CCN2-induced phospho-ERK. CCN2 slightly suppressed LEC cell growth at 24 hours. CCN2 enhanced the interaction between ERK and DUSP6. Knockdown of DUSP6 increased CCN2-induced phospho-ERK levels. In vivo, CCN2 increased the number of Podoplanin-positive vessels. Phospho-ERK and DUSP6 were detected in CCN2-treated Matrigel plugs.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
CCN2 activates ERK signaling via integrin av in LECs. DUSP6 acts as a negative modulator of ERK signaling. The enhanced ERK-DUSP6 interaction may prevent excessive ERK activation. CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo despite weak in vitro growth effects. Integrin av, ERK, and DUSP6 are potential therapeutic targets.

Contradictions And Limitations
CCN2 suppressed LEC proliferation in vitro but promoted lymphangiogenesis in vivo. The discrepancy may be due to ECM and MMP effects in Matrigel. The relationship between FOXC1/2 and DUSP6 was not analyzed. Itga5 expression was not investigated due to lack of prior reports.

Claims
CCN2 activates ERK signaling in LECs via integrin av. Phospho-ERK increased with CCN2 treatment. Integrin av knockdown reduced phospho-ERK. Integrin a9 knockdown did not reduce phospho-ERK. Integrin av is a key mediator of CCN2 signaling.
DUSP6 negatively regulates CCN2-induced ERK phosphorylation. CCN2 enhanced ERK-DUSP6 binding. DUSP6 knockdown increased phospho-ERK.  DUSP6 prevents excessive ERK activation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
siRNA knockdowns were used for integrins and DUSP6. Multiple concentrations of CCN2 were tested for dose-response. Time-course experiments showed transient ERK phosphorylation.

Ethical Considerations
Animal experiments were approved by the Fukuoka University committee.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows dose-dependent upregulation of LEC markers. Figure 2 shows CCN2-induced phospho-ERK increase. Figure 3 shows integrin knockdown effects on phospho-ERK. Figure 4 shows CCN2 effects on cell growth and time-course. Figure 5 shows ERK-DUSP6 interaction and DUSP6 knockdown. Figure 6 shows in vivo lymphangiogenesis in Matrigel plugs. Figure 7 shows phospho-ERK and DUSP6 in CCN2 plugs.

Three Takeaways
1. CCN2 activates ERK signaling in LECs via integrin av. 2. DUSP6 negatively regulates CCN2-induced ERK phosphorylation. 3. CCN2 promotes lymphangiogenesis in vivo through these mechanisms.

summary.title: Stem Cell Microarrays for Assessing Growth Factor Signaling in Engineered Glycan Microenvironments
summary.authors: Austen L Michalak, Greg W Trieger, Kelsey A Trieger, Kamil Godula
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a novel stem cell microarray platform designed to analyze the role of extracellular glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in growth factor signaling. The platform integrates GAG-protein conjugates into a hydrogel-supported microarray, allowing for the rapid development and optimization of functional glycomaterials for stem cell-based regenerative therapies. Extracellular glycans, particularly heparan sulfate (HS), are critical regulators of growth factor signaling but are difficult to study due to their structural complexity. The authors developed a method to immobilize HS polysaccharides onto polyacrylamide hydrogels via covalent crosslinking to gelatin, creating stable, ECM-mimetic microenvironments. Using murine embryonic stem cells (ESCs) lacking the Ext1 enzyme, which prevents endogenous HS synthesis, the study isolated the effects of arrayed GAGs on FGF2 signaling. The results demonstrated that covalently linked heparin provided significantly higher FGF2 binding capacity compared to non-covalent immobilization. Furthermore, the arrays retained approximately 40% of FGF2 binding activity after 48 hours under cell culture conditions. The platform successfully supported ESC growth and allowed for the quantification of MAPK pathway activation via immunofluorescence. Stimulation with FGF2 in the presence of immobilized heparin led to significant increases in Erk1/2 phosphorylation, confirming the platform's utility for assessing glycan-mediated signaling. This approach offers a powerful tool for integrating glycans into biomaterials to advance their biological properties and applications in tissue engineering.

claims.description: The developed microarray platform effectively assesses growth factor signaling in engineered glycan microenvironments.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a novel stem cell microarray platform designed to analyze the role of extracellular glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in growth factor signaling. The platform integrates GAG-protein conjugates into a hydrogel-supported microarray, allowing for the rapid development and optimization of functional glycomaterials for stem cell-based regenerative therapies. Extracellular glycans, particularly heparan sulfate (HS), are critical regulators of growth factor signaling but are difficult to study due to their structural complexity. The authors developed a method to immobilize HS polysaccharides onto polyacrylamide hydrogels via covalent crosslinking to gelatin, creating stable, ECM-mimetic microenvironments. Using murine embryonic stem cells (ESCs) lacking the Ext1 enzyme, which prevents endogenous HS synthesis, the study isolated the effects of arrayed GAGs on FGF2 signaling. The results demonstrated that covalently linked heparin provided significantly higher FGF2 binding capacity compared to non-covalent immobilization. Furthermore, the arrays retained approximately 40% of FGF2 binding activity after 48 hours under cell culture conditions. The platform successfully supported ESC growth and allowed for the quantification of MAPK pathway activation via immunofluorescence. Stimulation with FGF2 in the presence of immobilized heparin led to significant increases in Erk1/2 phosphorylation, confirming the platform's utility for assessing glycan-mediated signaling. This approach offers a powerful tool for integrating glycans into biomaterials to advance their biological properties and applications in tissue engineering.

Research Context
Extracellular glycans provide essential regulatory components during tissue development. Glycosaminoglycans harbor binding sites for growth factors and morphogens. The structural complexity of GAGs makes structure-function relationships difficult to establish. Recent advances in synthetic and recombinant technologies have produced well-defined GAG structures. Previous array platforms have been limited in analyzing HS-dependent cellular signaling.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to develop a platform to analyze growth factor binding and signaling. The hypothesis is that GAGs conjugated to adhesion proteins can direct cellular signaling. The platform is intended to streamline the discovery of biomaterials using ECM glycans. The method seeks to present HS structures in a spatially isolated format. The goal is to directly measure GAG contributions to growth factor signaling pathways.

Methodological Details
The study utilized murine embryonic stem cells lacking Exostosin 1 expression. Ext1 knockout cells lack cell surface HS structures and cannot engage FGF2. Hydrogels were composed of polyacrylamide with gelatin loaded in dehydrated form. Heparin was crosslinked to gelatin using NHS esters and EDC coupling. The crosslinking targeted approximately 15% carboxylic acid crosslinks per chain. Cells were seeded at a density of 40,000 cells per square centimeter. Culture conditions included 24 hours in serum-free media to establish baselines. FGF2 stimulation was performed at a concentration of 0.5 ng/mL.

Procedures And Architectures
Dry acrylamide substrates were spotted with gelatin and heparin solutions. Heparin was activated in HEPES buffer with EDC at 4°C for 18 hours. Arrays were washed for 3 hours prior to staining with fluorescent FGF2. Cells were fixed, permeabilized, and immunoassayed for MAPK activity. Fluorescence was detected using a microarray scanner and validated by microscopy. The ratio of phosphorylated-ERK1/2 to total ERK1/2 was used for quantification. Soluble heparin was used as a positive control for MAPK activity.

Key Results
NHS-crosslinked heparin provided 5-to 10-fold higher FGF2 binding signal. Heparin arrays retained approximately 40% of FGF2 binding activity after 48 hours. FGF2 binding showed the greatest preference for fully sulfated heparin. Removal of sulfates resulted in progressive loss of FGF2 binding activity. Only cells with immobilized or soluble heparin showed significant Erk1/2 phosphorylation. MAPK activity on arrayed heparin was lower than with soluble heparin. FGF2 stimulation showed a heparin dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The platform enables rapid development of functional glycomaterials for regenerative therapies. Covalent crosslinking facilitates GAG retention without altering protein-binding specificity. The array allows for systematic analysis of extracellular GAG biological activities. This approach capitalizes on the expanding repertoire of synthetic GAG structures. The study demonstrates the utility of engineered glycan microenvironments for signaling.

Contradictions And Limitations
MAPK activity on arrayed heparin was lower than with soluble heparin. This difference may be due to limited accessibility of immobilized heparin. The study focuses on murine ESCs, which may limit generalizability. The platform requires specific knockout cells to isolate GAG effects. The stability of arrays over longer periods is not fully characterized.

Claims
The developed microarray platform effectively assesses growth factor signaling in engineered glycan microenvironments. The platform allows for multiplexed analysis of glycan structures. Covalent crosslinking enhances stability of GAG displays. The array supports ESC culture and signaling assays. Signal intensity was lower compared to soluble heparin controls. This accelerates the development of bioactive glycomaterials. It provides a tool for integrating glycans into biomaterials.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study compared covalent and non-covalent immobilization strategies. Different sulfation patterns of heparin were tested for specificity. Seeding density was optimized to ensure consistent monolayer formation.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the cellular microarray approach for ECM-mediated signaling. Figure 2 shows the generation and characterization of hydrogel GAG arrays. Figure 3 details the optimization of ESC culture on the array. Figure 4 presents the FGF2 signaling assay results on the array.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a hydrogel-based GAG microarray for stem cell signaling analysis. 2. The strongest evidence is the dose-responsive ERK1/2 phosphorylation in Ext1-/- ESCs. 3. The future path involves using this platform to optimize glycomaterials for therapy.

summary.title: A Single-domain Protein Catenane of Dihydrofolate Reductase
summary.authors: Jing Fang, Tianzuo Li, Jiyeon Lee, Dahye Lim, Lianjie Xu, Yajie Liu, Jongcheol Seo, Wen-Bin Zhang
summary.executive_summary: This study reports the design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), a mechanically interlocked polypeptide structure that is extremely rare in nature. The authors achieved this by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, using the original fold as the entangling template. The synthesis was accomplished in cells using a series of programmed streamlined post-translational processing events involving mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs, without additional in vitro reactions. The resulting cat-DHFR was thoroughly characterized using LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to the linear control (l-DHFR), cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability, although with reduced activity (~5 U/mg vs ~14 U/mg) and lower substrate affinity. However, cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against thermal and chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction imposed by the mechanical interlocking. The study demonstrates that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents a new horizon in protein science, offering a unique scaffold for further engineering and evolution, and highlighting topology as a distinct dimension for protein design.

claims.description: A single-domain protein catenane of DHFR can be synthesized in cells without in vitro reactions.
cat-DHFR retains catalytic function but with reduced activity and affinity.
cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against thermal and chemical denaturation.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study reports the design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of dihydrofolate reductase (cat-DHFR), a mechanically interlocked polypeptide structure that is extremely rare in nature. The authors achieved this by rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs to introduce artificial entanglement, using the original fold as the entangling template. The synthesis was accomplished in cells using a series of programmed streamlined post-translational processing events involving mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs, without additional in vitro reactions. The resulting cat-DHFR was thoroughly characterized using LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry. Compared to the linear control (l-DHFR), cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability, although with reduced activity (~5 U/mg vs ~14 U/mg) and lower substrate affinity. However, cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against thermal and chemical denaturation due to conformational restriction imposed by the mechanical interlocking. The study demonstrates that linear proteins can be converted into concatenated single-domain counterparts with almost identical chemical composition, well-preserved function, and elevated stability. This represents a new horizon in protein science, offering a unique scaffold for further engineering and evolution, and highlighting topology as a distinct dimension for protein design.

Research Context
Natural protein domains are based on linear polypeptide chains with limited topological diversity. The discovery of natural topological proteins suggests unconventional topology could enhance stability. Topology has been recognized as a unique dimension for protein engineering. Previous artificial topological proteins often contain multiple domains, complicating structure-property studies. Ideally, a single-domain topological protein would exhibit the most profound impact of chemical topology. It remains challenging to prepare single-domain topological proteins, even for the simplest catenane. The need for exogenous entangling motifs may be eliminated by exploiting spatially entangled relationships. The goal is to design single-domain protein catenanes with identical composition to linear wild-type.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is whether a single-domain protein catenane can be designed and synthesized. The hypothesis is that rewiring connectivity between secondary motifs can introduce artificial entanglement. It is hypothesized that using the original fold as a template allows synthesis without exogenous motifs. The predicted outcome is a catenane with preserved function and elevated stability. The study aims to demonstrate the feasibility of converting DHFR into its catenane counterpart. It is expected that the catenane will retain catalytic capability despite topological changes. The design should ensure entangled conformation and high reconstitution efficiency. The active site and adjacent regions should be left intact to preserve activity.

Methodological Details
The study utilized dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) from Escherichia coli as the model enzyme. The design involved rewiring the connectivity between secondary motifs. The Gaussian linking number (GLN) matrix was used to identify splitting positions. Cleavage at residues 88 and 89 generated two highly intertwined segments. The design consisted of residues 1-88 as one ring and 89-159 as the other. Synthesis used two pairs of mutually orthogonal split-intein pairs. Ring I was circularly permutated to generate new termini between residues 23 and 24. The rewired loops were designed to be 16 residues long. A TEV protease recognition sequence was included for topology proof. A linear control (l-DHFR) with identical amino acid composition was designed. Genes were sub-cloned into pMCSG19 and pET21a vectors. Proteins were expressed in E. coli BL21(DE3) competent cells. Expression was carried out at 16 °C for 20 hours. Purification was performed using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography and size exclusion chromatography. Characterization included LC-MS, SDS-PAGE, protease cleavage, and ion mobility mass spectrometry.

Procedures And Architectures
The retrosynthetic analysis guided the choice of ring closure sites. Cyclization efficiency depends on the distance between new termini. The two bulky split-intein pairs were placed on opposite sides to avoid interference. The gene cassette contained two DHFR segments and two split-intein pairs. Protein expression was optimized for proper folding and complete reaction. SDS-PAGE showed a major band at less than 20 kDa for cat-DHFR. The faster mobility of cat-DHFR in SDS-PAGE indicates a more compact structure. SEC showed cat-DHFR elutes as a broader peak at a larger retention volume. LC-MS confirmed the accurate molecular weights of cat-DHFR and l-DHFR. Far-UV CD spectra showed reduced intensities of positive and negative peaks. Near-UV CD spectrum exhibited positive ellipticity at ~290 nm. Proteolytic digestion with TEV protease converted cat-DHFR to linear and cyclic fragments. Ion mobility spectrometry and collision-induced dissociation were used for topology proof. Kinetic parameters Km and kcat were determined by Michaelis curve fitting. Binding affinity was determined using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC).

Key Results
cat-DHFR retains catalytic capability with an activity of ~5 U/mg. The linear control l-DHFR has an activity of ~14 U/mg. cat-DHFR has a Km approximately 5-fold that of l-DHFR. The kcat of cat-DHFR is about 38% that of l-DHFR. The catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) of cat-DHFR is reduced by an order of magnitude. The dissociation constant for DHF is ~173-fold larger for cat-DHFR. The dissociation constant for NADPH is ~14-fold larger for cat-DHFR. The dissociation constant for THF is ~3.6-fold larger for cat-DHFR. cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against thermal denaturation. cat-DHFR preserved 87% activity in 5% DMSO, compared to 74% for l-DHFR. The GLN of cat-DHFR is +1.120. The GLN of the split DHFR segments is +0.726. The yield with the shortest linker is about one-fifth that of the longest. The yield with the longest linker is ~12 mg/L of culture.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Mechanical interlocking enhances the thermal resilience of the enzyme. The reduced activity is attributed to compromised affinity towards substrate and cofactor. Circular permutation causes minor local disturbance but overall structure is intact. The catenane topology reinforces the folded structure. This approach offers a new horizon in protein science. Linear proteins can be converted into concatenated counterparts with preserved function. Topology provides a unique dimension for protein engineering. The design allows for further engineering and evolution of the scaffold.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors failed to obtain a crystal structure of cat-DHFR. The lack of crystal structure limits unambiguous proof of topology. The approach requires extensive optimization for high-yield expression. Steric hindrance of split-intein pairs affects reconstitution efficiency. Shorter linkers lead to decreased yield and increased by-products. The reduced activity may be further restored by directed evolution. The dynamic structure of cat-DHFR suggests coupled movement of rings.

Claims
A single-domain protein catenane of DHFR can be synthesized in cells without in vitro reactions. Synthesis was accomplished by programmed post-translational processing. No additional in vitro reactions were required. The method uses orthogonal split-intein pairs. The process requires extensive optimization. Side products can form if linkers are too short. This enables the study of topological effects on single domains. It provides a new scaffold for protein engineering.
cat-DHFR retains catalytic function but with reduced activity and affinity. cat-DHFR has ~5 U/mg activity. Km is 5-fold higher than linear control. kcat is 38% of linear control. Previous rethreaded DHFR showed no activity. Split DHFR complex retained only 15% activity. Function is preserved despite topological change. Activity can potentially be restored by evolution.
cat-DHFR exhibits enhanced stability against thermal and chemical denaturation. Enhanced stability against thermal denaturation. 87% activity preserved in 5% DMSO. Mechanical interlocking enhances resilience. Secondary structure intensities are reduced. Topology can be used to stabilize proteins. This is a new dimension for protein design.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The method is robust before the linker becomes too short. Shorter linkers lead to decreased yield and more by-products. Circular permutation was necessary to place cyclization motifs on opposite sides. Different sites for ring closure were tested. The site between residues 23 and 24 was most efficient.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the molecular design and retrosynthetic analysis. Figure 2 shows SDS-PAGE, SEC, LC-MS, and CD spectra. Figure 4c shows kinetic curves of DHFR samples. Table 1 lists kinetic parameters and dissociation constants. Figure S1 shows GLN matrices of split DHFR and cat-DHFR. Figure S3 shows constructs with split-intein pairs on the same side. Figure S4 shows the effect of linker length on yield.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the design and synthesis of a single-domain protein catenane of DHFR. 2. The strongest evidence is the retention of catalytic activity and enhanced stability. 3. The future path is using directed evolution to restore or surpass linear control activity.
