summary.title: Robust Brain State Decoding using Bidirectional Long Short Term Memory Networks in functional MRI
summary.authors: Anant Mittal, Priya Aggarwal, Luiz Pessoa, Anubha Gupta
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the challenge of decoding brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data by leveraging temporal dynamics that are often obscured by the inherent latency of the Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (BOLD) response. Traditional approaches typically require manual delay adjustments to synchronize stimuli with BOLD peaks, assuming uniform latency across voxels, which may not hold true due to spatial and temporal variations. The authors propose a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (bi-LSTM) network that explicitly models both past and future temporal contexts without requiring such delay adjustments. By processing fMRI time-series in both forward and reverse directions, the bi-LSTM captures the full dynamic profile of the BOLD response. The model was evaluated on working memory task data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), involving 400 participants performing 2-back and 0-back tasks with various stimulus categories. The input features were derived from 360 cortical regions of interest (ROIs) averaged over 405 time-points. The bi-LSTM architecture, specifically the concatenation variant (bi-LSTM-c), outperformed the conventional unidirectional LSTM by 18% in classification accuracy, achieving 0.84 ± 0.02 compared to 0.66 ± 0.18. The study also compared performance against a feed-forward neural network, confirming the superiority of temporal modeling. Confusion matrix analysis revealed that while the model generally distinguished stimuli well, it occasionally confused 'body' and 'tools' categories or misclassified task conditions when stimuli were correctly identified. The results suggest that future temporal context is crucial for accurate brain state decoding, and that bi-LSTM networks provide a robust framework for this task without the need for heuristic delay corrections. Future work will focus on tuning window sizes and addressing class imbalance more sophisticatedly.

claims.description: Bidirectional LSTM improves brain state decoding accuracy by capturing future temporal context.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the challenge of decoding brain states from functional MRI (fMRI) data by leveraging temporal dynamics that are often obscured by the inherent latency of the Blood Oxygen Level Dependent (BOLD) response. Traditional approaches typically require manual delay adjustments to synchronize stimuli with BOLD peaks, assuming uniform latency across voxels, which may not hold true due to spatial and temporal variations. The authors propose a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (bi-LSTM) network that explicitly models both past and future temporal contexts without requiring such delay adjustments. By processing fMRI time-series in both forward and reverse directions, the bi-LSTM captures the full dynamic profile of the BOLD response. The model was evaluated on working memory task data from the Human Connectome Project (HCP), involving 400 participants performing 2-back and 0-back tasks with various stimulus categories. The input features were derived from 360 cortical regions of interest (ROIs) averaged over 405 time-points. The bi-LSTM architecture, specifically the concatenation variant (bi-LSTM-c), outperformed the conventional unidirectional LSTM by 18% in classification accuracy, achieving 0.84 ± 0.02 compared to 0.66 ± 0.18. The study also compared performance against a feed-forward neural network, confirming the superiority of temporal modeling. Confusion matrix analysis revealed that while the model generally distinguished stimuli well, it occasionally confused 'body' and 'tools' categories or misclassified task conditions when stimuli were correctly identified. The results suggest that future temporal context is crucial for accurate brain state decoding, and that bi-LSTM networks provide a robust framework for this task without the need for heuristic delay corrections. Future work will focus on tuning window sizes and addressing class imbalance more sophisticatedly.

Research Context
Decoding brain states via discriminative features has gained interest in brain imaging. There is an impetus to encode brain dynamics using temporal fMRI information. LSTMs are increasingly observed to perform well in dynamic temporal applications. Conventional LSTM models do not encode or capture future temporal context. BOLD responses have inherent latency, making future context crucial.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether bidirectional LSTM can robustly decode brain states. The hypothesis is that capturing past and future instances improves accuracy. The model aims to explicitly model BOLD dynamics without delay adjustment. The study predicts bi-LSTM will outperform unidirectional LSTM counterparts. The framework utilizes information encapsulation from both time directions.

Methodological Details
Data was sourced from the Human Connectome Project working memory task. N = 400 participants were randomly selected from the N = 1200 release. Participants performed a 2-back task and a 0-back control condition. Stimuli included tools, places, faces, and body parts in separate blocks. Each scan consisted of a 405 time-points long sequence of fMRI volumes. Preprocessing included distortion correction, alignment, and intensity normalization. Motion-related variables and low-frequency signals were regressed out using AFNI. Cortical data was parcellated into 360 regions of interest (ROIs). Input features were structured as a 360 by 405 2D-tensor. No stimuli and brain-state synchronization was performed for delay adjustment. Time-points in task blocks were marked as specific brain states. Fixation blocks were labelled as 'others', yielding S = 9 brain states.

Procedures And Architectures
The model is a Bidirectional LSTM with forward and reverse hidden layers. Forward hidden activation is computed using past temporal dependencies. Backward hidden activation is calculated using future temporal dependency. Activations are combined via concatenation, addition, or averaging. The last layer is a fully-connected layer with softmax activation. The bi-LSTM architecture had two hidden layers with 256 hidden activations. A fully-connected layer with S = 9 neurons predicted the brain states. Inter-subject 10-fold cross-validation was employed for evaluation. Data was split into 9 parts for development and 1 for testing. The development set was split into 80-20 training-validation sets. Training data was windowed with size w = 40 and overlap of 10. The model was implemented in the Keras deep learning framework. Training used a GeForce GTX 980 GPU with batch size 32. The ADAM optimizer was used with a learning rate of 0.001. The model was trained for 100 epochs without early stopping. A dropout of 0.3 was applied in LSTM layers to prevent over-fitting. Class weights were estimated using Sklearn's compute_class_weight routine.

Key Results
The overall accuracy of the unidirectional LSTM model was 0.66 ± 0.18. The classification accuracy of the bidirectional LSTM (bi-LSTM-c) was 0.84 ± 0.02. The bi-LSTM performed 18% better than the unidirectional counterpart. LSTM models miss-classify to a larger extent compared to bi-LSTM-c. Misclassification was highest for both models to the 'Others' class. Confusion occurred between 'faces' and 'places' stimuli with task conditions. The model also gets confused between the stimuli 'body' and 'tools'. The bi-LSTM-c variant was used for the primary comparison.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The results demonstrate superior performance of Bi-LSTM over unidirectional LSTM. The model works well without hard-coded delay adjustment. This emphasizes the availability of useful information in immediate future samples. The framework explicitly models the dynamics of BOLD response. Future temporal context is crucial for capturing BOLD dynamics accurately.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study used a fixed window length, which may not be optimal. Future work may involve tuning the window-size and overlap. The problem of class imbalance still requires more sophisticated handling. The model sometimes gets confused between 'body' and 'tools' stimuli. No early stopping was performed, relying on fixed epochs.

Claims
Bidirectional LSTM improves brain state decoding accuracy by capturing future temporal context. Bi-LSTM accuracy was 0.84 compared to LSTM's 0.66. The improvement was 18% over the unidirectional counterpart. The model captures information from both past and future instances. Confusion remains between specific stimuli like body and tools. Class imbalance issues persist despite weighting. Future temporal context is essential for accurate BOLD modeling. Delay adjustment is not required for this framework.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study compared bi-LSTM with unidirectional LSTM and feed-forward NN. Different bi-LSTM merging schemes were considered (concat, add, avg). Class weights were applied to handle imbalanced classes. Dropout was used to prevent over-fitting during training.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 provides a schematic illustration of the Bidirectional LSTM. Figure 2 illustrates mean normalized confusion matrices for classification. Confusion matrices compare miss-classifications of LSTM and bi-LSTM-c.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a bi-LSTM model for robust brain state decoding. 2. The strongest evidence is the 18% accuracy improvement over unidirectional LSTM. 3. The future path involves tuning window sizes and handling class imbalance.

summary.title: Spontaneous regression of micro-metastases following primary tumor excision: a critical role for primary tumor secretome
summary.authors: Shaashua Lee, Anabel Eckerling, Boaz Israeli, Gali Yanovich, Ella Rosenne, Suzana Fichman-Horn, Ido Ben Zvi, Liat Sorski, Ronit Satchi-Fainaro, Tamar Geiger, Erica K Sloan, Shamgar Ben-Eliyahu
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the mechanisms behind the spontaneous regression of metastases following primary tumor (PT) excision, a phenomenon previously documented in case studies but lacking a mechanistic model. Using a highly sensitive luciferase-expressing MDA-MB-231 HM breast cancer model in BALB/c nu/nu mice, the authors demonstrate that removing the primary tumor leads to a marked regression of early-stage micro-metastases, while larger metastases remain unaffected. This regression is not due to surgical trauma, as sham surgery did not induce similar effects. Instead, the study identifies the primary tumor secretome as a critical support system for early metastatic growth. In vitro, tumor-conditioned medium enhanced cancer cell viability, adhesion, and endothelial tube formation. In vivo, replenishing the secretome via osmotic minipumps after PT excision significantly diminished metastatic regression. Proteomic and cytokine array analyses identified four key secreted factors: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. In vivo neutralization of these four factors arrested micro-metastasis development even in the presence of the primary tumor. Furthermore, analysis of the TCGA lung adenocarcinoma dataset revealed that high protein levels of these four factors correlate with poor patient survival (hazard ratio 2.05). These findings suggest that the primary tumor actively supports early metastatic niches via secreted factors, and that targeting these factors during the perioperative period could be a novel strategy to control minimal residual disease.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the mechanisms behind the spontaneous regression of metastases following primary tumor (PT) excision, a phenomenon previously documented in case studies but lacking a mechanistic model. Using a highly sensitive luciferase-expressing MDA-MB-231 HM breast cancer model in BALB/c nu/nu mice, the authors demonstrate that removing the primary tumor leads to a marked regression of early-stage micro-metastases, while larger metastases remain unaffected. This regression is not due to surgical trauma, as sham surgery did not induce similar effects. Instead, the study identifies the primary tumor secretome as a critical support system for early metastatic growth. In vitro, tumor-conditioned medium enhanced cancer cell viability, adhesion, and endothelial tube formation. In vivo, replenishing the secretome via osmotic minipumps after PT excision significantly diminished metastatic regression. Proteomic and cytokine array analyses identified four key secreted factors: IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 (PAI-1), and MIF. In vivo neutralization of these four factors arrested micro-metastasis development even in the presence of the primary tumor. Furthermore, analysis of the TCGA lung adenocarcinoma dataset revealed that high protein levels of these four factors correlate with poor patient survival (hazard ratio 2.05). These findings suggest that the primary tumor actively supports early metastatic niches via secreted factors, and that targeting these factors during the perioperative period could be a novel strategy to control minimal residual disease.

Research Context
Surgical removal of the primary tumor is a cornerstone of cancer treatment. However, various case studies report the opposite effect; spontaneous postoperative regression of evident cancer metastasis. Unfortunately, postulated mechanisms have not been empirically tested, as no animal model of spontaneous regression exists. The need to study potential interactions between the primary tumor (PT) and metastases is stressed by the current realization that the presence of a primary tumor is a systemic disease.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Herein, for the first time, we present an animal model of spontaneous regression of metastases following PT removal. We found that development of micro-metastases is supported by the numerous factors secreted from the PT. We hypothesized that the primary tumor secretome supports the survival and growth of distant micro-metastases. We hypothesized that if these four factors are among those that drive metastatic growth, their in vivo blockade would partly mimic the effect of primary tumor removal.

Methodological Details
A highly metastatic variant of the triple-negative breast adenocarcinoma cell line, MDA-MB-231 HM, was transduced with a codon-optimized firefly luciferase-mCherry vector. Eight-week old female BALB/c nu/nu mice were injected with 2×10 5 cells in 20 μl PBS into the fourth mammary fat pad. Once metastatic foci reached a total count of 10 6 photons/s (~ 3-4 weeks post injection), the primary tumor (average size of 80mm 3 ) was excised. CM was produced by incubating ~80% confluent MDA-MB-231 HM cells with serum-free medium for 24 h at 37°C, 5% CO2. CM (and the same volume of SM as control) was then concentrated by 3 kDa Amicon filters to a final volume of 100 μl/mouse. Alzet osmotic minipumps (model 1003D) were loaded with either CM or SM and implanted i.p. immediately following tumor excision. Human Cytokine Array (R&D systems, Proteome Profiler TM Array, ARY022) was used to compare relative expression levels of 102 soluble human proteins. Mass spectrometry-based secretome analysis was performed using the Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer. Mouse anti-human monoclonal antibodies were used to neutralize CXCL8/IL-8, Serpin E1/PAI-1, PDGF-AA, and MIF. Using the public TCGA provisional dataset (cBioPortal), we studied patient outcome in a lung adenocarcinoma cohort.

Procedures And Architectures
Primary tumor resection was performed under anesthesia with 2% isoflurane. For the sham surgery, an identical incision was made, however the PT was untouched. Cells were imaged for 8 hours, in 20 min intervals, using the IncuCyte system. Cells were incubated in CM or SM for 24 hrs, then washed and stained for AnnexinV-FITC and 7AAD. Proteins were digested overnight with LysC/Trypsin mix and sequencing-grade modified Trypsin at room temperature. MS analysis was performed using a top10 method in which every high resolution MS scan was followed by fragmentation. Lung sections (6 μm) were stained for Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E). Survival curve was conducted according to Kaplan Meier Analysis, and a hazard ratio was calculated in the R software.

Key Results
A dramatic decrease in metastatic signal, of up to 100-fold, was evident in mice along the 24 h following tumor excision, p<0.0001. These metastases have regressed into latent foci, as no increase in in vivo bioluminescent signal occurred for 50 days post-excision. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases, p<0.000. Metastases regressed significantly following excision of the primary tumor, while continued to increase in mice subjected to sham surgery, p<0.05. Medium conditioned by MDA-MB-231 HM tumor cells enhanced viability, p<0.001 and adhesion, p<0.01 of cancer cells. Mice that were treated with tumor-cell conditioned medium showed 10-fold less regression than mice that received serum-free medium, p<0.005. We identified 28 cytokines that were highly expressed in cancer cell CM. Unbiased mass spectrometry proteomic analysis of CM identified 2,600 proteins, 359 of which were annotated as extracellular factors. Antibody neutralization of these factors completely blocked metastatic progression, p<0.0001. High protein levels of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1 and MIF were associated with significantly lower survival with a hazard ratio of 2.05, p<0.05.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The findings of this study indicate a crucial supportive role for MDA-MB-231 HM tumor secretome in survival and progression of distant metastatic foci. Our findings suggest that tumor-secreted factors may act through multiple mechanisms to affect both malignant cells and/or their microenvironment. The findings provide an opportunity to empirically study metastatic regression into latent foci, and to explore mediating mechanisms. The primary tumor secretome can be a vital factor in promoting metastasis during early stages of metastatic formation.

Contradictions And Limitations
We herein tested only the combined effect of blocking four key secreted factors known to promote malignant progression. Other secreted factors are likely to also be involved in supporting metastatic progression. Different tumors, specifically syngeneic lines, should be similarly studied to test the generalizability of the novel phenomenon. The prevalence of post-operative regression of micro-metastases in cancer patients is currently unknown due to technical limitations.

Claims
Primary tumor excision causes spontaneous regression of early-stage micro-metastases. A dramatic decrease in metastatic signal, of up to 100-fold, was evident in mice along the 24 h following tumor excision. No increase in in vivo bioluminescent signal occurred for 50 days post-excision. Regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases. 
The primary tumor secretome supports the survival and growth of distant micro-metastases. Mice that were treated with tumor-cell conditioned medium showed 10-fold less regression. Medium conditioned by MDA-MB-231 HM tumor cells enhanced viability and adhesion. Larger micrometastases showed lower or no regression, potentially given their ability to secrete sufficient amount of the necessary factors. Targeting secreted factors could be a strategy to control minimal residual disease.
Neutralization of IL-8, PDGFaa, Serpin E1, and MIF arrests micro-metastasis development. Antibody neutralization of these factors completely blocked metastatic progression. High protein levels of these four factors were associated with significantly lower survival. No difference in regression of metastases was evident between these two groups on post-excision day-1. These factors are crucial for survival of early stage micro-metastases.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
We identified 28 cytokines that were highly expressed in cancer cell CM. Unbiased mass spectrometry proteomic analysis of CM identified 2,600 proteins. Pathway enrichment analysis identified proteins engaged in key steps of metastasis including apoptosis, angiogenesis, growth factor activity, focal adhesion, and metalloenzyme regulation.

Ethical Considerations
All procedures were approved by Monash University or Tel-Aviv University Animal Ethics Committees.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1A-B shows a dramatic decrease in metastatic signal following tumor excision. Figure 1E shows that regression was significantly less prominent in larger metastases. Figure 2D shows that mice treated with tumor-cell conditioned medium showed 10-fold less regression. Figure 3B shows that antibody neutralization of these factors completely blocked metastatic progression. Figure 3D shows that high protein levels of these four factors were associated with significantly lower survival.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that primary tumor excision causes spontaneous regression of early micro-metastases. 3. The future path is to exploit the perioperative period to control minimal residual disease by targeting pro-metastatic factors.

summary.title: The structural basis for regulation of the glutathione transporter Ycf1 by regulatory domain phosphorylation
summary.authors: Nitesh Kumar Khandelwal; Cinthia R Millan; Samantha I Zangari; Samantha Avila; Dewight Williams; Tarjani M Thaker; Thomas M Tomasiak
summary.executive_summary: This study presents the first high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the yeast glutathione transporter Ycf1, revealing the structural basis for its regulation by phosphorylation. Ycf1, an ABCC transporter, sequesters heavy metals and oxidized glutathione into the vacuole to protect cells from stress. While phosphorylation is known to regulate many ABC transporters, the mechanism remains poorly understood due to the intrinsic disorder of their regulatory domains (R-domains). Here, the authors report two inward-facing conformations of Ycf1 at 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å resolution, capturing a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain. The structures show that the R-domain is phosphorylated at three sites (S908, T911, S914) and forms extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with Nucleotide Binding Domain 1 (NBD1) and the lasso domain. These interactions are conserved between the wide and narrow inward-facing states, which are related by rigid body movements of the NBD1/R-domain complex. Biochemical assays demonstrate that dephosphorylation of the R-domain significantly reduces ATPase activity and alters the protein's proteolytic profile, indicating that phosphorylation stabilizes an active architecture. The study challenges previous models suggesting that phosphorylation releases the R-domain into a disordered state, instead proposing that phosphorylation drives the R-domain to bind NBD1, stabilizing the transporter in a primed, active conformation. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how post-translational modifications regulate ABCC transporters and offer insights into related human diseases like cystic fibrosis.

claims.description: R-domain phosphorylation stabilizes an active conformation of Ycf1 required for maximal ATPase activity.
The R-domain is ordered and bound to NBD1 in the phosphorylated state, contrary to previous models.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents the first high-resolution cryo-EM structures of the yeast glutathione transporter Ycf1, revealing the structural basis for its regulation by phosphorylation. Ycf1, an ABCC transporter, sequesters heavy metals and oxidized glutathione into the vacuole to protect cells from stress. While phosphorylation is known to regulate many ABC transporters, the mechanism remains poorly understood due to the intrinsic disorder of their regulatory domains (R-domains). Here, the authors report two inward-facing conformations of Ycf1 at 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å resolution, capturing a previously unobserved ordered state of the R-domain. The structures show that the R-domain is phosphorylated at three sites (S908, T911, S914) and forms extensive electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with Nucleotide Binding Domain 1 (NBD1) and the lasso domain. These interactions are conserved between the wide and narrow inward-facing states, which are related by rigid body movements of the NBD1/R-domain complex. Biochemical assays demonstrate that dephosphorylation of the R-domain significantly reduces ATPase activity and alters the protein's proteolytic profile, indicating that phosphorylation stabilizes an active architecture. The study challenges previous models suggesting that phosphorylation releases the R-domain into a disordered state, instead proposing that phosphorylation drives the R-domain to bind NBD1, stabilizing the transporter in a primed, active conformation. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how post-translational modifications regulate ABCC transporters and offer insights into related human diseases like cystic fibrosis.

Research Context
Ycf1 transports glutathione and heavy metals into vacuoles to counter cell stress. Ycf1 belongs to the ABCC subfamily of ATP-binding cassette transporters. Many ABCC transporters are regulated by phosphorylation on intrinsically disordered domains. The regulatory mechanism of phosphorylation in these transporters is poorly understood. Previous cryo-EM structures of ABCC transporters showed mostly disordered R-domains. Lack of sequence assignment in previous models limited understanding of R-domain interactions. No structure of an intact R-domain with NBDs had been determined previously.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to determine how R-domain phosphorylation regulates Ycf1 activity. The authors hypothesize that phosphorylation induces structural changes in the R-domain. They predict that these structural changes affect ATPase activity. The study seeks to resolve the ordered state of the R-domain. The hypothesis is that phosphorylation stabilizes interactions between the R-domain and NBD1. The authors propose that this stabilization is required for maximal ATPase activity.

Methodological Details
Ycf1 was expressed in S. cerevisiae DSY5 strain. Two forms were purified: wild-type (WT) and NBD2 Walker B mutant E1435Q. Cryo-EM grids were prepared for both WT and E1435Q Ycf1 in apo conditions. Only the E1435Q dataset yielded homogenous particles for structure determination. Two inward-facing conformations were identified: IFwide and IFnarrow. The E1435Q mutant had substantially lowered ATPase activity compared to WT. Data processing was performed using RELION and cisTEM. Model building was guided by evolutionary coupling analysis. ATPase assays were conducted using an enzyme-coupled assay. Phosphorylation was characterized using mass spectrometry and phosphostaining.

Procedures And Architectures
The Ycf1 gene was codon-optimized and cloned into a yeast expression vector. Protein expression was induced by adding YPG media. Purification involved lysis, affinity chromatography, and size exclusion chromatography. Cryo-EM data was processed with drift correction and CTF estimation. Particle picking was performed manually and automatically using reference maps. 3D classification and refinement were performed in RELION. The final structures were refined using Phenix and CCP-EM modules. Evolutionary coupling analysis used 13,723 sequences from Uniref90. ATPase rates were determined at 30°C using NADH consumption monitoring. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 was generated using lambda phosphatase treatment.

Key Results
Two cryo-EM structures of Ycf1 were determined at 3.4 Å and 4.0 Å resolution. The structures captured an ordered state of the intrinsically disordered R-domain. R-domain phosphorylation was observed at S908, T911, and S914. Phosphorylation induced electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions with NBD1 and the lasso domain. These interactions were constant between the IFwide and IFnarrow states. Dephosphorylation of Ycf1 resulted in a drastic reduction in ATPase activity. Dephosphorylated Ycf1 showed increased protease accessibility in limited proteolysis assays. The R-domain buried ~1530 Å² and ~1338 Å² of surface area in IFnarrow and IFwide, respectively. The IFnarrow state showed occlusion of the non-functional ATP binding site in NBD1. GSSG stimulated ATPase activity at physiologically relevant concentrations.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The findings challenge the model where phosphorylation releases the R-domain into a disordered state. Instead, phosphorylation drives the R-domain to bind NBD1, stabilizing an active architecture. This stabilization is required for maximal ATPase activity. The R-domain acts as a regulatory "clutch" that engages the motor without performing work. The structures provide a plausible explanation for the inhibitory role of S251 phosphorylation. These insights may inform the development of allosteric modulators for ABCC transporters.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study does not rule out an inhibitory role for the unphosphorylated state. The NBD2 region was less ordered, limiting detailed modeling in some states. A third state, IFtransition, was insufficiently detailed for model building. The study focuses on Ycf1, so generalizability to other ABCC transporters requires further validation. The exact mechanism of how phosphorylation prevents protease accessibility is not fully resolved.

Claims
R-domain phosphorylation stabilizes an active conformation of Ycf1 required for maximal ATPase activity. Dephosphorylation drastically reduced ATPase activity. Phosphorylated R-domain formed extensive contacts with NBD1. Phosphorylation increased protease resistance. The unphosphorylated state may still have some activity. This mechanism may apply to other ABCC transporters.
The R-domain is ordered and bound to NBD1 in the phosphorylated state, contrary to previous models. Cryo-EM structures showed an ordered R-domain. Phosphorylation sites were resolved in the structure. Previous structures showed disordered R-domains. This provides a new model for ABCC regulation.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The E1435Q mutant was used to trap inward-facing conformations. Dephosphorylation experiments confirmed the functional role of phosphorylation. Evolutionary coupling analysis supported the R-domain/NBD1 interaction interface.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the cryo-EM structures of IFwide and IFnarrow states. Figure 2 details the R-domain phosphorylation and interactions. Figure 3 illustrates the hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions stabilizing the R-domain. Figure 4 compares the NBD orientation in IFwide and IFnarrow states.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the first high-resolution structures of Ycf1 with an ordered, phosphorylated R-domain. 2. The strongest evidence is the correlation between R-domain phosphorylation, structural stability, and ATPase activity. 3. The future path involves applying these insights to understand and modulate other ABCC transporters.

summary.title: Phylogenetic study of thermophilic genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, Parageobacillus, and proposal of a new classification Quasigeobacillus
summary.authors: Carling (University of Canberra); Blom (Diversity Arrays Technology Pty Ltd); Georges (University of Canberra); Berenice Talamantes Becerra
summary.executive_summary: This study presents a comprehensive phylogenomic analysis of the thermophilic bacterial genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus to resolve taxonomic ambiguities and propose a new genus, Quasigeobacillus. The research addresses the limitations of traditional 16S rRNA sequencing and DNA-DNA hybridization by employing high-resolution metrics, specifically Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) and Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI), alongside a maximum likelihood tree constructed from 662 orthologous core genes. A total of 113 genome assemblies were selected from public databases and recent isolates to ensure broad representation. The analysis revealed that the genomes split into two primary clades: Clade I, containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species, and Clade II, comprising the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Further partitioning of Clade I identified three distinct subclades. The authors propose that a specific subclade, previously assigned to Anoxybacillus or Geobacillus, should be elevated to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., based on its distinct phylogenetic positioning and unique genomic characteristics. The study highlights the critical importance of analyzing closely related genera together to avoid incongruent genus designations. Two species of Anoxybacillus, A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus, showed inconsistent positioning across different phylogenetic methods, leaving their affinities unresolved. The findings underscore the necessity of using combined phylogenomic approaches for accurate bacterial classification in the era of next-generation sequencing.

Combined phylogenomic analysis is necessary for accurate bacterial classification.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study presents a comprehensive phylogenomic analysis of the thermophilic bacterial genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus to resolve taxonomic ambiguities and propose a new genus, Quasigeobacillus. The research addresses the limitations of traditional 16S rRNA sequencing and DNA-DNA hybridization by employing high-resolution metrics, specifically Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) and Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI), alongside a maximum likelihood tree constructed from 662 orthologous core genes. A total of 113 genome assemblies were selected from public databases and recent isolates to ensure broad representation. The analysis revealed that the genomes split into two primary clades: Clade I, containing all Geobacillus, all Parageobacillus, and some Anoxybacillus species, and Clade II, comprising the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Further partitioning of Clade I identified three distinct subclades. The authors propose that a specific subclade, previously assigned to Anoxybacillus or Geobacillus, should be elevated to a new genus, Quasigeobacillus gen. nov., based on its distinct phylogenetic positioning and unique genomic characteristics. The study highlights the critical importance of analyzing closely related genera together to avoid incongruent genus designations. Two species of Anoxybacillus, A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus, showed inconsistent positioning across different phylogenetic methods, leaving their affinities unresolved. The findings underscore the necessity of using combined phylogenomic approaches for accurate bacterial classification in the era of next-generation sequencing.

Research Context
Next-generation sequencing allows researchers to establish thresholds for bacterial taxonomical scales. DNA-DNA hybridization was previously considered the gold standard for bacterial taxonomy. 16S rRNA gene sequencing has low resolution, limiting its usefulness for classification. Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) provides higher resolution to detect relatedness among genomes. Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI) is recommended for comparing distant genomes. The genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus belong to the family Bacillaceae. These genera are moderate thermophiles with the ability to form spores. Anoxybacillus species are mainly isolated from geothermal sources. Geobacillus species have been isolated from hot springs and oilfields. Parageobacillus is a thermophilic facultative anaerobe isolated from geothermal springs. Anoxybacillus was proposed in 2000 based on a strain from animal manure. Geobacillus was described in 2001 by splitting a group from Bacillus. Parageobacillus was defined in 2016 by reassigning a clade from Geobacillus. Previous studies suggested reclassification of G. galactosidasius to Parageobacillus. The current study aims to determine the placement of newly isolated strains.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question is how to accurately delimit the genera Anoxybacillus, Geobacillus, and Parageobacillus. The study hypothesizes that combined phylogenomic analysis reveals problems in genus delimitation. It is predicted that considering closely related genera together is essential for accurate phylogeny. The authors propose that a specific clade should be elevated to a new genus. The hypothesis is that ANI and AAI metrics provide better resolution than 16S rRNA. The study aims to resolve the affinities of two Anoxybacillus species with inconsistent positioning. The researchers suggest that A. tepidamans and a genomospecies belong to a new genus. The study tests whether core gene trees align with ANI and AAI dendrograms. The hypothesis is that unique genes can identify distinct clades. The study investigates the genomic characteristics of the proposed new genus. The authors aim to provide a preliminary placement of seven newly isolated strains. The research questions whether merging clades would support further genus mergers. The study seeks to clarify the phylogenetic position of Anoxybacillus within Clade I.

Methodological Details
A total of 113 genomes were selected for phylogenomic metrics. The study used publicly available whole genome sequences. Average Nucleotide Identity (ANI) and Average Amino Acid Identity (AAI) were calculated. A maximum likelihood tree was built from 662 orthologous core genes. Genomes were obtained from the RefSeq database. Thirty-two Anoxybacillus strains were included in the analysis. Seventy-three Geobacillus strains were included in the analysis. Eight Parageobacillus genomes were represented in the analysis. One Bacillus genome was included as an outgroup. Whole genome sequences of newly isolated strains were included. The group contained 31 chromosome level assemblies. The group contained 33 scaffold genomes. The group contained 49 genomes up to the contig level. Anomalous genome assemblies were excluded from the study. Core genes were identified using EDGAR 2.0. Geobacillus thermodenitrificans NG80-2 was used as a starting reference. Bacillus subtilis spizizenii TU-B-10T was included as an outgroup. Five assemblies with low CDS numbers were excluded. One duplicate assembly was removed. CDS were concatenated and aligned using MUSCLE. A maximum-likelihood tree was built using FastTree. ANI was calculated using the ani.rb script. AAI was calculated using the aai.rb script. Draft genomes were concatenated with 100 N bases between contigs. UPGMA dendrograms were constructed using the DendroUPGMA web server. Trees were plotted using Interactive Tree Of Life. Genes unique to clade I-c were identified using BLASTn. Relaxed BLASTn filtering criteria included 30% identity. The CDS from Anoxybacillus tepidamans PS2 were used for alignment.

Procedures And Architectures
Methods were based on the reassessment of the genus Geobacillus by Aliyu et al. A set of core genes was identified from the bacterial genomes. A maximum likelihood tree was constructed from the core genes. ANI and AAI scores were calculated for all genome pairs. UPGMA dendrograms were constructed from the similarity matrices. GC content and genome size were calculated for all genomes. Topology, GC contents, and ANI values were used for taxonomic delimitation. The core genome was identified using iterative BLAST comparisons. Orthologous genes were identified via BLAST against the reference assembly. The core genome consists of CDS with orthologs in all assemblies. Alignments were used to build the phylogenetic tree. Default parameters were selected for ANI calculation. Default parameters were selected for AAI calculation. Similarity values were arranged into matrices for clustering. Unweighted pair group with arithmetic mean clustering was used. BLASTn alignment was used to find genes unique to clade I-c. CDS were aligned against NCBI RefSeq and nt databases. Genes present in all clade I-c members were considered unique. The study followed the reclassification of G. galactosidasius to P. galactosidasius.

Key Results
The core gene set consisted of 662 orthologous genes per genome. The maximum likelihood tree included 114 genomes. The tree splits into three major groups: outgroup, Clade I, and Clade II. Clade I consists of eighty-seven genomes. Clade II consists of twenty-four Anoxybacillus genomes. Clade I contains all Geobacillus and all Parageobacillus. Clade I contains some species of Anoxybacillus. Clade II contains the majority of Anoxybacillus species. Clade I is partitioned into three clades. One clade consists of Geobacillus. One clade consists of Parageobacillus. A third clade is suggested for elevation to a new genus. The new genus is named Quasigeobacillus. Two Anoxybacillus species showed inconsistent positioning. Anoxybacillus sp. EFIL had an ANI of 97.99. Geobacillus sp. MMMUD3 had an ANI of 97.14. Geobacillus sp. DSP4a had an ANI of 97.64. Anoxybacillus sp. CHMUD had the most distant ANI of 95.03. The affinities of A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus remain unresolved.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study shows the importance of considering closely related genera together. Problems in genus delimitation are revealed by combined analysis. Genus designation can become incongruent without broader phylogenetic assessment. Clade I-c is seen to be outside of existing genera when analyzed together. Merging clades would support further genus mergers. The new genus Quasigeobacillus is distinct from existing genera. Phylogenetic assessment is an essential step in isolate identification. The breadth of species assessed requires further consideration. The study highlights the need for high-resolution metrics like ANI and AAI. The findings support the reclassification of certain species. The unique genes in clade I-c support its distinctiveness. The study provides a framework for future taxonomic revisions. The results emphasize the limitations of single-gene approaches. The study demonstrates the utility of core gene phylogenomics.

Two Anoxybacillus species showed inconsistent positioning among trees. The affinities of A. vitaminiphilus and A. amylolyticus remain unresolved. A new genus Quasigeobacillus should be established for clade I-c. Clade I-c is distinct from Geobacillus and Parageobacillus. Six unique CDS were found in clade I-c. ANI and AAI values support the separation. The core gene tree supports the new genus. The candidate new genus is closer to Parageobacillus. Merging with Parageobacillus might be an alternative. This clarifies the taxonomy of thermophilic bacilli. It prevents incongruent genus designations.
Combined phylogenomic analysis is necessary for accurate bacterial classification. Problems in delimitation are revealed by combined analysis. ANI and AAI provide higher resolution than 16S rRNA. Core gene trees provide vertical phylogenetic relationships. Some species remain unresolved despite combined analysis. Future studies should use multi-method approaches. Taxonomic revisions should consider closely related genera.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Five assemblies with low CDS numbers were excluded. One duplicate assembly was removed. Anomalous genome assemblies were excluded. The study used relaxed BLASTn filtering criteria. The study used default parameters for ANI and AAI.

1. The core contribution is the proposal of a new genus Quasigeobacillus. 2. The strongest evidence is the combined use of ANI, AAI, and core gene trees. 3. The future path is to consider closely related genera together in phylogenetic studies.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates whether the length of chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesions impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes following successful percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents (DES). A total of 235 consecutive patients were enrolled and divided into long CTO (≥30mm) and short CTO (<30mm) groups. Baseline characteristics were similar except for higher prior PCI in the long group and more bifurcation lesions in the short group. In-hospital complications were comparable, though intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. At six months, angiographic outcomes, including in-stent restenosis and binary restenosis, were statistically similar between groups, although a numerical trend toward higher restenosis was observed in the long group. Over two years, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including death and myocardial infarction, did not differ significantly. However, the incidence of repeat PCI, predominantly target vessel revascularization (TVR), was significantly higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%). Multivariate analysis identified long CTO as an independent predictor for repeat PCI (OR 4.26). The authors conclude that while long CTO lesions are associated with higher rates of repeat revascularization, they do not translate into worse hard endpoints like mortality or MI, suggesting similar overall safety and efficacy profiles in the DES era.

Research Context
Successful CTO PCI is associated with improved clinical outcomes compared to failed PCI. It remains unclear if long CTO lesions have different outcomes than short ones in the DES era. Long coronary artery lesions are known to be worse prognostic factors after PCI. Procedural success rates for CTO patients remain lower than for non-CTO patients. There are no definite answers regarding CTO PCI outcomes based on lesion length.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to investigate if CTO lesion length impacts six-month angiographic outcomes. The study also investigates the impact on two-year clinical outcomes following successful PCI. The authors predicted adverse clinical outcomes would be more frequent in the long CTO group. This prediction was based on worse clinical risk factors in the long CTO group. The use of newer generation DES was dominant in the short CTO group.

Methodological Details
A total of 235 consecutive CTO patients underwent successful PCI with DESs. Patients were enrolled from November 2004 to October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital. Patients were divided into long CTO (≥30mm) and short CTO (<30mm) groups. The long CTO group included 159 patients and the short CTO group 76. CTO was defined as complete obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0. The estimated duration of CTO was required to be at least 3 months. Only de novo lesions were included, excluding in-stent restenosis. Loading doses of clopidogrel and aspirin were administered before the index procedure. Maintenance dual antiplatelet therapy included aspirin 100mg and clopidogrel 75mg. Adjunctive cilostazol usage was at the physician's discretion. PCI procedures used standard techniques with various available guidewires. Atheroablative devices were not utilized, and simple pre-dilation was mostly performed. Procedural success was defined as final stenosis less than 30% and TIMI ≥2. Quantitative coronary angiography parameters were measured before, after, and at 6 months. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6-12 months. Follow-up data was collected via interview, medical records, or telephone. Primary clinical endpoint was MACE, including death, MI, and revascularization. Statistical analysis used Student's t-test, chi-square, and logistic regression.

Procedures And Architectures
PCI was performed using current guidelines and standard techniques. Various guidewires were used to cross the CTO lesion. Simple pre-dilation with balloon was performed to accommodate the stent. Adjunctive balloon dilatation was performed if necessary for optimal outcome. All PCI was performed using DES, with type decided by the operator. QCA measurement and analysis were performed at the Cardiovascular Center. Follow-up angiography was obtained in 99 long CTO and 45 short CTO patients. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 20 software. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Key Results
Baseline characteristics were similar except prior PCI was more frequent in the long group. Bifurcation lesions were more frequent in the short CTO group. Intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. Total death incidence was 3.1% in long and 5.2% in short groups. Cardiac death incidence was 1.2% in long and 2.6% in short groups. Myocardial infarction incidence was 1.8% in long and 2.6% in short groups. MACE incidence was 21.3% in long and 13.1% in short groups. Repeat PCI incidence was significantly higher in the long CTO group. Target vessel revascularization was 16.3% in long and 6.5% in short groups. Long CTO was an independent predictor for repeat PCI with OR 4.26. In-stent restenosis incidence was 33.3% in long and 26.6% in short groups. Binary restenosis incidence was 19.1% in long and 8.8% in short groups. Late loss was 0.65 mm in long and 0.46 mm in short groups.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Long CTO PCI with DES is similarly safe as short CTO PCI. Higher TVR in long CTO did not translate into increased mortality. Less myocardial viability and developed collaterals may lessen restenosis effects. The study suggests procedural safety and efficacy are similar between groups. Long-term studies with larger populations are needed for final conclusions.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study is not randomized and is a single-center registry. Baseline clinical and procedural characteristics were slightly different between groups. Newer generation DES was more frequent in the short CTO group. Unmeasured confounders and analytical bias could exist despite statistical adjustment. Follow-up angiography was not routinely performed in all patients. The sample size was relatively small, limiting power to detect angiographic differences. The two-year follow-up period was not long enough for long-term safety.

Claims
Long CTO lesion length is an independent predictor for repeat PCI. Multivariate analysis showed long CTO predicted repeat PCI. The odds ratio for repeat PCI was 4.26. Overall MACE rates were not significantly different between groups. Long CTO patients may require closer monitoring for revascularization.
Angiographic outcomes at 6 months are similar between long and short CTO groups. Binary restenosis rates were not statistically different. Late loss values were similar between the two groups. There was a numerical trend toward higher restenosis in the long group. DES implantation provides similar angiographic results regardless of length.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Logistic regression was used to adjust for risk factors. Risk factors included sex, age, hypertension, and diabetes. The study adjusted for prior PCI and bifurcation lesion.

Ethical Considerations
The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study.

Key Figures Tables

There is a unit inconsistency in the source text between abstract and results. The results section lists µM for others. I will report the abstract's value as written but note the context). Molecular docking studies indicated that compound 6h forms a stable ligand-α-glucosidase complex with a binding energy of -10.56 kcal/mol, facilitated by hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469, and hydrophobic interactions with Trp329. These findings suggest that the new tricyclic scaffold offers a promising lead for developing clinically effective antidiabetic drugs with potentially fewer gastrointestinal side effects compared to sugar mimetics.

Research Context
The global number of diabetic patients increased from 108 million in 1980 to 422 million in 2014. Prevalence among people over 18 years old rose from 4.7% in 1980 to 8.5% in 2014. α-Glucosidase inhibitors like acarbose delay carbohydrate hydrolysis to reduce postprandial glucose levels. Acarbose is associated with gastrointestinal side effects such as flatulence and diarrhea. These side effects are a major cause for reduced patient compliance. Most previously developed inhibitors were sugar mimetics requiring tedious synthesis. There is a high demand for effective antidiabetic agents with fewer side effects.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aimed to develop α-glucosidase inhibitors to overcome side effects of sugar mimetics. The authors hypothesized that modifying pyridine, triazole, and pyrimidine scaffolds would yield active inhibitors. The central research question was whether new tricyclic hybrids would exhibit significant inhibitory activity. It was predicted that the new compounds would have IC50 values comparable to or better than acarbose. Molecular docking was hypothesized to explain the binding modes and stability of the complexes.

Methodological Details
Twenty-five tricyclic 2-phenoxypyrido[3,2-e][1,2,4]triazolo[1,5-a]pyrimidin-5(4H)-ones were synthesized. The synthesis started with diphenoxy-N-cyanimidocarbonate reacting with 2-hydrazino-3-carboxylic pyridine. Triazole intermediate B was formed using triethylamine in ethanol at room temperature. Compound 1 was converted to thione 3 using phosphorous pentasulfide in pyridine. Imidoyl chloride 5 was prepared using phosphorous oxychloride in boiling benzene. Compounds 6a-d were synthesized by reacting 5 with aromatic amines in pyridine. Compound 6h was formed by hydrazinolysis of 5 followed by reaction with 2-methoxy benzaldehyde. In vitro screening used α-glucosidase enzyme from Baker's yeast. The substrate used was para-nitrophenyl-α-D-glucopyranoside (p-NPG) at 20 mM. Compounds were tested at 100 µg/mL initially, with serial dilutions for IC50 determination. Acarbose was used as the positive control in all assays.

Procedures And Architectures
The reaction mixture for intermediate B was stirred overnight at room temperature. Acidification with conc. HCl and heating at 80 °C yielded compound 1. N-alkylation of compound 1 used potassium carbonate in DMF for 18 hours. Thione 3 was obtained in 90% yield as a yellow amorphous powder. Chlorination to form 5 involved boiling benzene and POCl3. Reaction of 5 with amines was refluxed in pyridine for 5-7 hours. Hydrazone formation for 6h involved refluxing in ethanol for 3-5 hours. Molecular docking used the Autodock software package. The protein structure was downloaded from the RCSB data bank (PDB 3W37). Binding energies and hydrogen bonds were calculated for the docked complexes.

Key Results
The inhibitory activity of all tested compounds ranged between 30% and 63%. Eight compounds exhibited more than 50% average percent inhibition. Compound 3 showed an average percent inhibition of 60.38%. The IC50 of compound 3 was 167.82 µM. The IC50 of compound 2a was 304.13 µM. The IC50 of compound 2d was 173.83 µM. Compound 6h exhibited the highest inhibition with an IC50 of 104.07 mM (as stated in abstract). Compound 6h had the lowest binding energy of -10.56 kcal/mol. Compound 6a had a binding energy of -9.76 kcal/mol. Compound 6b had a binding energy of -9.17 kcal/mol. Acarbose established 10 hydrogen bonds with the enzyme. Compound 6h established three hydrogen bonds with Ala234, Arg552, and Asp469.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The introduction of a branch to the pyrimidine scaffold via a nitrogen bridge enhanced activity. Amino-bridge substitution at position 4 was responsible for strong inhibitory activity. The stability of the ligand-α-glucosidase complex correlates with inhibitory potency. Trp329 plays a significant role in directing the ligand in the binding site. The new scaffold offers a non-sugar-mimetic alternative for antidiabetic drug development.

Contradictions And Limitations
There is a unit discrepancy in the abstract (mM) versus results (µM) for IC50 values. The study only evaluated in vitro activity, lacking in vivo or clinical data. The mechanism of action relies on docking predictions, which require experimental validation. The gastrointestinal side effects of the new compounds were not tested.

Claims
Compound 6h is a more potent α-glucosidase inhibitor than acarbose. Compound 6h had an IC50 of 104.07 mM (abstract) or lower than acarbose. Compound 6h had the lowest binding energy (-10.56 kcal/mol). The unit in the abstract (mM) is inconsistent with typical µM values for such inhibitors. This suggests 6h is a promising lead compound for further development.
The tricyclic scaffold provides a novel mechanism for α-glucosidase inhibition. The compounds are not sugar mimetics. Binding is stabilized by specific hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions. The exact physiological relevance of the binding mode is not fully established. This opens new avenues for designing antidiabetic drugs with fewer side effects.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study compared multiple derivatives to isolate the effect of the amino-bridge. Binding energies were compared across compounds 6a, 6b, and 6h.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 illustrates the structure of acarbose and related compounds. Figure 2 illustrates the synthetic route towards fused pyrimidine derivatives. Figure 3 shows the average percent inhibition of compounds 6a-6i. Figure 4 displays the IC50 values of the active compounds. Figure 5 shows the binding modes of the docked compounds. Table 1 lists the binding energies and hydrogen bonds for the docked compounds.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the synthesis of 25 new tricyclic α-glucosidase inhibitors. 2. The strongest evidence is that compound 6h outperforms acarbose in IC50 and binding energy. 3. The future path involves developing these non-sugar-mimetic leads into clinical drugs.

summary.title: Tumor PD-L1 selectively suppresses type I interferon in myeloid cells to suppress CTL recruitment to promote lung metastasis
summary.authors: John D Klement, Priscilla S Redd, Chunwan Lu, Alyssa D Merting, Dakota B Poschel, Dafeng Yang, Gang Zhou, David H Munn, Kebin Liu
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the mechanism by which tumor-expressed PD-L1 (tPD-L1) promotes immune suppression, specifically focusing on lung metastasis in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and colorectal cancer (CRC) models. Contrary to the prevailing paradigm that tPD-L1 directly inhibits cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activity via PD-1 engagement, the authors demonstrate that tPD-L1 has no direct effect on CTL killing when only tumor cells and CTLs are present. Instead, tPD-L1 functions by engaging PD-1 on myeloid cells (mPD-1), creating an immunosuppressive niche that suppresses type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling. Using CRISPR-Cas9 knockout models of 4T1 and CT26 cells, the study shows that while PD-L1 loss does not affect primary tumor growth, it significantly reduces lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals that tPD-L1 engagement with mPD-1 activates SHP-2, which dephosphorylates STAT1, thereby repressing the expression of chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10. This repression impairs the recruitment of CTLs to the lung metastatic site. The study further validates these findings in human patient cohorts, showing that response to PD-1 blockade immunotherapy correlates with the restoration of IFN-I signaling in myeloid cells. The authors conclude that the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis is critical for controlling CTL infiltration in lung metastasis, providing a mechanistic basis for the efficacy of checkpoint blockade in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings. This work shifts the focus from direct CTL inhibition to myeloid-mediated suppression of chemokine production, highlighting the importance of the tumor microenvironment in metastatic progression.

claims.description: tPD-L1 does not directly suppress CTL activation or lytic function when only tumor cells and CTLs are present.
tPD-L1 promotes lung metastasis by engaging myeloid PD-1 to suppress type I interferon signaling.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the mechanism by which tumor-expressed PD-L1 (tPD-L1) promotes immune suppression, specifically focusing on lung metastasis in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and colorectal cancer (CRC) models. Contrary to the prevailing paradigm that tPD-L1 directly inhibits cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activity via PD-1 engagement, the authors demonstrate that tPD-L1 has no direct effect on CTL killing when only tumor cells and CTLs are present. Instead, tPD-L1 functions by engaging PD-1 on myeloid cells (mPD-1), creating an immunosuppressive niche that suppresses type I interferon (IFN-I) signaling. Using CRISPR-Cas9 knockout models of 4T1 and CT26 cells, the study shows that while PD-L1 loss does not affect primary tumor growth, it significantly reduces lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner. Single-cell RNA sequencing reveals that tPD-L1 engagement with mPD-1 activates SHP-2, which dephosphorylates STAT1, thereby repressing the expression of chemokines Cxcl9 and Cxcl10. This repression impairs the recruitment of CTLs to the lung metastatic site. The study further validates these findings in human patient cohorts, showing that response to PD-1 blockade immunotherapy correlates with the restoration of IFN-I signaling in myeloid cells. The authors conclude that the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis is critical for controlling CTL infiltration in lung metastasis, providing a mechanistic basis for the efficacy of checkpoint blockade in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings. This work shifts the focus from direct CTL inhibition to myeloid-mediated suppression of chemokine production, highlighting the importance of the tumor microenvironment in metastatic progression.

Research Context
The mechanism of tPD-L1 induction of immune suppression via an intermediate cell is incompletely understood. PD-L1 and PD-1 immune checkpoint blockade is believed to function by blocking PD-L1 to PD-1 engagement. Particular attention has been paid to the role of tumor-expressed PD-L1 as a direct molecular shield. Emerging data suggests response to PD-1/L1 blockade may depend on tumor anatomic sites. The dominant cause of mortality is metastatic growth, not primary tumor growth. How tPD-L1 might differentially drive metastasis from primary tumor is unknown. PD-1 expression in non-T cell populations is important for tumor immune evasion. How non-T cell-expressed PD-1 connects tPD-L1 to CTL suppression is incompletely understood.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether tPD-L1 directly protects tumor cells from CTL cytotoxicity. The authors hypothesize that tPD-L1 targets myeloid cell-expressed PD-1 to suppress type I IFN. This suppression represses Cxcl9 and Cxcl10 expression in myeloid cells. This impairs CTL recruitment to the lung niche to enhance established lung metastasis. The study aims to determine if tPD-L1 exhibits no direct effect on CTL activity. It is hypothesized that a third factor in the lung metastatic niche is necessary. The hypothesis is that tPD-L1 engages mPD-1 to antagonize type I interferon signaling. The predicted outcome is that PD-L1 loss will decrease lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner.

Methodological Details
The study used 4T1 murine triple negative breast cancer and CT26 colorectal cancer cell lines. Cd274 encoding PD-L1 was deleted using CRISPR-Cas9 in these cell lines. An in vitro CTL-tumor interaction system using 2/20 tumor-specific CTLs was utilized. 2/20 cells recognize the H2-Ld-restricted AH1 epitope of gp70 protein. In vivo models included orthotopic injection for primary tumors and tail vein injection for metastasis. Lung metastasis was quantified by harvesting lungs and inflating with India ink solution. RNA sequencing was performed on lungs colonized by WT and PD-L1-deficient 4T1 cells. Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on CD45+ leukocytes from colonized lungs. Approximately 7500 cells were analyzed using UMAP for dimensional reduction. Flow cytometry was used to validate transcriptomic data in 4T1-colonized lungs. Myeloid cells were depleted using clodronate liposomes in tumor-bearing mice. Human patient data from metastatic basal cell carcinoma was analyzed. Statistical analysis was conducted using Prism8 and two-tailed Student's t-test. Bulk RNA sequencing used STARv2.5 for alignment and DESeq2 for quantification. Single-cell libraries were generated using the Chromium Single Cell 3' Reagent Kit v3.

Procedures And Architectures
HEK293FT cells were co-transfected with pCMV-VSV-G, psPAX2, and lentiCRISPRv2 plasmids. Tumor cells were transduced with lentivirus and selected with puromycin. Cells were sorted for marker-negative cells using a BD FACSARIA. 4T1 orthotopic tumors were established by injection at the right second mammary gland. CT26 subcutaneous tumors were established by injection at the right flank. For experimental metastasis, tumor cells were injected into the lateral tail vein. Anti-CD8α or isotype control antibodies were injected i.v. every other day. Samples were blocked in FACS Buffer containing mouse FcBlock. Intracellular staining was performed using Cytofix/Cytoperm Plus kit. Data was acquired on FACSCalibur or LSRFortessa and analyzed with FlowJo v10.6.0. RNA was extracted using Direct-zol RNA microprep kit. Reads were aligned to mm10 reference genome using STARv2.5. scRNA-seq libraries were sequenced on Illumina NextSeq 500 platform. Cells were clustered using the first fifty principal components. Clusters were annotated by comparison to pre-existing RNA-sequencing datasets using SingleR.

Key Results
tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage when an antigen-specific effector CTL encounters a tumor cell. No difference was observed in primary tumor growth between PD-L1 WT and KO 4T1 cells. Knocking out PD-L1 in tumor cells significantly decreases lung metastasis. Increased infiltration of CD3+ cells was observed in the lung after loss of tPD-L1. No difference in initial tumor cell colonization was seen one day after tail vein injection. PD-L1-deficient and competent 4T1 metastasized equally in RAGII-KO mice. Genetic ablation of MHC class I and CD8+ T cell depletion revealed tPD-L1 drives metastasis. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed tPD-L1 engages myeloid PD-1 to antagonize type I IFN. Expression changes were observed in myeloid cells, not CTLs, in the metastatic niche. Enhanced antigen presentation machinery was detected in macrophages following tPD-L1 loss. Pdcd1lg2 encoding PD-L2 was identified as a marker for IFN-stimulated myeloid cells. Engagement with 4T1 tPD-L1 enhanced SHP-2 activation and decreased pSTAT1 levels. Disruption of RAW PD-1 or 4T1 PD-L1 expression enhanced IFNβ production. Depletion of myeloid cells diminished tPD-L1 function in promoting lung tumor growth. Human patient response to PD-1 blockade correlates with IFN-I response in myeloid cells.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The study uncouples the role of tPD-L1 at the metastatic site from primary tumor growth. tPD-L1 binds to mPD-1 to enforce an immunologically cold microenvironment. The tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis controls CTL tumor infiltration. This axis underlies the efficacy of ICB immunotherapy in neoadjuvant and adjuvant settings. The PD-1/L1 axis functions as a negative feedback circuit for type I interferon. Low response rates in interferon alpha therapies may be due to compensatory PD-1/L1 upregulation. Type I interferon signaling is essential for myeloid cell function in CTL recruitment. This work highlights the importance of myeloid cells in bridging tPD-L1 to CTL suppression.

Contradictions And Limitations
Conflicting findings for the role of tPD-L1 in PD-1 blockade efficacy have been reported. There is a consensus that tPD-L1 may be sufficient but not necessary for response. One limitation is that the study exclusively analyzed lung metastases. Lung metastases may have a uniquely inflamed microenvironment due to barrier tissue location. The mechanism underlying tPD-L1 induction of immune suppression via an intermediate cell is incompletely understood. How non-T cell-expressed PD-1 connects tPD-L1 to CTL suppression is incompletely understood.

Claims
tPD-L1 does not directly suppress CTL activation or lytic function when only tumor cells and CTLs are present. In vitro cytotoxicity results show no difference in killing between WT and KO cells. 2/20 CTLs exert antigen-specific cytotoxicity within minutes. Previous paradigms suggest tPD-L1 serves as a direct molecular shield against CTL lysis. This shifts the focus to indirect mechanisms involving other cell types.
tPD-L1 promotes lung metastasis by engaging myeloid PD-1 to suppress type I interferon signaling. PD-L1 loss significantly decreases lung metastasis in a CTL-dependent manner. Single-cell RNA sequencing shows tPD-L1 antagonizes type I IFN in myeloid cells. Depletion of myeloid cells impairs tPD-L1 promotion of lung metastasis. No difference in primary tumor growth was observed. This identifies a new axis for CTL recruitment control in metastasis.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Ablation of MHC class I and CD8+ T cells confirmed the CTL-dependent nature of the effect. Depletion of myeloid cells using clodronate liposomes validated the role of myeloid cells. Disruption of RAW PD-1 or 4T1 PD-L1 expression enhanced IFNβ production. The study used both bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing for robust validation.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows tPD-L1 confers no survival advantage in in vitro CTL-tumor interaction. Figure 2 shows no difference in primary tumor growth between WT and KO cells. Figure 3 shows increased CD3+ infiltration in lung after tPD-L1 loss. Figure 4 shows single-cell RNA sequencing of CD45+ leukocytes from colonized lungs. Figure 5 shows validation of transcriptomic data by flow cytometry. Figure 6 shows tPD-L1 engagement with mPD-1 creates an immunosuppressive niche. Figure 7 shows human patient response to PD-1 blockade correlates with IFN-I response.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of the tPD-L1/mPD-1/IFN-I/STAT1/Cxcl9/10 axis in lung metastasis. 2. The strongest evidence is the significant decrease in lung metastasis upon PD-L1 knockout in a CTL-dependent manner. 3. The future path involves exploring this axis in other metastatic sites and clinical trials.

summary.title: Inhibitor of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase impairs paramyxovirus replication
summary.authors: Naveen Kumar, Sanjay Barua, Nitin Khandelwal, Kundan Kumar Chaubey, Ram Kumar, Krishan Dutt, Yogesh Chander, Thachamvally Riyesh, Vir Shoor Singh, Bhupendra Nath
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the role of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) in paramyxovirus replication, specifically focusing on Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and Newcastle disease virus (NDV). The authors demonstrate for the first time that SERCA is a critical host factor facilitating paramyxovirus replication. Using the SERCA-specific inhibitor Thapsigargin, they show that treatment at non-cytotoxic concentrations significantly reduces viral replication in Vero cells. Conversely, overexpression of SERCA2 rescues the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin, confirming SERCA's supportive role. The study reveals that paramyxovirus infection induces SERCA expression, which can be blocked by Thapsigargin. Mechanistic investigations using time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays indicate that Thapsigargin primarily inhibits viral entry and disrupts the subcellular localization of viral proteins, causing them to remain in cytoplasmic foci rather than localizing to the cell surface for budding. Notably, the study reports a rare phenomenon where NDV, but not PPRV, acquires significant resistance to Thapsigargin after long-term passage (70 passages) in Vero cells. This suggests that viruses may evolve to bypass dependency on cellular factors targeted by inhibitors. The findings highlight SERCA as a potential novel target for broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics, offering a strategy to combat viral resistance by targeting host factors rather than viral proteins. The work contributes to the understanding of paramyxovirus replication mechanisms and the development of host-directed antiviral strategies.

claims.description: SERCA facilitates paramyxovirus replication.
NDV can acquire resistance to SERCA inhibitors.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the role of sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium-ATPase (SERCA) in paramyxovirus replication, specifically focusing on Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV) and Newcastle disease virus (NDV). The authors demonstrate for the first time that SERCA is a critical host factor facilitating paramyxovirus replication. Using the SERCA-specific inhibitor Thapsigargin, they show that treatment at non-cytotoxic concentrations significantly reduces viral replication in Vero cells. Conversely, overexpression of SERCA2 rescues the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin, confirming SERCA's supportive role. The study reveals that paramyxovirus infection induces SERCA expression, which can be blocked by Thapsigargin. Mechanistic investigations using time-of-addition and virus step-specific assays indicate that Thapsigargin primarily inhibits viral entry and disrupts the subcellular localization of viral proteins, causing them to remain in cytoplasmic foci rather than localizing to the cell surface for budding. Notably, the study reports a rare phenomenon where NDV, but not PPRV, acquires significant resistance to Thapsigargin after long-term passage (70 passages) in Vero cells. This suggests that viruses may evolve to bypass dependency on cellular factors targeted by inhibitors. The findings highlight SERCA as a potential novel target for broad-spectrum antiviral therapeutics, offering a strategy to combat viral resistance by targeting host factors rather than viral proteins. The work contributes to the understanding of paramyxovirus replication mechanisms and the development of host-directed antiviral strategies.

Research Context
Antiviral strategies have traditionally targeted essential viral proteins. High mutation rates in viral genomes lead to drug resistance. This resistance has prompted a shift toward targeting host factors. Host factors can be proviral or antiviral. SERCA regulates calcium uptake into the endoplasmic reticulum. The role of SERCA in virus replication was previously unknown. Recent studies suggest other calcium ATPases support virus replication.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to determine if SERCA regulates paramyxovirus replication. The hypothesis is that SERCA facilitates viral entry and protein localization. It is predicted that inhibiting SERCA will reduce viral titers. Overexpression of SERCA is expected to rescue viral replication. The study investigates whether viruses can acquire resistance to SERCA inhibitors. It is hypothesized that NDV may develop resistance upon long-term passage.

Methodological Details
Vero, 293T, HeLa, and goat kidney cells were used. Cells were grown in DMEM with 10% fetal bovine serum. PPRV and NDV were used as the viral models. Thapsigargin was used as the SERCA inhibitor. Cytotoxicity was assessed using the MTT assay. Antiviral efficacy was measured by plaque assay at MOI 0.1. Virucidal activity was tested by incubating virions with Thapsigargin. Time-of-addition assays were performed to identify inhibited viral steps. SERCA2 overexpression was achieved using pCR3-SERCA2 plasmids. Immunofluorescence assays were used to visualize viral protein localization. Viral resistance was selected by 70 passages in Thapsigargin.

Procedures And Architectures
Thapsigargin was applied at 0.5 µM, a non-cytotoxic concentration. Virus titers were determined by plaque assay. For entry assays, preattached virus was allowed to enter at 37°C. Immunofluorescence involved fixation with 4% paraformaldehyde. Cells were stained with primary and secondary antibodies. Resistance selection involved sequential passage in 0.25 µM Thapsigargin. Virus harvest times varied between 72-120 hours for passage. Western blotting was used to analyze SERCA2 expression levels. GAPDH was used as a housekeeping control.

Key Results
Thapsigargin did not affect cell viability at concentrations up to 2 µM. Thapsigargin significantly inhibited NDV and PPRV replication. Thapsigargin did not exhibit virucidal activity on cell-free virions. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued the inhibitory effect of Thapsigargin. PPRV infection induced SERCA2 expression at 3 hpi. Thapsigargin blocked virus-induced SERCA2 expression. Highest inhibition occurred when Thapsigargin was added 30 min pre-infection. Thapsigargin did not affect viral attachment, RNA synthesis, or budding. Thapsigargin treatment reduced NDV and PPRV entry. Defective subcellular localization was observed in ~70% of treated cells. NDV acquired significant resistance to Thapsigargin at passage 35. PPRV did not acquire resistance to Thapsigargin after 70 passages.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
SERCA is a crucial host factor for paramyxovirus replication. SERCA inhibition primarily impacts viral entry and protein localization. Targeting host factors may provide broad-spectrum antiviral activity. Viruses can acquire resistance to host-targeting agents. NDV resistance suggests a change in host factor requirement. SERCA is a potential candidate for antiviral drug development.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study could not determine direct interaction between SERCA and viral proteins. Co-immunoprecipitation assays were unsuccessful. The mechanism of NDV resistance is not yet understood. Fluctuations in viral titers occurred during passage experiments. The study did not identify specific viral mutations conferring resistance.

Claims
SERCA facilitates paramyxovirus replication. Overexpression of SERCA2 rescued Thapsigargin inhibition. Thapsigargin reduced viral titers. Thapsigargin did not affect viral attachment. SERCA is a potential antiviral target.
NDV can acquire resistance to SERCA inhibitors. NDV showed significant resistance at passage 35. PPRV did not show resistance. Complete resistance was not achieved. Viruses can evolve to bypass host factor dependency.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Control-passaged viruses did not exhibit resistance. Resistance was specific to Thapsigargin passage.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows Thapsigargin cytotoxicity and antiviral efficacy. Figure 2 shows SERCA2 overexpression rescues replication. Figure 3 shows virus-induced SERCA2 expression. Figure 4 shows time-of-addition assay results. Figure 5 shows Thapsigargin inhibits viral entry. Figure 6 shows defective subcellular localization. Figure 7 shows selection of resistant mutants.

Three Takeaways
1. SERCA is a critical host factor for paramyxovirus replication. 2. Thapsigargin inhibits viral entry and protein localization. 3. NDV can acquire resistance to SERCA inhibitors.
