summary.title: Lack of negative density-dependence regulation in a dominant oak tree from a neotropical highland forest
summary.authors: Irene Calderón-Sanou, Luis Diego Ríos, Alfredo Cascante-Marín, Gilbert Barrantes, Eric J Fuchs
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the mechanisms regulating seedling establishment of Quercus costaricensis, a monodominant oak species in the Talamanca highland forests of Costa Rica. Contrary to the widely accepted Janzen-Connell hypothesis, which posits that conspecific negative density-dependence (CNDD) drives species coexistence by reducing survival near conspecifics, this research finds no evidence of CNDD regulation on seedling survival or recruitment. The authors monitored 3,538 seedlings across four 400-m² plots between 2014 and 2017, analyzing the effects of conspecific density, distance to the nearest adult, bamboo density, and herbivory. Results indicate that while herbivory and Chusquea bamboo density significantly decreased seedling survival, conspecific density did not exert a negative effect. Instead, seedling survival was highest at intermediate distances from adult trees, suggesting a potential facilitative role of ectomycorrhizal transfer. The study argues that the lack of intraspecific density regulation, potentially due to predator satiation and symbiotic benefits, explains the dominance of Q. costaricensis in these highland forests. Local density is instead regulated by herbivory and interspecific competition with bamboo, rather than conspecific interactions.

claims.description: Conspecific negative density-dependence does not regulate seedling survival in Q. costaricensis.
Herbivory and bamboo density are the primary regulators of seedling density.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the mechanisms regulating seedling establishment of Quercus costaricensis, a monodominant oak species in the Talamanca highland forests of Costa Rica. Contrary to the widely accepted Janzen-Connell hypothesis, which posits that conspecific negative density-dependence (CNDD) drives species coexistence by reducing survival near conspecifics, this research finds no evidence of CNDD regulation on seedling survival or recruitment. The authors monitored 3,538 seedlings across four 400-m² plots between 2014 and 2017, analyzing the effects of conspecific density, distance to the nearest adult, bamboo density, and herbivory. Results indicate that while herbivory and Chusquea bamboo density significantly decreased seedling survival, conspecific density did not exert a negative effect. Instead, seedling survival was highest at intermediate distances from adult trees, suggesting a potential facilitative role of ectomycorrhizal transfer. The study argues that the lack of intraspecific density regulation, potentially due to predator satiation and symbiotic benefits, explains the dominance of Q. costaricensis in these highland forests. Local density is instead regulated by herbivory and interspecific competition with bamboo, rather than conspecific interactions.

Research Context
Conspecific negative density-dependence is a primary mechanism for species coexistence in tropical forests. Tropical highland forests are typically dominated by few tree species, unlike diverse lowlands. Previous studies in temperate oaks showed susceptibility to CNDD and distance to adults. Ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults may positively affect seedling density and survival. The specific dynamics of tropical oak communities remain scarcely studied.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study tests the importance of CNDD regulation on seedling survival and recruitment. The authors expected weak or no CNDD regulation on seedling survival. A positive effect of nearby adults on seedling recruitment was hypothesized. The effect of Chusquea bamboo density on survival was also investigated. Herbivory was included as a potential factor limiting seedling survival.

Methodological Details
The study was conducted at Cerro de la Muerte Biological Station in Costa Rica. Four 400-m² plots were established in old-growth forests undisturbed for 30 years. Plots were subdivided into 64 quadrats of 2.5 x 2.5 m for censuses. A total of 3,538 seedlings were tracked between 2014 and 2017. Seedling height, distance to nearest adult, and conspecific density were measured. Herbivory was estimated using the qualitative index of Núñez-Farfán and Dirzo. Bamboo stem density was counted in each quadrat. Spatial aggregation was analyzed using Ripley's L(t) transformation.

Procedures And Architectures
Annual survival probability was modeled using generalized linear mixed-effects models. A binomial distribution was used for the survival analysis. Quadrat and census year were included as random effects. A dummy variable identified seedlings from the 2014 census versus 2015 recruits. Recruitment was analyzed using a GLMM with a quasi-poisson distribution. The lme4 package in R was used for statistical analyses. Variables were standardized to facilitate comparison between effects.

Key Results
No significant effect of CNDD on seedling survival was found. Bamboo density and herbivory significantly decreased seedling survival. Annual seedling survival decreased from 73.2% in 2015 to 63.8% in 2017. Seedling height had the strongest positive effect on survival. Survival was highest at intermediate distances from adult trees. Herbivory decreased at higher seedling densities, contrary to Janzen-Connell predictions. 1,578 new recruits were recorded in 2015. Recruitment increased with conspecific seedling density but not adult density.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The lack of CNDD may explain the dominance of Q. costaricensis. Predator satiation may explain the lack of density-dependent regulation. Ectomycorrhizal transfer from adults may facilitate seedling survival at intermediate distances. High herbivory tolerance or long-lived leaves may explain observed damage levels. Interspecific competition with Chusquea bamboo is a key regulator of density.

Contradictions And Limitations
Results disagree with Janzen-Connell expectations of negative density regulation. Environmental factors like soil acidity and temperature were beyond the study scope. The study only analyzed recruitment after the 2014 masting event. Few recruits were recorded in 2016 and 2017, limiting recruitment analysis.

Claims
Conspecific negative density-dependence does not regulate seedling survival in Q. costaricensis. No effect of CNDD on seedling survival was detected. Survival was not related to conspecific density. Temperate oaks are typically susceptible to CNDD. This lack of regulation contributes to species dominance.
Herbivory and bamboo density are the primary regulators of seedling density. Bamboo density and herbivory decreased survival. Herbivory was present in over 99% of seedlings. Herbivory decreased at higher densities, suggesting satiation. Local density is controlled by these factors rather than conspecifics.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
A second-degree polynomial effect for distance to adults was tested. Interactions between seedling and Chusquea densities were significant. No significant interactions were found between herbivory and distance.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the distribution of herbivory indices. Figure 2 illustrates the effect of variables on survival. Table S1 lists the retained model variables and interactions. Figure S1 displays the spatial aggregation of seedlings.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration of absent CNDD in a dominant oak. 2. The strongest evidence is the significant negative effect of bamboo and herbivory. 3. The future path involves understanding how predator satiation and ECM drive dominance.

summary.title: Influence of plant growth regulators and nitrogen sources on the production and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk Hormonal treatment and fertilization to plant development
summary.authors: Leone Campos Rocha; Fábio Andrade; Teixeira; Márcio Dos; Santos Pedreira; Daniela Deitos Fries; Giovanna Evely; Leite Costa; Ana Cláudia; Maia Soares; Daniel Lucas; Santos Dias; Abdias José De Figueiredo; Angel Amaral; Seixas; Camile Carvalho Pacheco
summary.executive_summary: This study evaluated the effects of seed treatment with plant growth regulators (PGR) and nitrogen fertilization methods on the growth and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. The research aimed to optimize pasture establishment by analyzing germination characteristics, dry matter yield, and physiological composition. Two experiments were conducted: one focusing on germination and initial growth at 30 days after sowing (DAS), and another on dry mass production and pigment content under different fertilization regimes. The PGR used was a mixture of auxin, cytokinin, and gibberellin. Results indicated that PGR treatment increased germination percentages and root dry mass, with optimal levels estimated at 10.3 mL.kg-1 for germination and 12.8 mL.kg-1 for root mass. A significant interaction was found between seed type (coated vs. conventional) and PGR levels for leaf and pseudostem dry mass, where coated seeds performed better at lower PGR concentrations. In the second experiment, soil nitrogen fertilization resulted in higher dry mass productions of leaf, stem, shoot, and root compared to foliar or no fertilization. The combination of PGR and soil fertilization yielded the highest dry mass for stem, leaf, and shoot. PGR also increased chlorophyll a content, suggesting enhanced photosynthetic efficiency. The study concludes that exogenous hormonal compounds act on organogenesis and increase development, while soil N-fertilization maximizes photosynthetic processes and growth rates. Lower PGR levels are recommended for coated seeds due to their higher embryo quality and protection.

claims.description: Plant growth regulators increase germination and root dry mass in Brachiaria decumbens.
Soil nitrogen fertilization is more effective than foliar fertilization for dry mass production.
Coated seeds perform better at lower PGR levels than conventional seeds.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study evaluated the effects of seed treatment with plant growth regulators (PGR) and nitrogen fertilization methods on the growth and development of Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk. The research aimed to optimize pasture establishment by analyzing germination characteristics, dry matter yield, and physiological composition. Two experiments were conducted: one focusing on germination and initial growth at 30 days after sowing (DAS), and another on dry mass production and pigment content under different fertilization regimes. The PGR used was a mixture of auxin, cytokinin, and gibberellin. Results indicated that PGR treatment increased germination percentages and root dry mass, with optimal levels estimated at 10.3 mL.kg-1 for germination and 12.8 mL.kg-1 for root mass. A significant interaction was found between seed type (coated vs. conventional) and PGR levels for leaf and pseudostem dry mass, where coated seeds performed better at lower PGR concentrations. In the second experiment, soil nitrogen fertilization resulted in higher dry mass productions of leaf, stem, shoot, and root compared to foliar or no fertilization. The combination of PGR and soil fertilization yielded the highest dry mass for stem, leaf, and shoot. PGR also increased chlorophyll a content, suggesting enhanced photosynthetic efficiency. The study concludes that exogenous hormonal compounds act on organogenesis and increase development, while soil N-fertilization maximizes photosynthetic processes and growth rates. Lower PGR levels are recommended for coated seeds due to their higher embryo quality and protection.

Research Context
Adverse climatic factors shorten the soil preparation and planting window. This reduction necessitates greater seed efficiency in germination and emergence speed. Management practices are essential to improve herbage production using favorable climatic conditions. Synthetic compounds act as growth promoters with effects similar to phytohormones. Phytohormones regulate homeostasis through signaling networks and intermediary metabolites. High levels of gibberellic compounds are uneconomical and reduce forage mass. Low concentrations of gibberellin positively affect forage yield. PGRs show potential under stress by regulating growth-related genes. Nitrogen expands the plant lifecycle and increases vegetative growth rates. Increased photoassimilate production maximizes structural characteristics and post-defoliation recovery. Nitrogen is an indispensable constituent in organic compounds and cell division. Nitrogen applications to degraded pastures increase water use efficiency and soil cover.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The aim was to evaluate the effect of seed treatment with PGR and nitrogen fertilization. The study focused on Brachiaria decumbens cv. Basilisk growth and development. Germinative characteristics were assessed as a primary outcome. Dry matter yield was a key metric for evaluating growth. Physiological composition, including pigments, was analyzed to assess health. It was hypothesized that PGR would increase germination and mass yields. It was expected that soil N-fertilization would increase dry mass productions. The interaction between seed type and PGR levels was a specific focus. Coated seeds were hypothesized to perform better at lower PGR levels. Embryo quality was expected to contribute to greater tissue formation. Soil fertilization was predicted to maximize photosynthetic processes. Exogenous hormonal compounds were expected to act on organogenesis.

Methodological Details
Experiments were performed at UESB, Itapetinga-BA, between June and September 2017. Germination was conducted in a Mangelsdorf germination chamber (MA-401). Germination conditions included a 12h photoperiod and constant 28ºC temperature. Growth evaluations were performed in a greenhouse using pots with 12 kg dry soil. Soil was collected at 0-20 cm depth and passed through a 4-mm sieve. Fertilization recommendations were based on the Soil Fertility Commission for Minas Gerais. A 2 x 4 factorial scheme in a completely randomized design (CRD) was used. Two commercial seed types (coated and conventional) were tested. Four levels of growth regulator (0, 8, 16, 24 mL.kg-1) were applied. Seeds were imbibed in PGR for approximately two hours. The PGR contained auxin (0.05 mg.L-1), cytokinin (0.09 mg.L-1), and gibberellin (0.05 mg.L-1). Initial growth assessments were done at 30 days after sowing (DAS). Sowing was performed in seedling trays with 32 cells per replicate. Sterilized coconut residue was used as the substrate for initial growth. The second experiment evaluated PGR (0, 24 mL.kg-1) and four nitrogen fertilization methods. Eight treatments were used with four plants per replicate and four replicates. A standardization cut was performed at 30 DAS with a 15 cm residue height. Data collection followed two periods of 28 days after the cut. Soil and foliar nitrogen fertilization rates were 75 kg.ha-1 N and 3 L.ha-1. Data were analyzed using the MIXED procedure of SAS. Significance was declared when P ≤ 0.05. Germination percentage and speed index (GSI) were determined over 14 days. Chlorophylls and carotenoids were quantified using DMSO extraction and spectrophotometry.

Procedures And Architectures
Germination was monitored daily for 14 days to determine percentage and GSI. Whole-plant yield was determined at the end of the experimental period. Fresh and dry mass of root, stem, and leaf were measured. The third fully expanded leaf was collected at 10 a.m. for pigment analysis. An aliquot of 200 mg fresh mass was prepared for pigment extraction. 5 mL of DMSO was added to the leaf aliquot for extraction. Readings were taken at wavelengths of 665, 649, and 480 nm. Pigment values were adjusted to mg.g-1 of fresh mass. Regression equations were used to estimate maximum points for PGR effects. Tukey test was used for comparison of means in Experiment 2. Single-degree-of-freedom contrast statements analyzed linear and quadratic PGR effects. Seed, PGR, and interaction effects were analyzed as fixed effects. The foliar fertilizer composition included N, P2O5, Mg, S, Zn, Mn, Cu, B, Mo, Co. The density of the foliar spray was 1.37 g.mL-1. Soil fertilization was applied after the standardization cut. Foliar fertilization was applied as a spray. Multiple fertilization combined soil and foliar methods. Greenhouse temperature and humidity were recorded using a digital thermo-hygrometer.

Key Results
The interaction between seed type and PGR levels was not significant for germination. There was a quadratic effect of PGR levels on germination. Treatment with 10.3 mL.kg-1 PGR promoted greater germination. Coated seeds had higher germination values than conventional seeds. Treatment with 12.8 mL.kg-1 PGR resulted in higher root dry mass. There was an interaction between seed type and PGR for leaf and pseudostem mass. Coated seeds performed better at 8.85 mL.kg-1 for leaf mass. Coated seeds performed better at 9.57 mL.kg-1 for pseudostem mass. Conventional seeds required 15.5 mL.kg-1 for leaf mass. Conventional seeds required 18.1 mL.kg-1 for pseudostem mass. Soil fertilization resulted in higher dry mass of leaf, stem, shoot, and root. Combining PGR and soil fertilization yielded the greatest stem, leaf, and shoot mass. PGR reduced leaf, stem, and shoot production when combined with multiple fertilization. PGR increased root dry mass only when combined with multiple fertilization. PGR had a significant effect on chlorophyll a content. Fertilization methods influenced levels of chlorophyll a, b, and carotenoids.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Exogenous hormones change hormonal balance and biosynthesis levels. Increased gibberellin concentration implies greater intracellular transport of metabolites. Gibberellin acts on genes responsible for germinative characteristics. Gibberellin reduces abscisic acid concentrations, overcoming dormancy. Coated seeds have higher germination due to protection and nutrient provision. Auxin in PGR increases rhizogenesis by stimulating stem cell multiplication. PIN proteins enable intracellular transport of auxins. Conventional seeds require higher PGR levels due to reduced efficiency. Hormonal interactions are comprised of a signaling network. Soil fertilization is more efficient for photosynthetic processes than foliar. Combined PGR and soil fertilization reflect in higher dry mass accumulation. Higher chlorophyll a levels favor ATP synthesis in chloroplasts. Foliar nitrogen may participate in cytokinin synthesis and chlorophyll production.

Claims
Plant growth regulators increase germination and root dry mass in Brachiaria decumbens. PGR increased germination percentages for both seed types. Optimal PGR level for germination was 10.3 mL.kg-1. Optimal PGR level for root mass was 12.8 mL.kg-1. Some studies found no significant response to specific hormone sets. PGR is a key tool in pasture establishment.
Soil nitrogen fertilization is more effective than foliar fertilization for dry mass production. Soil fertilization resulted in higher dry mass of all structures. Combining PGR and soil fertilization yielded the greatest mass. PGR reduced mass when combined with multiple fertilization. Soil N-fertilization maximizes photosynthetic processes and growth rates.
Coated seeds perform better at lower PGR levels than conventional seeds. Coated seeds had higher germination and GSI. Coated seeds performed better at 8.85 mL.kg-1 for leaf mass. Conventional seeds required higher PGR levels for optimal mass. Lower PGR levels are recommended for coated seeds.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Regression equations were used to estimate maximum points for PGR effects. Tukey test was used for comparison of means. Single-degree-of-freedom contrast statements analyzed PGR effects.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows average, minimum, and maximum temperatures and relative humidity. Table 1 describes the composition of the foliar spray. Table 2 presents germination characteristics for different seed types. Table 3 shows root dry mass production. Table 4 details leaf and pseudostem dry mass production. Table 5 presents dry mass production under different fertilization methods. Table 6 shows contents of chlorophylls and carotenoids.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the evaluation of PGR and nitrogen fertilization effects on Brachiaria decumbens. 2. The strongest evidence is the significant increase in dry mass with soil fertilization and PGR. 3. The future path involves optimizing PGR levels for different seed types.

summary.title: Toxicity of TiO2, SiO2, ZnO, CuO, Au and Ag engineered nanoparticles on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp
summary.authors: Ch Lakshmi N Murthy; Mohammed M Idris; Shashi Singh
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three soluble salts on the hatching and early development of Artemia sp. Given the increasing environmental release of nanomaterials, a simple and efficient test to estimate acute toxicity is required. The authors utilized Artemia cysts and nauplii as model organisms due to their robustness and cost-effectiveness. The study employed two parallel assays: a hatching rate test using hydrated and bleached cysts, and a standard Artemia toxicity test monitoring nauplii viability. Physicochemical characterization via TEM and DLS revealed that nanoparticles exhibited different behaviors in salt water, with some showing flocculation. The results demonstrated a clear order of toxicity: Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2. Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles showed the highest toxicity, significantly reducing hatching rates and increasing larval mortality. A strong inverse correlation was found between hatching rates and larval mortality, suggesting that the hatching test can serve as a valid pre-screening tool for nanoparticle hazard assessment. The study also observed oxidative stress markers (ROS) in exposed nauplii, particularly with silver nanoparticles. The findings highlight the utility of Artemia assays for high-throughput screening of nanomaterial toxicity in aquatic environments.

claims.description: Artemia hatching rate is a sensitive indicator of nanoparticle toxicity.
Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles are the most toxic to Artemia.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three soluble salts on the hatching and early development of Artemia sp. Given the increasing environmental release of nanomaterials, a simple and efficient test to estimate acute toxicity is required. The authors utilized Artemia cysts and nauplii as model organisms due to their robustness and cost-effectiveness. The study employed two parallel assays: a hatching rate test using hydrated and bleached cysts, and a standard Artemia toxicity test monitoring nauplii viability. Physicochemical characterization via TEM and DLS revealed that nanoparticles exhibited different behaviors in salt water, with some showing flocculation. The results demonstrated a clear order of toxicity: Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2. Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles showed the highest toxicity, significantly reducing hatching rates and increasing larval mortality. A strong inverse correlation was found between hatching rates and larval mortality, suggesting that the hatching test can serve as a valid pre-screening tool for nanoparticle hazard assessment. The study also observed oxidative stress markers (ROS) in exposed nauplii, particularly with silver nanoparticles. The findings highlight the utility of Artemia assays for high-throughput screening of nanomaterial toxicity in aquatic environments.

Research Context
Nanomaterials pose risks to the environment and human health due to expanding applications. There is a lack of information on the impact of nanoscale objects on ecosystems. Aquatic systems are the primary receptacles for released nanomaterials. Artemia sp. are used as a model organism for toxicological assays. Previous studies rarely used hatching of hydrated cysts as a toxicity endpoint.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to estimate the acute toxicity of six nanoparticles on Artemia hatching and nauplii. The hypothesis is that nanoparticles will affect hatching rates and larval viability. The study predicts an order of toxicity based on nanoparticle type. It is hypothesized that hatching rate correlates with larval mortality. The goal is to validate the hatching test as a hazard assessment tool.

Methodological Details
Six nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three salts were tested. Nanoparticles were sourced from the NANOVALID project consortium. Artemia cysts (San Francisco Bay strain) were used for cultures. Cysts were hydrated in distilled water and bleached with sodium hypochlorite. Hatching occurred in 25% salt water at 28°C for 24 hours. Nanoparticle concentrations of 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L were used. The standard Artemia toxicity test used concentrations from 100 to 0.01 mg/L. Viability was counted at 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours. Oxidative stress was measured using DCFDA staining. Experiments were repeated six times for statistical validity.

Procedures And Architectures
Nanoparticle suspensions were sonicated at 30W for 10 minutes. TEM was used to characterize nanoparticles on copper grids. DLS was used to measure particle size in water and salt water. Artemia cysts were decapsulated using 20% sodium hypochlorite for 15 minutes. Hatching was monitored under continuous light and aeration. Nauplii were transferred to six-well plates for the toxicity test. Mortality was defined as cessation of swimming or movement. LD50 was calculated using GraphPad software. DCFDA fluorescence was imaged using a Zeiss Axiovert imager. Data was analyzed for correlation using Microsoft Excel.

Key Results
The order of toxicity was estimated as Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2. Control hatching rate was 74% ± 5.5 with 97% viability. Silver and CuO reduced hatching rate to about 29% at 100 mg/L. Viability of hatched nauplii in Ag/CuO was 50% at 100 mg/L. Silver nitrate showed 80% mortality in 24 hours. LC50 of silver nanoparticles was around 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. TiO2 hatching rate was 41.50% at 100 mg/L with 67.8% viability. SiO2 at 10 mg/L showed hatching and viability equivalent to controls. A strong inverse correlation (-0.7853) was found between hatching and mortality. No statistically significant difference was found in mean values (P=0.683).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The hatching test serves as a valid pre-screening tool for nanoparticle toxicity. Toxicity may be due to ionic forms or gut clogging by nanoparticles. Artemia is a suitable model for assessing nanoparticle behavior in aquatic environments. The assays are easy, short-term, and use mortality as an endpoint. The method allows for high-throughput hazard identification of nanomaterials.

Contradictions And Limitations
Sedimentation and flocculation of nanoparticles may vary between particles. Ionic components may precipitate due to high salinity. The study focuses on acute toxicity, not chronic effects. Morphological abnormalities were not observed despite high toxicity.

Claims
Artemia hatching rate is a sensitive indicator of nanoparticle toxicity. Hatching rate dropped drastically in the presence of nanoparticles. There is a strong correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality. SiO2 at low concentration showed better hatching than control. This assay can be used for high-throughput screening.
Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles are the most toxic to Artemia. Silver and CuO showed the highest effect on hatching. Silver nitrate caused 80% mortality in 24 hours. Viability was better at lower concentrations (10 mg/L). These nanoparticles pose a higher risk to aquatic ecosystems.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Experiments were repeated six times to ensure validity. Validity criterion was low mortality in the control. Correlation tests were performed using online software.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows TEM images of nanoparticles. Figure 2 shows DLS values in water and salt water. Table 1 presents hatching rates and viability data. Figure 3 illustrates hatching rate changes. Table 2 presents larval toxicity and LC50 data. Figure 4 shows mortality over time. Figure 5 shows nanoparticle accumulation in gut. Figure 6 shows correlation between hatching and mortality.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the validation of Artemia hatching as a nanoparticle toxicity assay. 2. The strongest evidence is the strong inverse correlation (-0.7853) between hatching and mortality. 3. The future path is using this assay for high-throughput hazard identification.

summary.title: Major concerns with the integrity of the mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier in dodecyl-phosphocholine used for solution NMR studies
summary.authors: Martin S King; Paul G Crichton; Jonathan J Ruprecht; Edmund R S Kunji
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a critical analysis of a previous study by Brüschweiler et al. that claimed to refold the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3) from inclusion bodies using the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC) for solution NMR studies. The authors argue that DPC is too harsh for AAC3, leading to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation. They present evidence from isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), NMR, and thermostability assays demonstrating that the binding affinities reported for the DPC-refolded protein are orders of magnitude weaker than those observed for native, membrane-embedded AAC3. Specifically, the Kd for carboxyatractyloside (CATR) binding to DPC-refolded AAC3 was reported as ~150 µM, whereas the authors' measurements on native AAC3 show a Kd of ~72 nM, a difference of 200 to 2000-fold. Furthermore, functional reconstitution assays showed that AAC3 diluted into DPC prior to reconstitution lost its ability to transport ADP, whereas control samples in mild detergent retained activity. The authors conclude that the DPC-refolded protein is in a non-native, unfolded state, rendering the NMR data biologically irrelevant. They highlight that the high positive charge of AAC3 and the negative charge of ligands at neutral pH may lead to non-specific interactions in the DPC environment, further complicating the interpretation of the previous NMR results. The paper underscores the importance of using mild detergents like dodecyl-maltoside for studying membrane proteins to preserve their native structure and function.

claims.description: DPC-refolded AAC3 is in a non-native, unfolded state.
The binding affinities reported for DPC-refolded AAC3 are significantly weaker than for native AAC3.

summary.title: MicroRNA-196a is regulated by ER and is a prognostic biomarker in ER+ Breast Cancer
summary.authors: Michael J G Milevskiy, Udai Gujral, Carolina Del Lama Marques, Andrew Stone, Korinne Northwood, Lez J Burke, Julia M W Gee, Kenneth Nephew, Susan Clark, Melissa A Brown, Mjg Milevskiy
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the transcriptional regulation of MicroRNA-196a (MIR196A) and its role as a prognostic biomarker in breast cancer. The authors demonstrate that MIR196A expression is dynamically controlled by the oestrogen receptor (ERα) through complex long-range transcriptional interactions between promoter and enhancer elements. Specifically, the MIR196A2 locus, located within the HOXC cluster, is upregulated by oestradiol in MCF7 cells, a process mediated by ERα and its pioneer factor FOXA1 binding to putative promoters and distal enhancers, including the HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE). Chromatin conformation capture (3C) and ChIA-PET analyses confirm physical interactions between these enhancers and the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter region. Clinically, MIR196A expression is significantly increased in models of hormone receptor-positive disease resistance, including tamoxifen-resistant and chemotherapeutic-resistant cell lines. In patient cohorts, high MIR196A expression correlates with poor survival in post-menopausal ER+ breast cancer, whereas it associates with better outcomes in pre-menopausal ER+ disease and triple-negative breast cancer. The study further reveals that DNA methylation patterns at the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters change in response to endocrine therapy resistance, suggesting that de-repression of these regulatory elements contributes to the development of therapeutic resistance. These findings establish MIR196A as a robust prognostic factor for advanced ER+ disease and provide insights into the epigenetic and transcriptional mechanisms driving breast cancer progression and resistance.

documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the transcriptional regulation of MicroRNA-196a (MIR196A) and its role as a prognostic biomarker in breast cancer. The authors demonstrate that MIR196A expression is dynamically controlled by the oestrogen receptor (ERα) through complex long-range transcriptional interactions between promoter and enhancer elements. Specifically, the MIR196A2 locus, located within the HOXC cluster, is upregulated by oestradiol in MCF7 cells, a process mediated by ERα and its pioneer factor FOXA1 binding to putative promoters and distal enhancers, including the HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE). Chromatin conformation capture (3C) and ChIA-PET analyses confirm physical interactions between these enhancers and the MIR196A2/HOXC10 promoter region. Clinically, MIR196A expression is significantly increased in models of hormone receptor-positive disease resistance, including tamoxifen-resistant and chemotherapeutic-resistant cell lines. In patient cohorts, high MIR196A expression correlates with poor survival in post-menopausal ER+ breast cancer, whereas it associates with better outcomes in pre-menopausal ER+ disease and triple-negative breast cancer. The study further reveals that DNA methylation patterns at the HOXC10/MIR196A2 promoters change in response to endocrine therapy resistance, suggesting that de-repression of these regulatory elements contributes to the development of therapeutic resistance. These findings establish MIR196A as a robust prognostic factor for advanced ER+ disease and provide insights into the epigenetic and transcriptional mechanisms driving breast cancer progression and resistance.

Research Context
MicroRNAs are short non-coding RNAs that post-transcriptionally regulate gene expression. MIR196A is transcribed from two loci, HOXC and HOXB. MIR196A has been implicated in a wide range of developmental and pathogenic processes. Genetic variants and altered expression of miR196a are associated with risk and progression of multiple cancers. Little is known about the regulation of the genes encoding this miRNA. The transcriptional regulation of miR-196a remains poorly understood. Promoters for miRNAs can be identified similarly to protein coding genes. Instances of miRNA regulation by enhancers have been described but are in their infancy.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aimed to characterise the expression landscape of MIR196A. The authors sought to determine if oestrogen regulates MIR196A2. It was hypothesized that MIR196A transcription may be controlled by the oestrogen receptor. The hypothesis was that MIR196A2 is controlled by long-range transcriptional regulation. The study explored potential roles of regulatory elements in breast cancer prognostication. The authors investigated the effects of menopause on the stratification of survival. The study examined whether therapeutic resistance leads to increases in MIR196A expression.

Methodological Details
MCF7 cells and endocrine resistance sub-lines were obtained from AstraZeneca. Cell lines were cultured for less than 6 months after authentication. Authentication was performed by short-tandem repeat (STR) profiling. PCR products were ligated into Invitrogen's pCR-Blunt plasmid. Enhancers and promoters were cloned into the luciferase reporter plasmid pGL3-Basic. MCF7 cells were transfected with 500 ng of modified pGL3 reporter constructs. Transfection included 20 ng of pRL-TK and 0.5μL of Lipofectamine 3000. Luciferase readings were measured using a DTX-880 luminometer. RNA was extracted using Life Technologies TRIzol reagent. RNA for miRNA analysis was reverse transcribed using the miScript RT II kit. Expression data for miRNAs was normalised to the snoRNA RNU6b. qRT-PCRs were performed on a Corbet Rotorgene-6000. RNA-Seq on MCF7 cells following oestradiol treatment was performed as described previously. RNA-Seq from Adriamycin and paclitaxel resistant cells was sourced from GSE68815. MCF7 ChIP-Seq data was sourced from GSE14664. GRO-Seq data was sourced from GSE27463. ChIA-PET data was sourced from GSE39495. Breast tumour ERα ChIP-Seq data was sourced from GSE32222. ChIP-Seq data was mapped with Bowtie and peaks called by MACS. DNA methylation of breast tumours was sourced from The Cancer Genome Atlas. METABRIC expression and clinical information were sourced from EGAS00000083. Clustering was performed using the Multiple Experiment Viewer (MeV). Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazard regression analyses were performed. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was done using GraphPad Prism. Optimal cutoffs were determined using receiver operator characteristic (ROC) curves. Chromosome conformation capture (3C) was adapted from Vakoc 2005. Cells were fixed with 1% formaldehyde for 3C. Libraries were generated using HindIII digestion.

Procedures And Architectures
Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP-Seq) for RNA polymerase II was used. Global-run-on sequencing (GRO-Seq) was used to measure nascent RNA. ChIA-PET was used to identify genome-wide chromatin interactions. Chromosome conformation capture (3C) digestion was performed on the HOXC locus. 3C-qPCR demonstrated that enhancer elements physically interact with promoters. Cloning of fragments into luciferase reporters demonstrated transcriptional augmentation. DNA methylation analysis was performed on MCF10A, MCF7, and HMEC cells. Hierarchical clustering of breast tumour RNA-Seq data was performed. Survival analysis stratified ER+ tumours by MIR196A expression. The study utilized expression data from the METABRIC cohort.

Key Results
MIR196A expression highly correlates to HOXC genes, particularly HOXC10. MIR196A expression is mostly within basal stem-cell derived cells. RNA production in the MIR196A2 region peaks at 40 mins following E2 addition. MIR196A2 is transcriptionally regulated by oestrogen. ERα and FOXA1 bind to putative promoters 1 and 3. PP1 is the most active promoter in MCF7 cells. Two major sites of interaction with MIR196A2 promoters were identified. One interacting partner is the HOTAIR distal enhancer (HDE). The other is a novel interacting partner (MIR196A2-Enhancer, mE). HDE appears to be the most active enhancer in MCF7 cells. The CpG island is mostly methylated in MCF10A and MCF7 cells. The CpG island is unmethylated in human mammary epithelial cells. MIR196A is significantly over-expressed in breast tumours compared to normal tissue. Over-expression is associated with an increase in tumour stage. High MIR196A expression is associated with poor survival in ER+ breast cancer. High expression associates with better outcome in triple-negative breast cancer. Women with low MIR196A expression had >95% survival at 10 years. Most women in the high expression group died within 17 years. 61% of high expression group died at 10 years. In premenopausal women, high MIR196A expression is associated with good outcome. In post-menopausal women, high MIR196A expression is associated with poor outcome. MIR196A expression is significantly increased in tamoxifen resistant MCF7 cells. MIR196A is almost depleted in fulvestrant resistance. MIR196A expression increases in resistant cell lines compared to sensitive lines. An increase in ERα occupancy is seen at enhancer and promoter regions.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
MIR196A displays complex and dynamic expression patterns. Expression is controlled by long range transcriptional regulation. The regulation involves ERα bound promoter and enhancer elements. Changes in regulation are associated with breast cancer progression. The pathway to resistance involves de-repression of promoter and enhancer elements. HOX genes may help tumour cells sustain a stem-cell like state. There is a change in regulation through and following menopause. MIR196A is a possible biomarker for progression to resistance.

Contradictions And Limitations
The association between MIR196A and HOXC genes is not significant in normal tissues. It is currently unclear how dual-encoded miRs are regulated. The effects of menopause on the human breast are largely unknown. PP3 is not able to increase luciferase expression in reporter assays. The study relies on cell line models which may not fully represent patient heterogeneity.

Claims
MIR196A is transcriptionally regulated by oestrogen via ERα binding to specific promoter and enhancer elements. ChIP-Seq shows polymerase binding is dependent on oestrogen. GRO-Seq indicates dramatic increase in RNA production after E2. ERα and FOXA1 bind to putative promoters 1 and 3. 3C-qPCR demonstrates physical interaction between enhancers and promoters. PP3 does not increase luciferase expression in reporter assays. 
High MIR196A expression is a prognostic biomarker for poor survival in post-menopausal ER+ breast cancer. High expression associates with poor survival in ER+ disease. 61% of high expression group died at 10 years. High expression is associated with poor outcome in post-menopausal women. High expression associates with good outcome in premenopausal women. High expression associates with better outcome in TNBC. MIR196A can be used for stratification of therapeutically resistant breast cancer.
Therapeutic resistance leads to increased MIR196A expression and changes in DNA methylation. MIR196A is significantly increased in tamoxifen resistant cells. Expression patterns match changes in DNA methylation. ERα occupancy increases in non-responders and metastases. MIR196A is almost depleted in fulvestrant resistance. De-repression of regulatory elements contributes to resistance.

Data And Code Availability
Accession codes for publically available data were provided. Data was sourced from ENCODE, TCGA, and GEO.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Validation was performed using qRT-PCR and RNA-Seq. 3C-qPCR was used to validate chromatin interactions. Luciferase reporter assays were used to test promoter/enhancer activity.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows ChIP-Seq, GRO-Seq, and qRT-PCR data for E2 regulation. Figure 2 shows ChIA-PET and 3C data for chromatin interactions. Figure 3 shows clustering of MIR196A expression in breast tumours. Figure 4 shows METABRIC expression and survival analysis. Figure 5 shows survival stratification and resistance models. Table 1 shows multivariate analysis for premenopausal women.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the elucidation of ERα-mediated long-range transcriptional regulation of MIR196A. 2. The strongest evidence is the correlation of high MIR196A expression with poor survival in post-menopausal ER+ patients. 3. The future path is to uncover the purpose of increased MIR196A expression in resistance.

summary.title: Atmospheric pressure continuous flow methane oxidation to methanol and acetic acid using H 2 O 2 over Au-Fe catalyst
summary.authors: Anuradha V Jagtap, Pawan Kumar, Sharad Gupta, N Abharana, S N Jha, D Bhattacharyya, T G Ajithkumar, C P Vinod
summary.executive_summary: The direct partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol and acetic acid is a significant catalytic challenge due to the thermodynamic drive towards complete oxidation to CO2. This study presents a modified silica-supported bimetallic catalyst (AuFeHS) that achieves high-yield methane conversion under mild, atmospheric pressure conditions in a continuous flow reactor. The catalyst, synthesized via a modified deposition precipitation method, features atomic Fe clusters and small Au nanoparticles (1.3-3.0 nm) on a hydrophobic silica support. Characterization techniques including XPS, XANES, and HRTEM reveal that the synergy between Au and Fe is crucial, with Au stabilizing low-valent Fe species (Fe 3-δ+) that are active for methane activation. In batch experiments at 10 bar, the AuFeHS catalyst achieved a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity. documents.judge_context:
Executive Summary
The direct partial oxidation of methane (POM) to methanol and acetic acid is a significant catalytic challenge due to the thermodynamic drive towards complete oxidation to CO2. This study presents a modified silica-supported bimetallic catalyst (AuFeHS) that achieves high-yield methane conversion under mild, atmospheric pressure conditions in a continuous flow reactor. The catalyst, synthesized via a modified deposition precipitation method, features atomic Fe clusters and small Au nanoparticles (1.3-3.0 nm) on a hydrophobic silica support. Characterization techniques including XPS, XANES, and HRTEM reveal that the synergy between Au and Fe is crucial, with Au stabilizing low-valent Fe species (Fe 3-δ+) that are active for methane activation. In batch experiments at 10 bar, the AuFeHS catalyst achieved a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity. When CO was co-fed, the selectivity switched to acetic acid, yielding 3403 µmol/gcat. In the continuous flow process at atmospheric pressure, the catalyst produced methanol with a yield of 224 mmol/gFe+Au over 4 hours, significantly outperforming previous high-pressure batch processes. The hydrophobic nature of the support was identified as critical for maintaining peroxide proximity to active sites and facilitating product desorption. Isotope labeling experiments confirmed that the methanol carbon originates from methane, not the support. This work demonstrates a viable pathway for the commercialization of methane-to-oxygenates technologies under benign conditions, highlighting the importance of bimetallic modulation and support hydrophobicity in stabilizing active catalytic species.

Research Context
Methane activation is difficult due to its non-polar tetrahedral structure. Partial oxidation to methanol is a 'holy grail' problem in catalysis. Previous methods often require harsh high-pressure and high-temperature conditions. Molecular oxygen yields are generally poor for commercialization. Hydrogen peroxide is a promising green oxidant for this conversion. Single-site catalysts have shown promise but often suffer from low selectivity. Continuous flow reports for POM to methanol are limited. Existing continuous flow processes often use high pressures.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to develop a catalyst for POM at atmospheric pressure. It hypothesizes that a bimetallic Au-Fe system on hydrophobic silica will enhance activity. The hypothesis includes that hydrophobicity helps peroxide stay near active sites. It predicts that co-feeding CO will switch selectivity to acetic acid. The goal is to surpass high-pressure batch process yields. The study seeks to stabilize active Fe species using Au. It aims to demonstrate continuous flow operation at mild conditions.

Methodological Details
A modified deposition precipitation method was used for catalyst synthesis. The support was hydrophobic silica (HS). The optimal catalyst had 0.46 wt% Fe and 0.23 wt% Au. Hydrophobicity was confirmed by a contact angle of 118 degrees. HRTEM showed Au nanoparticles of 1.3-3.0 nm. XPS identified Fe 3+ and low-valent Fe 3-δ+ species. XPS showed 85% Au 0 and 15% Au δ+ species. Batch reactions were conducted at 10 bar methane pressure. Continuous flow reactions were conducted at atmospheric pressure. H2O2 (15% w/v) was used as the oxidant. CO was co-fed to produce acetic acid. Isotope labeling with CD4 was used to verify product origin.

Procedures And Architectures
The catalyst was synthesized by depositing Fe onto hydrophobic silica. Au was added via a NaOH-assisted deposition process. Batch screening was performed at 10 bar and optimized temperature. Continuous flow used a fixed-bed reactor. The continuous flow process ran for up to 7 hours. Products were analyzed using GC and NMR. XANES and EXAFS were used to probe electronic structure. In-situ IR spectroscopy probed CO adsorption states.

Key Results
Batch methanol yield was 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity. Batch acetic acid yield was 3403 µmol/gcat with CO co-feed. Continuous flow methanol yield was 224 mmol/gFe+Au. Continuous flow acetic acid yield was 648 µmol/gcat. The continuous flow rate was 0.42 molmethanol kgcatalyst -1 h -1. This rate is higher than previous O2-based continuous flow reports. FeHS alone produced 285 mmol/gFe in batch. AuHS alone produced 47.6 mmol/gAu in batch. No product was detected without methane, oxidant, or catalyst.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The synergy between Au and Fe is key to high activity. Au stabilizes low-valent Fe species necessary for methane activation. Hydrophobicity facilitates peroxide proximity and product desorption. Lewis acid sites help in C-H sigma complex formation. The mechanism involves CH3 and OH radical formation. This approach offers a path to commercial M2O technologies.

Contradictions And Limitations
The role of Na and Lewis acid sites is not fully explored. The study focuses on specific bimetallic compositions. Long-term stability in continuous flow is not extensively detailed. The mechanism for acetic acid formation is inferred from prior work.

Claims
AuFeHS catalyst achieves high-yield methane oxidation at atmospheric pressure. Yield of 224 mmol/gFe+Au in continuous flow. Selectivity of 95% for methanol in batch. Previous high-pressure processes had higher absolute yields in some cases. Enables milder, potentially more scalable industrial processes.
Co-feeding CO switches selectivity to acetic acid. Acetic acid yield of 3403 µmol/gcat in batch. Acetic acid yield of 648 µmol/gcat in flow. Methanol is still formed as a side product. Provides a route to higher-value acetic acid from methane.

Data And Code Availability
Supporting information is available via ChemRxiv.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Control experiments showed no product without reactants or catalyst. Isotope labeling confirmed methane origin of methanol. Comparison with SBA-15 support showed lower activity.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows HRTEM images and elemental mapping. Figure 2 shows XPS and XANES spectra. Figure 3 shows batch catalytic activity and selectivity. Figure 4 shows continuous flow results. Table S6 compares literature values.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a high-yield Au-Fe catalyst for atmospheric POM. 2. The strongest evidence is the 224 mmol/gFe+Au yield in flow. 3. The future path is commercialization of methane-to-oxygenates tech.

"title": "QED⊗QCD Resummation and Shower/ME Matching for LHC Physics",
"authors": "B.F.L. Ward and S.A. Yost",
"field_subfield": "High Energy Physics - Phenomenology (hep-ph)",
"type_of_paper": "Theoretical Physics / Conference Proceedings",
"executive_summary": "This paper presents a theoretical framework for the simultaneous resummation of Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) and Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) effects, termed QED⊗QCD resummation, aimed at achieving high-precision predictions for LHC luminosity processes. The authors argue that to match the expected 2% experimental luminosity precision, theoretical predictions for single heavy gauge boson production (W, Z) must reach a 0.67% precision level. This requires controlling multiple gluon and photon radiative effects. The study extends the Yennie-Frautschi-Suura (YFS) exponentiation theory, originally for QED, to non-Abelian QCD, and further to the combined QED⊗QCD sector. The core contribution is an exact rearrangement of the perturbative series that allows for the simultaneous resummation of soft and collinear divergences in both αs and α without double-counting. The authors demonstrate how this exact resummation can be matched with standard parton shower Monte Carlo generators like HERWIG and PYTHIA. They propose two matching strategies: a standard pT matching and a more precise 'shower-subtracted' residual method. {
  "title": "Characteristics of EGRET Blazars in the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS)",
  "authors": "G. B. Taylor, S. E. Healey, J. F. Helmboldt, S. Tremblay, C. D. Fassnacht, R. C. Walker, L. O. Sjouwerman, T. J. Pearson, A. C. S. Readhead, L. Weintraub, N. Gehrels, R. W. Romani, P. F. Michelson, R. D. Blandford, G. Cotter",
  "field_subfield": "Astrophysics / Radio Astronomy",
  "type_of_paper": "Research Article",
  "executive_summary": "This study investigates the radio properties of blazars detected by the EGRET instrument on the Compton Gamma-Ray Observatory, utilizing data from the VLBA Imaging and Polarimetry Survey (VIPS). VIPS provides a uniform sample of 1127 flat-spectrum sources with a flux limit significantly lower than previous surveys like MOJAVE, allowing for a more unbiased comparison between gamma-ray loud and quiet blazars. The authors compare 31 EGRET candidate blazars within the VIPS field to the broader VIPS population. The primary finding is that at lower radio flux levels, radio flux density does not directly correlate with gamma-ray flux density. Instead, EGRET-detected blazars exhibit distinct morphological and physical characteristics: they tend to have higher core brightness temperatures, greater core fractions (indicating more core-dominated emission), and possibly larger jet opening angles. A weak correlation is also observed with jet length and polarization. draft_summary.title: Atmospheric pressure continuous flow methane oxidation to methanol and acetic acid using H 2 O 2 over Au-Fe catalyst
draft_summary.authors: Anuradha V Jagtap, Pawan Kumar, Sharad Gupta, N Abharana, S N Jha, D Bhattacharyya, T G Ajithkumar, C P Vinod
draft_summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the 'holy grail' challenge of catalytic methane partial oxidation (POM) to methanol and acetic acid under mild, atmospheric pressure conditions. The authors developed a bimetallic Au-Fe catalyst supported on hydrophobic silica (AuFeHS) to achieve high selectivity and yield using hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as the oxidant. The catalyst was synthesized via a modified deposition precipitation method, featuring atomic dispersion of Fe and small Au nanoparticles (1.3-3.0 nm). Characterization techniques including XPS, XANES, and HRTEM confirmed the presence of low-valent Fe species (Fe3-δ+) stabilized by Au, which are critical for methane activation. In batch reactions at 10 bar, the AuFeHS catalyst achieved a methanol yield of 1666 mmol/gFe+Au with 95% selectivity. More significantly, in a continuous flow reactor at atmospheric pressure, the catalyst produced methanol with a yield of 224 mmol/gFe+Au over 4 hours, surpassing previous high-pressure batch reports. The introduction of CO into the feed stream enabled a selectivity switch to acetic acid, yielding 648 µmol/gcat in the continuous process. The hydrophobic nature of the silica support was identified as crucial for maintaining peroxide proximity to active sites and preventing catalyst deactivation. Isotope labeling experiments confirmed that the methanol carbon originated from methane, not the support. The study demonstrates that bimetallic modulation of Fe species by Au, combined with a hydrophobic support, enables efficient methane conversion to value-added oxygenates under benign conditions, offering a pathway toward commercialization of methane-to-oxygenates technologies.
draft_summary.contradictions_and_limitations: The role of Na and Lewis acid sites in the overall POM reaction is worth exploring and is beyond the scope of this study.
